lessons.plain: Identity and Access Management, usually called IAM, is the system that answers three questions for every request to a cloud resource: who is asking, what they want to do, and which thing they want to do it to. Instead of handing out keys to every door, you grant access in small bundles called roles and attach those bundles to a person, a group of people, or a service account, which is a robot identity that software runs as. An organization policy is a different tool. It sets rules on how the whole company's cloud may be configured, such as which regions data may be stored in. Designing these well means giving each identity only the access its job needs, at the level where that access belongs.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly data pipeline runs under a robot account. It only needs to read one table and write its results to another table. Would you give it the Owner role on the whole company project so it never breaks, or something narrower? Explain your choice in a sentence or two.
lessons.teach:
An IAM policy is a list of bindings. Each binding ties a principal (a user, a group, or a service account) to a role. A role is a named set of permissions, such as permission to read rows from a table or to create a new dataset. A permission is the smallest unit: it allows one action on one kind of resource. Google Cloud arranges resources in a hierarchy: the organization at the top, then folders, then projects, then individual resources such as datasets and tables. A binding made at one level applies to everything beneath it. This inheritance is convenient, and it is also the most common source of too much access.

Why it works: access is allow-only and additive. A principal can perform an action if any binding on the path from the resource up to the top grants it. A lower level cannot take back a permission granted above it, except through separate deny policies, which are an advanced tool. So the safest design places each grant as low in the hierarchy as the job allows.

Organization policies work differently. They are constraints, not grants. One might restrict where resources can be created or block the creation of long-lived service account keys. They limit what configuration is possible for everyone under the organization, whatever roles they hold.

Worked example: a pipeline service account must read the orders dataset and write to the reports dataset. Step 1: identify the principal, which is the pipeline's own service account. Step 2: list the minimum permissions, read on orders and write on reports. Step 3: choose predefined roles that match those permissions and bind them on each dataset, not on the project. Step 4: confirm that nothing else in the project is reachable through that account.

Common mistake: granting a broad basic role such as Editor at the project level because the pipeline once failed with a permission error. This makes every dataset in the project writable by that robot, so a leaked key could delete data far outside the pipeline.

When access is over-granted, a failure in one job becomes an incident across the whole data estate. When access is narrow, a failure stays contained and is easier to audit.

questions.prompt: A nightly loader at a hospital group needs to write new rows into the claims_staging dataset in project clinic-analytics-prod. It must not touch any other dataset in that project. Step 1: the principal is the loader's own service account. Step 2: the minimum permission is write on claims_staging. Step 3 is missing and you must supply it. Step 4: confirm the account cannot reach the other datasets in the project.
choices: Grant the Owner role on the whole clinic-analytics-prod project so the loader never hits a permission error again.
Bind a predefined role that allows writing to claims_staging on that dataset only, not on the project.
Create a long-lived key for the loader's service account and store it in the job's configuration file.
Set an organization policy that allows every service account in the company to write to any dataset.
questions.why: Step 3 is where the grant is chosen and placed, and the narrow role bound on the one dataset matches the minimum permission from Step 2 while keeping the grant as low in the hierarchy as the job allows.

questions.prompt: In IAM, what is a binding?
choices: A rule that ties one principal, such as a user, group, or service account, to a role.
A constraint that restricts which regions resources may be created in.
A folder that groups several projects together under one owner.
A single permission that allows one action on one kind of resource.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a binding as the tie between a principal and a role, distinct from the permission (the smallest unit), the constraint type of organization policy, and the hierarchy level of a folder.

questions.prompt: A group is granted a read role on the folder Retail-EU. The folder contains projects retail-eu-sales-2 and retail-eu-returns. Which statement is true?
choices: The group can read only the single dataset it was first asked about, because folders hold no grants of their own.
The group can read datasets in both projects only if an organization policy also names each dataset.
The group is blocked from the returns project, because each project must be granted access separately.
The group can read datasets in both projects, because a binding made at a folder applies to everything beneath it.
questions.why: Bindings apply downward through the hierarchy, so a grant on a folder reaches every project and resource beneath it, which is why the teaching text calls inheritance a common source of too much access.

questions.prompt: An organization policy blocks the creation of long-lived service account keys. A team lead holds the Owner role on the project where a service account lives and wants to create such a key anyway. What happens?
choices: The creation succeeds, because a role granted on a project is higher in the hierarchy than an organization policy and overrides it.
The creation is blocked, because an organization policy is a constraint that limits configuration for everyone under the organization regardless of the roles they hold.
The creation succeeds only if the lead also holds a predefined role for keys, since roles and constraints are checked separately and the role is enough.
The creation succeeds, because Owner allows the lead to edit organization policies and remove the restriction for that project.
questions.why: The teaching text states that organization policies are constraints rather than grants, so they cap what configuration is possible for all principals, and holding a broad role does not lift them.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would give a new analytics service account read access to one dataset without exposing the rest of the project. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would create a dedicated service account for the analytics job, so the access belongs to the job and not to a person. Then I would bind a predefined reader-style role on the one dataset it needs, not at the project level. Because IAM access is additive and inherited downward, the account gets nothing from other datasets, and nothing from the project unless I add a binding there. The tradeoff is operational. Every new dataset needs its own binding, so access reviews take longer as the estate grows. Groups can reduce that work, but adding a broad group to a parent folder makes over-granting easy. I would verify the result by checking the access on that dataset and recording why each binding exists.
rubricPoints: Names a dedicated service account as the principal, not a shared or personal login.
Grants a predefined role at the dataset level rather than a basic role at the project level.
Explains that IAM access is allow-only and inherited downward, so a higher-level grant reaches lower resources.
States a real limit: per-dataset bindings add review work, and broad parent-level grants risk over-access.

suggested.rationale: An authorization policy evaluator would let the learner test who can reach which dataset under inherited and additive rules, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: Encryption scrambles data so that only someone holding the right key can read it. A key is a secret value that the scrambling process uses, so the real design question is who controls the keys and where they are stored. In Google Cloud, most data is already encrypted when it is stored and while it moves between services, with no setup from you. Designing data security means deciding whether that default is enough, or whether your organization must hold and manage its own keys, rotate them on a schedule, and be able to cut off access to the data by controlling the key.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a warehouse table is encrypted at rest and a user with read permission queries it, does the user see scrambled bytes or readable rows, and why?
lessons.teach:
Encryption at rest means data is encrypted while it sits in storage. Encryption in transit means it is encrypted while moving over a network, usually with TLS. Key management is the set of practices for creating, storing, rotating (replacing on a schedule), disabling, and destroying keys. Google Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS) is the managed service that holds keys, organized into key rings grouped by location.

Most services use envelope encryption. Each piece of data gets its own data encryption key (DEK). That DEK is then encrypted by a key encryption key (KEK) that lives in Cloud KMS. The KEK never leaves the service, and rotating it only means re-wrapping the small DEKs, not re-encrypting all the data.

There are three key choices. Google-managed keys are the default and need no configuration. Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) mean you create the KEK in Cloud KMS and point a service such as BigQuery or Cloud Storage at it. Customer-supplied keys (CSEK) mean you hold the key material yourself and send it with each request.

Worked example: a nightly export is written to a Cloud Storage bucket that uses a CMEK key. Step 1: the service generates a new DEK for the object. Step 2: it encrypts the object bytes with that DEK. Step 3: it asks Cloud KMS to encrypt the DEK with the KEK, and stores the wrapped DEK beside the ciphertext. Step 4: when an authorized reader asks for the object, the service asks Cloud KMS to unwrap the DEK, and the reader receives plaintext. Step 5: if the KEK is disabled, the unwrap fails and the data cannot be read.

Common mistake: assuming encryption alone blocks access. Encryption protects against exposure at the storage layer, but anyone with permission to read the data gets plaintext, so over-broad access permissions still expose it. Consequence in a running system: if a team disables or destroys a CMEK key used by a production warehouse, queries and pipelines fail across the system, and destroyed key material cannot be recovered. Key control is therefore a reliability decision as well as a security one.

questions.prompt: A payments startup stores scanned receipts in a Cloud Storage bucket that uses a CMEK key named receipt-kek in key ring pay-ring. A receipt is uploaded and the following steps happen. Step 1: the service generates a new DEK for that receipt object. Step 2: the service encrypts the receipt bytes with that DEK. Step 3 is missing and you must supply it: the service ______. Step 4: an authorized auditor opens the receipt, the service asks Cloud KMS to unwrap the DEK, and the auditor gets plaintext. Step 5: if receipt-kek is disabled, the unwrap in step 4 fails.
choices: encrypts the DEK with the DEK itself and stores that result in the bucket
sends the receipt-kek key material to the auditor's laptop so the auditor can decrypt locally
re-encrypts every receipt in the bucket with receipt-kek each time a new receipt arrives
asks Cloud KMS to encrypt the DEK with receipt-kek and stores the wrapped DEK beside the ciphertext
questions.why: In envelope encryption the service asks Cloud KMS to wrap the per-object DEK with the KEK, and the wrapped DEK is stored alongside the ciphertext, which is what step 4 later unwraps.

questions.prompt: In envelope encryption, what is the role of the key encryption key (KEK)?
choices: It encrypts data while it travels over a network, which is why it is called a transit key
It is a new key generated for every object, then discarded after the write finishes
It encrypts each per-object data encryption key (DEK), and it stays inside Cloud KMS rather than leaving the service
It is the key the reader must type in to see plaintext, so it is held by the user
questions.why: The KEK wraps the small DEKs and never leaves the service, which is why rotating it only re-wraps DEKs instead of re-encrypting all the data.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's Cloud Storage bucket uses a CMEK key. Over a weekend, an engineer disables that key intending to re-enable it on Monday. What happens to reads from the bucket while the key is disabled?
choices: Reads return encrypted bytes that the readers must decrypt themselves with the old key
Reads are automatically moved to a Google-managed key until the CMEK key is re-enabled
Reads fail because the DEKs cannot be unwrapped, and they succeed again once the key is re-enabled
Reads continue normally because the plaintext was already cached when the key was disabled
questions.why: Disabling the KEK makes the unwrap step fail, so the data cannot be read until the key is re-enabled, and nothing falls back to another key automatically.

questions.prompt: A school district reasons that because its Cloud Storage bucket is encrypted at rest, any service account with read access is safe from seeing student records. Which statement correctly identifies the flaw in this reasoning?
choices: Encryption at rest only applies to data moving over the network, so the bucket is not encrypted at rest at all
Encryption at rest is turned off whenever a service account reads the data
Encryption at rest is enough on its own, so read permissions do not need to be reviewed
Encryption at rest protects storage, but any authorized reader receives plaintext, so over-broad access still exposes the data
questions.why: Encryption at rest protects against exposure at the storage layer, but anyone with permission to read the data gets decrypted content, so access permissions must still be controlled.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between Google-managed keys and customer-managed keys for a warehouse holding regulated customer records, and name one limit or tradeoff of the customer-managed option.
lessons.modelAnswer: With Google-managed keys, Google creates, stores, and rotates the keys for us, so there is nothing to configure and the data is encrypted at rest by default. With customer-managed keys, we create the key encryption key in Cloud KMS and the warehouse uses it, so we control rotation, can disable the key, and can show an auditor who holds control. For regulated records that is often the requirement. The tradeoff is that we now own availability: if someone disables or destroys that key, queries and loads fail, and destroyed key material cannot be recovered. We also have to grant the service account permission to use the key and monitor it. So CMEK adds control and some operational risk, and the team needs a clear key-lifecycle process before turning it on.
rubricPoints: Google-managed keys are the default with no setup, and the provider handles their lifecycle.
Customer-managed keys let the organization create, rotate, and disable the key in Cloud KMS.
A real tradeoff is operational: disabling or destroying the key makes the data unreadable and can break pipelines.
Access to decrypt still depends on IAM permissions, so encryption is not a substitute for access control.

suggested.rationale: Envelope encryption is a mechanism best practiced by wrapping and unwrapping data keys hands-on, which the planned envelope-crypto lab would provide.

lessons.plain: Personally identifiable information, or PII, is any data that can point to a specific person, such as a name, email address, phone number, or home address. A privacy strategy is a plan for deciding which of that data a system really needs, who may see it, and how it is hidden or shortened when people only need patterns. Think of a hospital ward roster: the nurse on shift needs to know which bed a patient is in, but a research team studying infection rates only needs counts by age group. Designing privacy means building that separation into the data pipeline from the start, not adding it after a leak.
lessons.guessPrompt: A marketing team wants to count how many customers signed up each week in each city, but the raw sign-up table contains full names and email addresses. Before the team gets access, what is the least risky change you would make, and why?
lessons.teach:
Personally identifiable information (PII) is any field that identifies a person, either alone or combined with others. Direct identifiers include names, email addresses, and national ID numbers. Quasi-identifiers, such as postcode, birth date, and gender, become identifying when combined. A privacy strategy decides, for each field, whether it is needed at all (minimization), where it is stored, who can read it, and whether the analysis can work on a masked version instead.

Pseudonymization replaces an identifier with a stand-in value, such as a random key, that someone holding a separate mapping can still link back. Anonymization removes that link, for example by dropping or generalizing fields. Masking hides part of a value, such as showing only the last four digits. Tokenization swaps a value for a token that a secured service can reverse on request. Each keeps a different balance of usefulness and risk.

It works because most analytics questions only need patterns, not people. You split the data: keep identifying columns in a restricted table, and give analysts a stand-in key they can count and join on.

Worked example: a sign-up table holds name, email, city, and signup_date. Step 1: drop name and email from the analytics copy, since the team counts sign-ups by city. Step 2: replace email with a keyed hash, meaning a hash computed with a secret key, so repeat sign-ups by one person can still be counted. Step 3: generalize signup_date to the week. The result answers the question and cannot be used as a contact list.

Common mistake: hashing emails without a secret key. Anyone holding a list of known emails can hash it and match the values, so the output is still identifying.

On Google Cloud, Sensitive Data Protection scans data for PII patterns and applies transformations such as masking or tokenization, and BigQuery policy tags restrict who can read a sensitive column. Controls must sit where the data lands and is queried, because masking one copy does nothing if a raw copy is readable elsewhere.

Designing for privacy means deciding which fields exist in each copy of the data, and placing controls so the most sensitive copy is the smallest one people can reach.

questions.prompt: A clinic keeps a visits table with patient_name, phone, postcode, patient_id, and visit_date. The analytics copy exists only to count visits per district per month. Step 1: drop patient_name and phone from the analytics copy, since no count needs them. Step 2: replace patient_id with a keyed hash, where the secret key sits in a restricted key store, so repeat visits by one patient still count once. Step 3 is missing: decide what happens to postcode and visit_date, which can single someone out when combined. Which completion correctly finishes step 3?
choices: Keep postcode exact and visit_date exact, since neither is a direct identifier like a name or phone
Generalize postcode to its district and visit_date to the month, since these combined fields could still identify someone
Delete postcode and visit_date from every copy of the data, including the restricted table
Replace postcode with an unkeyed hash so it can still be grouped by area
questions.why: Postcode and visit_date are quasi-identifiers, so generalizing them in the analytics copy keeps district-by-month counts usable while reducing how easily a person can be picked out.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm replaces each driver's licence number with a random code. A separately locked file links each code back to its licence number. Which term describes this approach?
choices: Minimization
Pseudonymization
Anonymization
Masking
questions.why: A stand-in value that someone holding a separate mapping can link back to the identifier is pseudonymization; anonymization would remove that link.

questions.prompt: A staff-analytics table replaces badge IDs with unkeyed SHA-256 hashes and is shared with a wider team. Which statement is correct?
choices: Safe because SHA-256 output is a fixed length
Safe once the table is encrypted at rest
Safe, because hashing cannot be reversed
Still identifying: known IDs can be hashed and matched
questions.why: Without a secret key, anyone holding a list of known badge IDs can compute the same hashes and match them, so the values still identify people.

questions.prompt: A bank's card table in BigQuery must show analysts only the last four digits of each card number, while only a compliance group may see the full column. Which combination fits?
choices: A BigQuery view that renames the column and hides nothing else
Exporting the table to a shared spreadsheet for analysts to filter by hand
Sensitive Data Protection masking plus a BigQuery policy tag on the column
Dataset-level read access for analysts, with the full card column left open to every reader in the project
questions.why: Masking transforms the value analysts see to the last four digits, and a policy tag restricts who can read the sensitive column, with both controls placed where the data is queried.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would protect a table of customer names and emails so analysts can still count customers by city. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would split the table in two. The original stays in a restricted dataset that only a small support group can read, and holds names and emails. For analysts, I would build a copy with names and emails removed, a city field, a signup week instead of the exact date, and a customer key made with a keyed hash so repeat signups still match. That lets them count and join without seeing anyone's identity. The main tradeoff is that the keyed hash is still a pseudonym: anyone with the secret key and the original table can re-link the rows, so the key and the restricted table need tight access control. Also, generalizing dates and cities reduces accuracy, so if a question needs exact timing, the team has to ask for a separate, more restricted view.
rubricPoints: Separates direct identifiers from the analytics copy
Explains that a keyed hash or token is pseudonymization, not full anonymization
Names a tradeoff such as loss of precision or the need to protect the key
Says controls must sit where the data is stored and queried

suggested.rationale: Choosing which privacy technique fits a given scenario is best practiced by reasoning through exam-style situations, which no current mission covers.

lessons.plain: Data sovereignty means a law or contract says certain data must stay within a country or region, and must only be reached by people or systems located or approved there. Designing for it means deciding, before anything is built, where the data is physically stored, where it is processed, and who can reach it from where. A common mistake is to assume that choosing a storage region also controls access. In practice you need several layers, each doing one job, and each placed correctly in the architecture.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company must keep its customer data inside the European Union. It stores the data in an EU region, but an engineer copies a nightly export to a bucket in the United States. Does the company still meet the requirement, and what single change would have prevented the copy?
lessons.teach:
Regional data sovereignty is the requirement that data stays inside a named geographic boundary, and that access to it also comes only from inside that boundary. Two questions follow. Where are the bytes stored and processed? Who or what can reach them, and from where? A region is one specific geographic location where cloud resources run, such as Frankfurt. A multi-region is a larger grouping, such as the European Union, that spreads copies across several regions inside it. Each choice must match the boundary the requirement names.

Why it works: you fix the location when resources are created, then use controls that make the wrong location impossible rather than merely discouraged. An organization policy that restricts resource locations stops anyone from creating a bucket or dataset outside an approved list. A service perimeter, from VPC Service Controls, wraps a set of projects so that data cannot be copied to a project outside it, and requests from outside approved networks are refused. Identity and Access Management, or IAM, the system that grants roles to people and services, then decides who inside the boundary may read.

Worked example: a German bank keeps transaction tables in BigQuery. Step 1: create the dataset in europe-west3 (Frankfurt). Its location cannot be changed later. Step 2: set the organization location policy to allow only europe-west3 and the EU multi-region. Step 3: place the project inside a service perimeter. Step 4: grant read access to one named analyst group. A query from a laptop on an unapproved network is now refused.

Common mistake: securing the dataset's region and forgetting the surrounding path. A nightly export to a Cloud Storage bucket in another region, or a backup copy, moves the same data out of the boundary even though the main table is compliant.

Consequence: that copy happens silently and is usually found only in a later audit, which is why the location policy should block the bucket from being created at all. Data is only sovereign when every copy, job, and reader sits inside the boundary too.

questions.prompt: A Canadian clinic stores scanned imaging files in Cloud Storage. The requirement is that the data and every copy of it stay inside Canada, and that only the radiology group can read it. Step 1: create the bucket in northamerica-northeast1 (Montreal), because its location is fixed when the bucket is created. Step 2: set the organization location policy to allow only northamerica-northeast1 and northamerica-northeast2 (Toronto). Step 3: point the nightly backup job at a bucket in northamerica-northeast2, so the backup copy stays inside Canada. Step 4: [missing]. Which completion finishes the design?
choices: Place the project inside a service perimeter so that copies cannot leave it and requests from outside approved networks are refused.
Grant the Owner role to every clinician so that audits are easier to run.
Change the bucket's storage class to Coldline so that older scans cost less to keep.
Enable object versioning on the bucket so that deleted scans can be recovered.
questions.why: A service perimeter is the control that stops data being copied out of the project and refuses reads from unapproved networks, which completes the boundary on the access path, while the other choices concern recovery, cost, or over-broad permissions and do not enforce location at all.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is the difference between a region and a multi-region when you are setting a data sovereignty boundary?
choices: A region is a single named geographic location where resources run, while a multi-region is a larger grouping that spreads copies across several regions inside it.
A region is a global network of data centres, while a multi-region is one building in a single city.
A region and a multi-region are the same thing, differing only in the price charged per gigabyte.
A region is chosen after data is uploaded, while a multi-region is chosen only when the project is deleted.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a region as one specific geographic location and a multi-region as a larger grouping that spreads copies across several regions within it, which is the distinction the first choice states in plain words.

questions.prompt: An Indian fintech must keep customer records physically inside India. Which setup meets that requirement at creation time and with an enforced control?
choices: Create the bucket in asia-south1 with no organization location policy, since the team will remember the rule.
Create the bucket in asia-south1 (Mumbai) and set an organization location policy that allows only asia-south1 and asia-south2 (Delhi).
Create the storage bucket in us-central1 and rely on encryption so the records are unreadable outside India.
Create the bucket as the ASIA multi-region for resilience, because it is inside the same continent.
questions.why: Fixing the location at creation and using an organization location policy that only allows Indian regions makes the wrong location impossible, whereas encryption, reliance on memory, or a wider continental multi-region do not keep the bytes inside India.

questions.prompt: A Japanese retailer keeps its sales dataset in asia-northeast1 (Tokyo), which meets its rule that data stays in Japan. A weekly export job writes a copy of the dataset to a bucket in us-west1. What is the consequence for the sovereignty requirement?
choices: Nothing changes, because the original dataset is still compliant and the copy is only a backup.
The requirement is broken, because the copy has left the boundary, even though the main dataset stays compliant.
The requirement is met because IAM roles on the bucket limit who can read the copy.
The requirement is met as long as the copy is encrypted with a key held in Japan.
questions.why: Data sovereignty applies to every copy, job, and reader, so a copy written to a region outside Japan breaks the boundary even when the primary dataset is compliant, and neither encryption nor IAM roles change where the bytes are stored.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would keep a customer dataset inside one region, the controls you would use and where each one lives, and name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would set the dataset location to the required region when it is created, since that cannot be changed later. Then I would add an organization policy that only allows resources in that region or the approved multi-region, so nobody can create a bucket or dataset elsewhere by mistake. I would put the projects holding the data inside a service perimeter so copies to outside projects and requests from unapproved networks are blocked. Access itself would go through IAM groups, limited to people who need it. The main limit is that these controls are only as good as the boundary definition: they stop data leaving through Google Cloud paths I have covered, but they do not stop someone photographing a screen, and a legitimate need for a cross-region service may force an exception that must be reviewed rather than quietly allowed.
rubricPoints: Dataset or storage location is set at creation and must match the required boundary
An organization policy restricts where resources can be created
A service perimeter blocks copies and access from outside the approved boundary
IAM controls who inside the boundary can read the data
Every copy, export, and backup must also stay inside the boundary

suggested.rationale: Matching a sovereignty requirement to the right control and its placement is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario with several possible copy paths.

lessons.plain: Legal and regulatory compliance means the way you build a data system must meet the rules that govern it, such as laws on how long data may be kept, who may read it, and whether you can prove what happened to it. Think of a bank vault: a locked door is not enough. You also need a logbook of who came in, a schedule for when records must be destroyed, and a way to show an inspector that all of it works. In cloud data work, each rule is met by a specific control, and each control has to sit at the right layer of the design, because a retention rule cannot be satisfied by a password setting.
lessons.guessPrompt: A regulator asks you to prove that nobody has changed a customer's transaction records in the past three years, and that those records cannot be deleted before seven years. Which kinds of evidence and which kinds of settings would you reach for first, and why?
lessons.teach:
Compliance means a data system must satisfy a legal or regulatory rule, and a rule is only met when a specific control exists and sits in the right place in the architecture. A control is a setting, policy, or process that enforces a rule. Four kinds matter most here. Retention controls decide how long data must be kept and whether it can be deleted early. Immutability controls stop anyone from changing or removing records during the retention period, including administrators; a retention policy with a lock is one example. Audit logs record who accessed or changed data and when, so you can prove compliance later. Perimeter controls, such as a service perimeter, block data from being copied out of an approved boundary.

Worked example: a rule says transaction records must be kept seven years, must be unalterable, and every read must be traceable. Step one: store the records in a location with a locked seven-year retention period, so early deletion is refused. Step two: turn on data access audit logs for the warehouse and the storage, because the default administrative logs do not record reads. Step three: export those logs to a separate project that the data team cannot edit. Step four: place the projects inside a perimeter so the records cannot be copied to an outside account. Each control lives at a different layer, and the rule is met only when all four exist.

Common mistake: treating a retention setting as a default that can be lowered at will. Without a lock, an administrator can shorten or remove it, so the rule is not really met.

Consequence: a locked retention period also blocks legitimate deletion, so a bad ingest of regulated data stays until the period ends. Confirm the retention rule and the deletion obligations together before you apply a lock.

Compliance is proven by controls you can show working, not by intentions written in a design document.

questions.prompt: A clinic network must keep imaging scans for 15 years, must not allow early deletion, and must be able to show later who read each scan. The team does four things. Step one: they place the scans in an archive bucket with a locked 15-year retention period, so nobody can shorten it. Step two: they turn on data access audit logs for that archive, because the default administrative logs do not record reads. Step three is missing. Step four: they put the projects inside a service perimeter so scans cannot be copied to an outside account. What should step three be?
choices: Set a lifecycle rule that deletes scan objects automatically after 15 years
Add a compliance label to the archive bucket so auditors can filter for it
Store the audit logs in a separate sink whose bucket also has a locked retention period, so the log records cannot be altered or erased
Turn on the default administrative activity logs as well, since they already show reads
questions.why: The rule requires every read to be provable later, so the log records themselves need an immutability control, which a locked retention period on their storage provides.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between a plain retention setting and a retention policy with a lock?
choices: A plain setting applies only to one project, while a locked one applies to an entire organisation
A plain setting deletes data at the end of the period, while a locked one archives it
A plain setting can be shortened or removed by an administrator, while a locked one cannot be shortened or removed during the retention period
A plain setting stops reads, while a locked one stops writes
questions.why: A lock is an immutability control that prevents anyone, including administrators, from shortening or removing the retention period while it runs, whereas an unlocked setting can be lowered at will.

questions.prompt: A payments startup keeps refund records in a data warehouse for 7 years. Its auditor asks for proof that every read of those refund records is traceable. The engineer answers that the default administrative logs are enabled on the project, so reads are covered. What is wrong with that answer?
choices: Audit logs cannot be used in a warehouse at all, so the team must export the data to a spreadsheet
The retention period is the problem, because seven years is too short for an audit
Nothing is wrong, because administrative logs record every read of stored data
Administrative logs do not record data reads, so the team must enable data access audit logs for the warehouse to prove who read the records
questions.why: The default administrative logs record configuration changes, not data reads, so the read-level proof requires data access audit logs turned on for the warehouse.

questions.prompt: A weather network applied a locked 5-year retention period to a sensor dataset. Later it found that a faulty feed had ingested corrupted readings that the law does not require it to keep. What is the main consequence the team now faces?
choices: The corrupted readings stay until the locked period ends, so the team must check the deletion obligations before applying a lock
The corrupted readings can be deleted immediately because the lock only protects valid data
The perimeter must be dissolved so the readings can be copied out and deleted
The lock is automatically removed once the data is found to be wrong
questions.why: A locked retention period blocks deletion of everything in it, including bad data, until the period ends, which is why deletion obligations should be confirmed before the lock is applied.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would meet a rule that financial records must be kept for seven years and cannot be altered, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would store the records in a bucket or table with a locked retention period of seven years, so nobody can delete or shorten it early, even an admin. Retention and immutability are the controls for the 'kept and unaltered' part. For the 'provable' part, I would turn on data access audit logs, because the default admin logs do not show reads, and send them to a separate project that the data team cannot edit. I would also put the projects inside a service perimeter so the records cannot be copied out. The main tradeoff is that a locked period also blocks legitimate deletion, such as removing personal data someone asks us to erase, so we must check those obligations before locking anything. Storage costs also grow until the period ends.
rubricPoints: Names a retention control that is locked, not just a default setting
Explains that audit logs must record reads and live where the team cannot edit them
Places controls at the correct layer, such as storage, logging project, or perimeter
States a real limit, such as conflict with deletion obligations or growing cost

suggested.rationale: Choosing controls for a stated rule is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario that forces the learner to place each control at the right layer.

lessons.plain: Think of a company's data like a filing cabinet in a building with several locked rooms. Governance design means deciding how to split that cabinet: which rooms exist, who holds the keys to each, and which drawers hold sensitive papers. On Google Cloud, data sits in tables, tables sit inside datasets, and datasets sit inside projects. Each of those levels is a place where you can attach an access rule. If you attach a rule at the wrong level, it either covers too much or leaks through. This lesson is about choosing those containers so that access rules, cost tracking, and audit records line up with how the organisation actually needs to control its data.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company has one table with customer names and another with anonymous trip counts. Analysts should see the counts but never the names. Would you put both tables in one dataset and try to hide the name column, or split them into separate containers? Say why in a sentence.
lessons.teach:
A project is the top-level container in Google Cloud. It owns resources, carries billing, and sets quotas. A dataset is a named group of tables and views inside a project in BigQuery, Google's analytics data warehouse. A dataset is usually the unit where you grant people access to data. A table holds the rows and columns themselves. Access rules attached to a container generally flow downward: a grant at the project level reaches every dataset in it, and a grant on a dataset reaches its tables. That inheritance is why placement matters. Granting a broad role on a whole project to fix one narrow problem exposes everything else in that project.

Governance design therefore asks three questions about each piece of data: who must be able to read it, who pays for it, and how long it must be kept. Answer them by splitting data into containers whose boundaries match those answers. Keep sensitive or regulated data in its own dataset, or in its own project when the boundary must be stronger, so access can be granted to that data alone. Use labels, which are key-value tags on resources, to record owner and classification so reports can group things. When only some rows or columns should be visible, use an authorized view, which is a saved query that exposes a result without giving users direct access to the source table.

Worked example. A ride company stores trip records with rider names in a raw table, and anonymised trip counts in another. Step one: create a restricted dataset for the raw table. Step two: create an analytics dataset that holds an authorized view returning only the anonymised columns. Step three: grant analysts access to the analytics dataset only. Analysts can query the view, but they cannot read the raw names, because the view is authorized to read the restricted dataset on their behalf.

Common mistake: putting everything in one dataset and hiding columns with saved queries that people are asked to follow. Anyone with read access to that dataset can still query the names directly, and the audit trail shows no clear boundary.

The boundary has to be a container that the platform enforces, not a habit that people remember to follow.

questions.prompt: Harbor Dental runs clinics in three cities. Its billing table holds patient names and card last-four digits, and a second table holds monthly payment totals per clinic. The setup so far: step one, create a restricted dataset called billing_raw for the billing table. Step two, create a dataset called reporting for the totals. Step three, create an authorized view in reporting that returns only clinic, month and total. Step four is missing, and it is needed before analysts can query the view. Step five, grant the analysts reader access on the reporting dataset only. Which action completes step four?
choices: Grant the analysts the project-level viewer role so they inherit access to every dataset in the project.
Grant the analysts reader access on billing_raw so the view can pass their queries through to it.
Authorize the view to read the billing_raw dataset, so the view can read the source on the analysts' behalf.
Add owner and classification labels to the billing_raw dataset so that reports can group it.
questions.why: An authorized view must itself be allowed to read the restricted source dataset; without that permission the view cannot return rows, and the analysts still have no direct path to the raw names.

questions.prompt: Northwind Logistics has one project containing four datasets: payroll, shipping, marketing and sales. An analyst is given the Viewer role on the project itself, and no grant on any individual dataset. Which statement describes what that grant reaches?
choices: Only the payroll dataset, because it was created first in the project.
Only tables that carry a label with the value analyst.
Every dataset in the project and the tables inside each of them.
Nothing, until the analyst is also granted access to each dataset separately.
questions.why: Access rules attached to a project flow down to every dataset in it and to the tables inside those datasets, which is why a broad project-level grant exposes everything in the project.

questions.prompt: A health app keeps patient ID and diagnosis code in one table inside a dataset called ops. To protect patients, support staff are told to use a saved query that leaves out the ID column. What problem remains?
choices: The table has no labels, so the audit report cannot count how often the query was run.
The project quota is too low to hold the results of the saved query for every support agent.
Anyone with read access to ops can query the ID column directly; the boundary is a habit, not a container.
The saved query runs more slowly than a direct table read, which may lead staff to skip it during busy shifts.
questions.why: Because the sensitive column sits in a dataset that users can read, the protection depends on people following the saved query, not on the platform enforcing a boundary.

questions.prompt: Ferro Retail stores loyalty rows that include full card numbers. Compliance says only two named people may read those card numbers. Forty analysts also need monthly visit counts drawn from the same loyalty data. Which design meets both needs?
choices: Grant the forty analysts project-level Viewer, then remove that grant only on the loyalty table so they keep access to everything else.
Keep the loyalty rows in the shared analytics dataset and give the analysts a saved query that hides the card column.
Put the card-number rows in their own restricted dataset granted only to the two named people, and give the analysts an authorized view that returns visit counts without the card columns.
Add a label marking the card column as sensitive and rely on regular reports to flag any analyst who reads it.
questions.why: Placing the sensitive rows in a restricted dataset makes the boundary a container the platform enforces, and an authorized view gives analysts the counts they need without exposing the card numbers.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate proposes putting all company data into one dataset so it is easy to find, and hiding sensitive columns with a saved query that analysts are told to use. Explain in your own words why this placement is risky, what placement you would use instead, and one tradeoff your alternative creates.
lessons.modelAnswer: The risk is that access is granted at the dataset level, so anyone who can read that dataset can query the sensitive columns directly. A saved query is only a convention; nothing stops someone from running a different query against the raw table. I would split the data into a restricted dataset holding the raw sensitive table and an analytics dataset holding an authorized view that exposes only the non-sensitive columns. Analysts get access to the analytics dataset only. The tradeoff is more containers to manage and some extra setup, because the view has to be authorized to read the restricted source, and people who need raw data must be granted access to the restricted dataset separately. That friction is the point: it makes the boundary something the platform enforces and an auditor can check.
rubricPoints: Dataset-level access exposes every table in that dataset, so a convention to use a saved query does not enforce anything.
Sensitive data should sit in a separate restricted container, with access granted to that container only.
An authorized view can expose a subset of columns or rows without giving direct access to the source table.
Separating containers adds administration overhead, which is a real tradeoff to name.

suggested.rationale: Deciding where a governance control must live is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario with competing access needs, which the mission list does not cover directly.

lessons.plain: A development environment is a separate copy of your system where engineers build and test changes safely. A production environment is the live copy that real users and business reports depend on. For data work, this means a practice pipeline and practice storage that never touch the real data, so a mistake in a test cannot corrupt the numbers the business relies on. Designing for multiple environments means deciding what is separate, what is shared, and how a change travels from the first to the second.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team builds a pipeline that loads sales data nightly into a reporting table. Someone tests a change by pointing it at that same reporting table. What could go wrong, and what would you do differently?
lessons.teach:
An environment is a complete set of resources (storage, pipeline jobs, compute, and settings) that serves one purpose. Development, often shortened to dev, is where engineers change and test things. Production, or prod, is the live environment whose outputs people act on. Multi-environment design means you deliberately keep these apart and define how work moves between them.

Why it works: a pipeline that fails in dev hurts only dev. The separation limits the blast radius of a mistake, and it lets you test with data that is safe to break. Each environment gets its own storage locations, its own job definitions, and its own configuration values such as table names, bucket paths, and job sizes. The code stays the same; the settings change. Moving a tested version forward to the next environment is called promotion.

Worked example: a team has a streaming pipeline that writes ride counts to a warehouse table. Step 1: build a dev copy of the pipeline that writes to a dev table. Step 2: run the new transformation against a sample of last week's data in dev and check the row counts. Step 3: the checks pass, so the same version is deployed to prod with the prod table name supplied as configuration. Step 4: the prod dashboards are checked after the first run.

Common mistake: testing in production, or copying real production data into dev without protection. Dev often has looser access and fewer people watching it, so a copy of customer data there can leak it. Use masked or synthetic data in dev.

Consequence: if a dev job writes to the prod table, a bad transformation can overwrite or duplicate figures that finance uses the next morning, and rebuilding those figures can take hours.

questions.prompt: A payroll-reporting team runs a nightly job that writes employee pay summaries to a table called payroll_summary_prod. They have a corrected version of the job. Step 1: they build a dev copy of the job that writes to payroll_summary_dev, with its table name and job size held in a separate settings file. Step 2: they run the corrected version in dev against masked sample records and compare the total pay per department with the previous run. The totals match after they fix a duplicate-join bug. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the next morning, they compare the prod totals with the source system's control total and find no gap.
choices: Edit the job's code directly in production so the table name matches prod, then run it once to check.
Promote the same tested version to prod, supplying the prod table name and job size through the prod settings file.
Skip the prod deployment and point the dev job at payroll_summary_prod on its nightly schedule.
Copy the dev job definition into prod and change its table name by hand before the first run.
questions.why: Promotion moves the same tested version forward, with only the environment-specific settings changed, so the prod run matches what was tested in dev.

questions.prompt: In the context of dev and prod environments, what does 'promotion' mean?
choices: Copying real customer records from production into dev for realistic testing.
Moving a tested version of a pipeline forward to the next environment without changing its code.
Giving a senior engineer admin rights over the production project.
Doubling the size of a production job to handle a traffic spike.
questions.why: Promotion is defined as moving a tested version forward to the next environment, with the code staying the same and only the settings changing.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's dev job is misconfigured and reads from the prod storage bucket because the bucket path was typed into the shared job definition. Which design choice would have prevented this?
choices: Keeping each environment's bucket path and table names in its own configuration values, separate from the shared code.
Running dev jobs only at night so they never overlap with production.
Giving dev engineers read-only access to the prod bucket so they cannot write to it.
Renaming the prod bucket every week so the dev job loses track of it.
questions.why: Each environment should have its own configuration values such as bucket paths and table names, so a single shared definition cannot point dev at prod.

questions.prompt: A retail company wants realistic test results, so it copies last quarter's full customer payment records into its dev project, which has looser access and fewer monitoring alerts. What is the safer approach?
choices: Use masked or synthetic data in dev instead of real customer records.
Share the dev project's access list with the whole engineering department.
Move the dev project into the production network so monitoring covers it.
Keep the full copy but delete it after each test run.
questions.why: Dev environments often have looser controls, so real customer data should be replaced with masked or synthetic data that is safe to break.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we keep a separate development environment for our data pipelines instead of testing changes directly against production. Name one tradeoff of running separate environments.
lessons.modelAnswer: We keep dev separate so a broken change only hurts a practice copy, not the tables finance and dashboards read from. Dev gets its own storage, its own job definitions, and its own config values, so the same pipeline code points at different targets. We test there with sample or masked data rather than real customer records, because dev usually has looser access and fewer people watching it. The tradeoff is cost and drift: a second environment costs money to run, and if dev settings differ from prod in ways nobody tracks, a job that passes in dev can still fail in prod. So we keep the differences small and explicit, and we promote the same tested version forward rather than rebuilding it by hand.
rubricPoints: States that dev isolates failures so a mistake does not reach live outputs
Explains that the same code runs in each environment with different configuration
Notes that dev should use masked or sample data, not raw production data
Names a tradeoff such as extra cost or configuration drift between environments

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a realistic promotion scenario with a dev and prod mix-up adds the most on top of the reading.

lessons.plain: Raw data often arrives messy: the same record appears twice, numbers are stored as text, dates use inconsistent formats, and some fields are blank. Preparing and cleaning data means turning that raw material into a consistent, trustworthy set that analysts and models can rely on. On Google Cloud, several tools do this work in different ways. Some let you write cleaning steps as SQL that runs inside the data warehouse. Some run records through code, in batches or as a continuous stream. Some offer a visual, drag-and-drop builder. Some use a language model to draft a query from a plain-language request. The skill is choosing the right fit for the job and checking the result.
lessons.guessPrompt: A file of customer orders has the same order appearing twice, some amounts stored as text like '12,50', and some dates written as 03/04/2024, which could mean March or April. Before learning anything here, which problem would you fix first, and what would you check afterwards to know the fix worked?
lessons.teach:
Cleaning means finding values that are wrong, duplicated, or in the wrong shape, and correcting or flagging them before anyone uses the data. Deduplication removes repeated records, usually by matching on a key such as an order ID. Type casting converts a value to the type it should have, such as text to a decimal number. A transformation is any step that changes data from one form to another, and a pipeline is a chain of such steps run in order.

The tools differ mainly in where the work runs and how it is written. Dataform manages SQL transformations inside BigQuery, the warehouse, as versioned definitions that depend on each other. Dataflow is a managed service that runs code-based pipelines written with Apache Beam, in batch or streaming mode, and suits high volume or continuous data. Cloud Data Fusion is a visual builder for assembling pipelines from connectors, useful when many sources must be joined without much code. LLM-prompted query generation means a language model drafts SQL from a description. Its output is a draft that must be reviewed and tested.

Worked example. Three raw order rows: order 101 with amount '12,50' and date 03/04/2024, order 101 again, and order 102 with a blank amount. Step one: deduplicate on order_id, keeping one row for 101. Step two: replace the comma with a period and cast to a decimal, giving 12.50. Step three: parse the date using the format the source documents, and flag order 102's blank amount rather than inventing a zero. The result is one clean row per order with an explicit flag for the gap.

The common mistake is silently turning bad values into zeros or nulls with no record of it, which hides the problem. A running system pays for this: a dashboard double-counts revenue when duplicates survive, or a model learns that missing amounts mean free orders.

Good cleaning keeps a record of what was changed and checks row counts before and after each step.

questions.prompt: A parking operator exports payment rows from two files. Session P-40 appears twice with fee '3,00'. Session P-41 has fee 'N/A'. Session P-42 has fee '5,50' and date 14/02/2024 written day first. The cleaner works in this order: Step 1, deduplicate on session_id and keep one row for P-40. Step 2, replace the comma with a period and cast the fees for P-40 and P-42 to decimal numbers, giving 3.00 and 5.50. Step 3, parse the P-42 date using the day-first format the source documents. Step 4 is missing. What should it be, to deal with the 'N/A' fee on P-41?
choices: Delete P-41 without a note so the output contains only complete rows.
Run the decimal cast again on the P-40 duplicate so both copies match.
Flag P-41 with an explicit missing-fee marker, keep the row, and record the before and after row counts.
Replace 'N/A' with 0.00 so that the column totals add up cleanly.
questions.why: The text says a blank or unknown value should be flagged rather than turned into a zero or dropped silently, and that good cleaning records what changed and checks row counts.

questions.prompt: A hotel booking export contains repeated rows for the same reservation, because the same booking was sent twice. Which field is the best key for deduplication?
choices: Guest surname, since guests rarely share one.
Total amount paid, since duplicates have identical totals.
Booking reference, because each reservation has one unique reference that repeats only in duplicates.
Room type, because it is always a short fixed list.
questions.why: Deduplication matches on a key that identifies one real-world record, and a unique booking reference does that, while the other fields are shared by different bookings.

questions.prompt: A school enrolment team replaces every blank attendance value with 0 before computing the average attendance rate. Classes with many missing entries now show very low averages. What is the main problem?
choices: The zeros are real attendance, so the averages are correct and only the chart needs changing.
The team should have converted the blanks to text so that the average skips them automatically.
Averages cannot be computed when any value is zero, so the team should use the median instead.
Blanks mean the value is unknown, so writing zeros records absence that never happened and hides the gap, which should be flagged instead.
questions.why: Turning unknown values into zeros invents data, which distorts the average and hides the missing records, so the correct approach is to flag them.

questions.prompt: A logistics company receives about 40 million sensor readings an hour that need type casting, deduplication, and range checks before they reach storage. The work must run continuously and the team wants code-based control. Which tool best fits this requirement?
choices: An LLM-prompted query generator, because it can draft the cleaning SQL from a description.
Dataflow, because it is a managed service that runs code-based batch or streaming pipelines at high volume.
Dataform, because it runs SQL transformations as versioned definitions inside the warehouse.
Cloud Data Fusion, because its visual builder is best for joining many sources with little code.
questions.why: Dataflow runs code-based pipelines in streaming mode at high volume, which matches a continuous, high-throughput cleaning requirement, while the other options are better suited to other situations.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between a SQL transformation tool, a managed batch and stream processing service, a visual pipeline builder, and a language model that drafts a query, for cleaning a nightly sales feed. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not pick first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from where the data lives and how fast it arrives. If the nightly feed lands in the warehouse and the cleaning is mostly SQL, a SQL transformation tool keeps the logic in one place, versioned and testable. If the volume is very large or the feed streams in continuously, a managed batch and stream processing service fits better, though it means writing and maintaining code. A visual builder suits teams that need many connectors and little custom logic, but complex rules get harder to review and version. A language model can speed up drafting a query, but its output can be subtly wrong, so I would never run it unreviewed. Whichever I pick, I would compare row counts and totals before and after cleaning, and record every change so the numbers can be audited later.
rubricPoints: Matches the tool to where the data lives and whether it is batch or streaming
Names a concrete limit of the option not chosen first, such as code maintenance or hard-to-review visual logic
Treats language-model output as a draft that needs review and testing
Describes checking row counts or totals and recording changes

suggested.rationale: A planned SQL lab would let the learner write and check cleaning queries against messy sample tables, which is the hands-on core of SQL-based preparation.

lessons.plain: A data pipeline is a chain of steps that moves data from where it starts to where people use it, such as collecting sales records, cleaning them, and loading them into a report. Monitoring means watching that chain with measurements and logs so you notice when a step is slow, failing, or quietly producing nothing. Orchestrating means a scheduler that decides when each step runs, in what order, what to do when one fails, and when to try again. Think of a kitchen: monitoring is the timer and the taste test, and orchestration is the head chef telling each cook what to start next. Together they let a data team run pipelines every night without someone babysitting them.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job copies orders into a report table. One night the job finishes with no error, but the report shows zero new rows. What would you check first, and why is 'the job finished' not enough evidence that the pipeline worked?
lessons.teach:
Orchestration is the layer that runs a pipeline's steps on a schedule and in dependency order. A dependency means one step needs another step's output first. The steps are usually arranged as a DAG, a directed acyclic graph: a set of tasks with arrows showing which must finish before which, with no loops. Managed services such as Cloud Composer, which runs Apache Airflow, let you describe that graph in code and handle the scheduling. Monitoring is the measurement side. Metrics are numbers sampled over time, such as run duration, rows processed, or the age of the oldest unprocessed message. Logs are the text records each step writes. An alert is a rule that notifies a person when a metric crosses a threshold. Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging are Google Cloud's tools for these jobs.

Why it works: the orchestrator knows the graph, so when a task fails it can stop the tasks that depend on it, retry the failed task with increasing waits (called backoff), and record the outcome. Monitoring then tells people about the failure instead of leaving them to discover stale data later.

Worked example: a nightly job has three tasks, extract, transform, and load. First, at 02:00 the scheduler starts extract. Second, extract succeeds, so transform starts. Third, transform fails on a malformed row. Fourth, the orchestrator retries transform after one minute, then after two minutes, and both attempts fail. Fifth, load never starts, so the warehouse keeps yesterday's data. Sixth, an alert fires on a failed-run metric and an on-call engineer is paged before 06:00.

Common mistake: alerting only when the job process exits with an error, while missing the case where a job succeeds but loads zero rows or runs hours late. Watch outcome metrics such as data freshness and row counts as well as run status.

Consequence: a silently stale table feeds dashboards and decisions for days before anyone notices. Good monitoring measures whether the data arrived, not only whether the code ran.

questions.prompt: A retail company runs a batch pipeline for its sales table each morning. It is a nightly orchestrated job with three tasks, pull, clean, and publish, in that order. Each task only starts after the one before it has finished. At 04:00 the scheduler starts pull. Pull finishes, so clean starts. Clean fails on a changed column name. The orchestrator retries clean twice, with waits of 30 seconds and then 60 seconds, and both retries fail. Publish never starts, so the reporting dashboard keeps showing the previous day's figures. Now consider a second morning. At 04:00 the scheduler starts the same job. The job exits with success status because the source file was empty, so it loads zero rows into the sales table. Nothing failed as a process, so run status still reads success. Fifth, ___.
choices: The dashboard automatically switches to the figures from the previous week
A rule on the rows-loaded metric crosses its threshold and notifies an engineer
The orchestrator treats the zero-row load as a failure and retries it with longer waits
The logs for the run are deleted once the run is marked successful
questions.why: Rows loaded is an outcome metric, and an alert rule that fires when it crosses a threshold is what notifies a person, since run status alone reports success.

questions.prompt: In orchestration, what is a DAG?
choices: A rule that pages a person when a number passes a threshold
A set of tasks with arrows showing which must finish before which, with no loops
A retry policy that doubles the wait after each failed attempt
A log file that records each step's text output in order
questions.why: The teaching text defines a DAG as a directed acyclic graph of tasks whose arrows show ordering dependencies with no loops.

questions.prompt: A data team wants a number that is sampled over time and shows how long the oldest unprocessed message has been waiting in a queue. Which kind of measurement is this, and what does a log or an alert contribute instead?
choices: A log, which is the text record each step writes as it runs
A metric, which is a number sampled over time, while logs are text and alerts are notification rules
A DAG, which fixes the order in which tasks must run
An alert, which notifies a person when a rule is triggered
questions.why: The teaching text describes metrics as numbers sampled over time, such as the age of the oldest unprocessed message, whereas logs are text records and alerts are threshold notifications.

questions.prompt: A task that failed is set to retry three times, with waits of 15 seconds, then 30 seconds, then 60 seconds. What is this pattern called, and why does it help?
choices: Sharding: the data is split into smaller pieces so each retry handles less work
Backoff: the waits lengthen between attempts, giving a struggling dependency time to recover instead of being hit repeatedly
Fan-out: the single failed task is copied into several parallel tasks so one of them is likely to succeed
Idempotence: each retry is guaranteed to produce the same rows as the first attempt
questions.why: The teaching text names increasing waits between retries as backoff, which lets a failing step or its upstream service recover rather than being overwhelmed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an orchestrator and monitoring work together for a nightly data pipeline. Name one limit or tradeoff of alerting too often versus too rarely.
lessons.modelAnswer: The orchestrator holds the pipeline as a graph of tasks and runs them in dependency order. If a task fails, it retries with increasing waits, and it stops the tasks that depend on the failed one so nothing downstream runs on bad input. Monitoring watches two kinds of signal. Run status tells us whether each task succeeded. Outcome metrics such as data freshness, row counts, and the age of the oldest unprocessed message tell us whether the data actually arrived and looks right. Alerts turn threshold breaches into notifications for a person. The tradeoff is in the thresholds. Alert too often and people get flooded with noise and start ignoring pages. Alert too rarely and stale data can sit unnoticed for hours. Retries also need care: if a step is not safe to run twice, a retry can duplicate records, so the step should be designed to be repeatable.
rubricPoints: Orchestrator runs tasks in dependency order and stops downstream tasks when an upstream task fails.
Retries with backoff handle transient failures, and the retried steps must be safe to repeat.
Monitoring should track outcome signals such as freshness and row counts, not only job exit status.
Alert thresholds involve a tradeoff between noisy alerts and missed problems.

suggested.rationale: That mission has you spot a growing backlog and a stalled consumer, which is the monitoring half of keeping a pipeline draining.

lessons.plain: Disaster recovery means planning for the day something important breaks badly: a data center fails, a whole region goes dark, or someone deletes a table by mistake. Fault tolerance means the system keeps working, possibly with less capacity, when one of its parts fails. Think of a bakery with a spare oven and a copy of its recipe book kept at another shop. One broken oven does not stop bread, and if the main shop burns down, you can still rebuild. For a data platform, this means choosing where copies of data live, how often they are made, and how quickly you can switch to a working copy. The core design question is how much data you can afford to lose and how long you can afford to be down.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your nightly sales report reads from a database in one city. If that city's data center loses power for two days, what would you need to have set up in advance so the report can still run, and how much recent data would you expect to be missing?
lessons.teach:
Disaster recovery (DR) is the set of copies, plans, and procedures that let a data system come back after a serious failure. Fault tolerance is the design property that lets a system keep serving when one component fails, often without users noticing. Two terms make DR measurable. The recovery point objective (RPO) is the most data, measured in time, that you accept losing: an RPO of one hour means the newest usable copy must be no more than an hour behind. The recovery time objective (RTO) is how long the service may stay down before it must be running again.

Why it works: you cannot prevent every failure, so you spread risk. Redundancy means keeping a second copy of data or a second instance of a service in a separate failure domain, such as another zone or another region. Replication copies changes continuously, which gives a small RPO, but it also copies mistakes almost instantly. Backups and snapshots are point-in-time copies that protect against bad writes and deletions, which replication alone does not.

Worked example: a warehouse ingests ride events hourly, with an RPO of one hour and an RTO of four hours. First, the raw files are stored in a multi-region storage location, so one region's outage does not lose them. Second, a scheduled job exports the warehouse tables to that storage every hour, which keeps the newest copy within the RPO. Third, a region outage occurs at 10:00. Fourth, the team restores from the latest export, at most one hour old, and reloads the tables within four hours, which meets the RTO. Had the team relied only on replication, a bad deletion at 09:55 would have been copied to the second location too.

Common mistake: treating a replica as a backup. A replica follows every change, including destructive ones, so it cannot take you back in time.

Consequence: if the copy schedule is slower than the RPO, a failover silently loses the gap, and downstream dashboards show numbers that skip hours without any error.

questions.prompt: A parcel-tracking team stores scan events in a database in one region. Their recovery point objective (RPO, the most data in time they accept losing) is 30 minutes, and their recovery time objective (RTO, how long the service may be down) is 2 hours. Step 1: they keep a second copy of the event archive in a different region, so one region's outage does not destroy it. Step 2: a job exports the database to that archive every 15 minutes, keeping the newest copy within the RPO. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: when a region outage hits, they restore from the newest export and reload the data within 2 hours, meeting the RTO. Which missing step is needed so that a bad delete made earlier in the day can still be undone?
choices: Nothing is missing, because the second-region copy already protects against deletions.
Keep dated point-in-time snapshots of the export, so that a state from before the bad delete can be restored.
Change the export job to run every minute, so the RPO becomes zero and deletions are caught sooner.
Lower the RTO to 30 minutes so the restore finishes before the bad delete spreads.
questions.why: Replication copies deletions as well as good data, so only point-in-time snapshots or backups taken before the bad change can recover it.

questions.prompt: In disaster recovery, what does the recovery time objective (RTO, the longest time a service may stay down before it must be running again) measure?
choices: The maximum time the service may be unavailable before it must be restored.
The share of component failures a system can absorb without users noticing.
The number of independent copies of data kept in separate zones.
The most recent data that can be lost, measured in time.
questions.why: RTO is the allowed downtime, while RPO is the allowed data loss, and redundancy and fault tolerance are separate ideas.

questions.prompt: A file store is replicated continuously to a second region. At 08:40 a user accidentally deletes a folder, and by 08:45 the replica also lacks it. Which control would have let the team recover the folder?
choices: Making the replication run more frequently than it already does.
Shortening the recovery time objective for the service.
A point-in-time backup or snapshot taken before 08:40.
Replicating the store to a third region at the same time.
questions.why: Continuous replication copies the deletion almost instantly, so only a backup or snapshot from before the change can restore the lost folder.

questions.prompt: A team has an RPO of 6 hours. It runs one export to cold storage each night at 02:00. A region outage happens at 19:00 the same day, and the team restores from the newest export. What is the worst-case data loss, and does the plan meet the RPO?
choices: 17 hours of data is lost, but the RPO is met because exports are nightly.
6 hours of data is lost, so the RPO is met exactly.
17 hours of data is lost, so the RPO is violated.
5 hours of data is lost, so the RPO is met with an hour to spare.
questions.why: The newest usable copy is from 02:00, 17 hours before the 19:00 outage, which exceeds the 6-hour RPO, so the schedule must be faster.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between RPO and RTO, why a replica alone does not count as a backup, and one tradeoff involved in placing copies of data in a different region.
lessons.modelAnswer: RPO is how much recent data we can afford to lose, measured as time. If the RPO is one hour, the newest copy we can recover from must be less than an hour old. RTO is how long the service can be down before it has to be serving again. They are independent: a system can have a tight RPO but a loose RTO if it copies data constantly yet takes a day to rebuild. A replica is not a backup because replication copies every change as it happens, including a bad delete or a corrupted write, so the damage reaches every copy within seconds. A backup or snapshot is a point-in-time copy you can return to. The tradeoff of spreading copies across regions is cost and latency. Cross-region copies cost more to store and move, and synchronous writes to a distant region slow every request, so teams often accept asynchronous copies that leave a small gap in the RPO.
rubricPoints: RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time, and RTO is the maximum acceptable downtime.
Replicas protect against hardware or regional failure but also copy mistakes, so backups or snapshots are needed too.
Placing copies in separate failure domains such as zones or regions is what provides fault tolerance.
Cross-region designs trade higher cost and latency for lower risk and tighter recovery targets.

suggested.rationale: A planned disaster-recovery planner engine would let the learner set RPO and RTO targets and check whether a proposed copy schedule meets them.

lessons.plain: Some data changes must either all happen or not happen at all, and some systems must keep answering even when part of the system breaks. These two wishes often pull against each other. Choosing a storage system means deciding how much you need the all-or-nothing, always-correct promise and how much you need the always-up-and-answering promise, then accepting what the other choice costs. A bank transfer usually needs the first. A stream of sensor readings usually needs the second. This lesson shows how to tell which one a job needs and what each choice gives up.
