lessons.guessPrompt: An online store saves a customer's order and then reduces the stock count in a separate step. If the server crashes between those two steps, what could the customer or the warehouse see, and would you rather the store refuse orders for a few seconds or risk that mismatch?
lessons.teach:
ACID is a set of promises a database makes about transactions, which are groups of reads and writes treated as one unit. Atomicity means every step in the group happens or none does. Consistency means the data still obeys its rules after the group finishes. Isolation means concurrent groups do not see each other's half-finished work. Durability means a committed change survives a crash. Availability is the share of time a system accepts requests and answers them. The two goals conflict because keeping copies of data in several places, often far apart, means a write must wait for the other copies to agree before it counts as committed. That waiting makes commits slower, and when the network between copies breaks, the system must either refuse writes or accept writes that may later disagree.

Worked example: an order reserves 2 units of stock and creates an order row in one transaction. Step 1, the database locks the stock row. Step 2, it checks that at least 2 units exist. Step 3, it subtracts 2 and inserts the order. Step 4, it commits. If step 3 fails, the whole group rolls back, so you never end up with an order whose stock was not reduced.

Common mistake: assuming a read from a replica always returns the latest committed value. A read replica can lag behind the primary by seconds, so a read right after a write may show old data.

Consequence: a single-region relational database gives strong ACID but stops accepting writes during a regional outage until failover completes. A globally distributed database can keep ACID across regions but adds latency to every commit. A high-throughput key-value store may give up multi-row transactions to keep writes fast. The right choice depends on which promise the workload cannot afford to lose.

questions.prompt: A clinic books appointment slots in one transaction, which is a group of reads and writes that the database treats as a single unit. The steps are: Step 1, lock the slot row so no other booking can change it. Step 2, check that the slot is still free. Step 3, [missing step]. Step 4, commit, which makes the group's changes permanent. Which step completes the group so that a slot is never marked as booked without a matching booking record existing?
choices: Mark the slot as taken and insert the booking row inside the same transaction.
Read the slot again from a different table to confirm it is still free.
Copy the slot's status to a read replica, which is a second copy of the data, and wait for it to catch up.
Send the patient a confirmation email before committing, so the patient knows the slot is theirs.
questions.why: Putting both the status change and the booking insert inside the same transaction means they either both happen or neither does, which is the atomicity promise in the teaching text.

questions.prompt: A courier company's app writes two changes in one transaction: it moves a parcel to 'out for delivery' and it adds a driver assignment record. The database crashes after the first change is written but before the group commits. What does the database promise about the result?
choices: Durability, so the first change is kept after the restart.
Availability, so the app keeps accepting the parcel update during the crash.
Atomicity, so neither change is kept because the group never committed.
Isolation, so other drivers cannot see the parcel while it is being updated.
questions.why: Atomicity means a group either fully happens or not at all, and since the group never committed, the teaching text's rules imply neither change survives the crash.

questions.prompt: A ride-sharing company stores driver location pings in a key-value store that is set up for very fast single-key writes and does not support multi-row transactions. The team wants to also update a driver's earnings total and a trip record together, always as one unit. What is the most accurate assessment?
choices: The store will automatically add isolation between the two updates, so no change is needed.
The store is a poor fit for that joint update, because it gave up multi-row transactions to keep writes fast.
The store can do this safely as long as writes are sent in parallel.
The store will keep both updates consistent because it uses replicas.
questions.why: The teaching text notes that a high-throughput key-value store may give up multi-row transactions for speed, so a workload needing a multi-row all-or-nothing update needs a different system or design.

questions.prompt: A loyalty app saves a customer's new points balance to the primary database, then immediately reads the balance from a read replica, which is a copy that can lag behind the primary by a few seconds. The customer sees the old balance and files a complaint. Which explanation best fits the situation described?
choices: The transaction was not isolated, so another customer's update overwrote the balance.
The app failed to commit, so the write was rolled back before the read happened.
The primary database lost the committed write because it was not durable enough.
The read replica lagged behind the primary, so the read returned an older committed value.
questions.why: A replica can lag behind the primary by seconds, so a read right after a write may return old data even though the write was committed on the primary.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between a strongly consistent transactional database and a more available, eventually consistent store for a new feature. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by asking what breaks if a reader or a crash sees a half-finished change. If the answer is money moving, stock being oversold, or a booking being double-counted, I need ACID on the write path, so I pick a transactional database. The cost is that a cross-region commit is slower, and during a regional outage writes may block until the system fails over. If the answer is that a slightly old value is acceptable, such as a dashboard tile or a vehicle position refreshed every few seconds, I pick the more available store and let reads lag. The tradeoff I would name to the team is that the availability option cannot promise that a read right after a write sees that write, so the application has to tolerate stale reads or the feature needs a fallback.
rubricPoints: Defines atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability in plain words
Explains that copies in several places make commits slower or force a choice during a network failure
Gives one case where all-or-nothing matters and one where staleness is acceptable
Names a concrete tradeoff of the chosen option, such as stale replica reads or blocked writes during failover

suggested.rationale: That mission has you reason about stale reads from a replica, the availability side of this trade-off, though it does not cover transaction guarantees.

lessons.plain: Data validation means checking incoming data against rules before you trust it or store it. Think of a checkout clerk who scans each item and sets aside anything with a missing price instead of letting it into the till. In a data pipeline, a pipeline is the chain of steps that moves data from where it is produced to where it is used. Designing validation into a pipeline means deciding which checks run, where they run in the chain, and what happens to records that fail: they are rejected, fixed, or set aside for review. Good design catches bad data early, before it spoils reports or models.
lessons.guessPrompt: A sensor sends a temperature of 900 degrees Celsius once an hour from a building that is normally around 20 degrees. Where in a data pipeline would you want to catch that reading, and why would waiting until the monthly report be a poor choice?
lessons.teach:
Validation in a pipeline means automatic checks that every record must pass, or be handled in a defined way, before it moves on to storage or analysis. A rule is one check, such as 'latitude must be between -90 and 90' or 'the timestamp field must be present'. A schema is the agreed description of a record's fields and their types. A quarantine, sometimes called a dead-letter destination, is a separate place where failed records are kept along with the reason they failed, so nothing disappears silently. Validation works because each check runs at a boundary, the point where data enters a new stage, so a bad record is stopped once instead of spreading into every downstream table and report. Rejected records are also counted, so a sudden rise in failures appears as a metric rather than as a wrong number nobody notices.

Worked example. A feed of vehicle positions arrives as a batch. Record A is vehicle V12 with latitude 51.5 and a timestamp present. Record B is vehicle V13 with latitude 151.2 and a timestamp present. Step 1: the pipeline checks record A against the schema and range rules; it passes and goes to the positions table. Step 2: record B passes the schema check but fails the range rule, because latitude cannot exceed 90. Step 3: B is written to the quarantine with the reason 'latitude out of range', and the failure counter rises by one. Step 4: the batch completes, and the failure count is reviewed.

Common mistake: validating only after loading into the warehouse. Bad rows are then already in reports and must be cleaned up later with deletes, which is slow and error-prone. Another mistake is dropping failures silently.

Consequence in a running system: if one bad row halts the whole stage, every valid record waits behind it. Choose per rule whether to reject one record or stop the stage, and monitor the rejection rate.

questions.prompt: A retailer's order feed arrives as a batch. Each order record must have a quantity of at least 1. Order O-881 has quantity 3 and passes; it goes to the orders table. Order O-882 has quantity -2 and fails the rule. Step 1: O-881 passes the rule and is written to the orders table. Step 2: O-882 fails the quantity rule. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the batch finishes and the failure count is reviewed. Which action completes step 3?
choices: Load O-882 into the orders table and flag it for review later
Stop the whole batch so that O-881 is also held back
Write O-882 to the quarantine with the reason 'quantity below minimum' and raise the failure counter by one
Delete O-882 from the feed without recording anything
questions.why: A failed record is kept in the quarantine with its failure reason and counted in the failure metric, so the rejection is visible and nothing vanishes silently.

questions.prompt: A payments team agrees that every transaction record must name a three-letter currency code and an amount stored as a number. What is that agreed description of the fields and their types called?
choices: A batch window
A quarantine
A schema
A failure counter
questions.why: A schema is the agreed description of a record's fields and their types, which is exactly what the team has written down.

questions.prompt: A clinic feed loads appointment records into a reporting table first, and only then runs its validation checks. What is the most likely problem with this order?
choices: Valid records wait behind one bad record in the same stage
Failed rows are sent to a quarantine automatically before they are loaded
The validation rules stop being needed once data is in a table
Incorrect rows appear in reports before anyone checks them, so they must be removed later with deletes
questions.why: Validating after loading lets bad rows reach reports, and cleaning them up afterwards means slow, error-prone deletes, which is the core mistake of checking too late.

questions.prompt: A shipping pipeline has a rule that every parcel must have a destination country code. A team wants bad parcel records handled without losing any evidence and without stalling good records. Which design best fits?
choices: Remove the country-code rule so that every parcel keeps flowing into storage
Halt the entire stage whenever any single parcel is missing a country code
Store all parcels first and count the missing codes once a week
Send individual parcels missing a country code to a quarantine with the reason, and track how many are rejected
questions.why: Rejecting only the failing records to a quarantine with reasons, and monitoring the rejection count, keeps evidence and keeps valid records moving.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate proposes validating vehicle positions only once a day, inside the reporting query. Explain to them where validation should sit in the pipeline instead, how failed records should be handled, and one limit or tradeoff of strict checking.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would move the checks to the ingestion boundary, the first step where data enters our processing stage, so each record is tested once as it arrives. The checks are rules such as required fields, correct types, and value ranges like latitude between -90 and 90. A record that fails goes into a quarantine store with the reason attached, rather than being dropped or loaded. Valid records continue to the warehouse, and we count rejections so a spike shows up on a dashboard. The tradeoff is that strict rules can reject real but unusual data, such as a new sensor format, so we need a review path and a way to update rules without losing records. A daily check inside the report is too late, because bad rows have already been used by then.
rubricPoints: Validation belongs at the ingestion boundary, before data reaches storage or reports.
Rules check things like required fields, types, and valid value ranges.
Failed records go to a quarantine with the failure reason, not silently dropped or loaded.
Strict rules carry a tradeoff: they can reject legitimate new or unusual data, so rules need review and monitoring.

suggested.rationale: Choosing where validation sits and how failures are handled is best shown by explaining it back, since no listed mission or planned engine covers data pipeline validation directly.

lessons.plain: Mapping business requirements to a data architecture means turning what a business says it needs into a design for how data is collected, moved, stored, and used. A business might say managers need yesterday's sales by 8 am, or that the company will open ten new cities next year. Each sentence hides technical demands: how fresh the data must be, how much of it there will be, who reads it and how, and how much downtime or cost is acceptable. The skill is pulling those demands out of ordinary sentences, writing them as measurable targets, and choosing parts that meet them now and still work as the business grows. It is less about memorising product names and more about asking the right questions first.
lessons.guessPrompt: A retail company says: 'Store managers must see today's sales by 9 am tomorrow, and head office wants to ask any question about three years of sales history.' Before reading on, what two different demands do these sentences place on the data design, and why might one system struggle to meet both?
lessons.teach:
A business requirement is a plain statement of what the business needs, such as a deadline or a question people must be able to answer. A technical requirement is a measurable version of it, such as data no more than 24 hours old or a query finishing in under 30 seconds. Freshness means how old data may be when someone uses it. Volume means how much data exists and how fast it grows. Access pattern means how people read it: a single record looked up by ID, or a large scan across years of rows. An analytical warehouse is a system built to scan many rows quickly for questions and summaries, usually storing data by column. An operational database is built to read and write small numbers of rows for live applications.

The method works because each measurable demand points toward a family of designs. Once you have the numbers, the choice of batch versus streaming, warehouse versus operational store, and cheap archive versus fast storage follows from them, and you can explain each choice back to a requirement.

Worked example. Take the retail sentences above. Step 1: 'by 9 am tomorrow' means data may be about a day old, so a nightly batch load is enough. Step 2: 'ask any question about three years' means large ad hoc scans over history, which points to an analytical warehouse such as BigQuery rather than the checkout database. Step 3: if sales double each year, the design must not need rebuilding, so pick managed services that scale without manual resizing. Step 4: keep raw files in object storage, a cheap store for files, so the history can be reloaded if the warehouse design changes.

Common mistake: choosing tools the team already knows, then reading the requirements to fit them. Consequence in a running system: running three years of analytical scans against the live checkout database slows payments for customers, because both workloads compete for the same resources.

A requirement that is never turned into a number cannot be checked, so every architecture decision should trace back to a measured demand.

questions.prompt: A regional bus operator needs its live dashboard to show each vehicle's position no more than 10 seconds old. Its planners also need to ask questions about five years of ridership counts, and the raw GPS logs must be kept so the history can be reloaded later. Work through it. Step 1: 10 seconds old means data must arrive as a continuous stream, not in a nightly batch. Step 2: five years of ridership questions are large scans over history, which points to an analytical warehouse, a system built to scan many rows quickly. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: keep the raw GPS logs in object storage, a cheap store for whole files, so the history can be rebuilt if the warehouse design changes. Which statement correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Because the warehouse already stores data by column, the live dashboard should also read from the warehouse, since one system is simpler to run.
Each vehicle's latest position is read as a single record lookup, which points to an operational store built for small, frequent reads and writes, kept separate from the warehouse.
Because raw GPS logs are cheap in object storage, the dashboard should query those files directly on every refresh.
Because the dashboard only needs data 10 seconds old, a batch job every ten minutes is the cheapest way to meet the requirement without any store for live reads.
questions.why: The dashboard reads one vehicle's latest position at a time, which is a single-record access pattern that an operational store handles, while the warehouse is for large scans; the other options either misread the access pattern or fail the 10-second freshness requirement.

questions.prompt: In data architecture, what does freshness mean?
choices: How old data may be when someone uses it.
The number of people who are allowed to read a dataset.
The total number of rows a system can store before it must be resized.
The speed at which a query returns its first result to the user.
questions.why: Freshness is the measure of how old data may be at the moment it is used, which is why a stated limit such as no more than 24 hours old is a usable technical requirement.

questions.prompt: A hospital lab must give managers a report covering ten years of test results, delivered in under two minutes. The team proposes running that report directly against the live lab system, because its engineers already know that database well. What is the main flaw in this proposal?
choices: Test results should never be stored in a database that engineers know.
The report is a large scan across years of rows, which competes with live lab work and reverses the usual order of choosing a design from the requirements.
The live system cannot be queried by managers under any circumstances.
Ten years of data is too small to need any analytical system at all.
questions.why: A ten-year report is an analytical access pattern, so the design should follow from that demand; running it on the live system lets the scan slow the work the system exists to do, and choosing the tool first is the common mistake.

questions.prompt: An energy company tells its team that its usage data must be no more than 24 hours old, but the requirement is only spoken in meetings and never written as a measurable target in the design documents. Why is this a problem for the architecture?
choices: Spoken requirements are legally binding, so the documents are unnecessary.
Measurable targets always make a system more expensive, so leaving them unwritten saves money.
A requirement that is never turned into a number cannot be checked, so no design decision can be traced back to it or verified.
Twenty-four hours is a standard value, so it does not need to be documented for each project.
questions.why: A requirement that is never measured cannot be tested, and architecture decisions cannot be traced back to a demand that was never stated as a number, so the design cannot be confirmed to meet it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would take a vague request such as 'make our reports faster and keep everything forever' and turn it into an architecture decision. Name at least one limit or tradeoff your approach does not remove.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking what each sentence actually measures. 'Faster' becomes numbers: how old the data may be when someone reads it, and how long a query may take. 'Keep everything forever' becomes a retention rule for each type of data, plus an estimate of current volume and yearly growth, because those decide storage cost and query cost. Then I would match each measured demand to a pattern: batch loads for data that can be a day old, streaming for anything needing minutes, an analytical warehouse for large scans and ad hoc SQL, and cheap object storage for raw history rarely read. I would write the mapping down so every design choice points back to a requirement. The tradeoff is that my growth and usage estimates are guesses until real traffic shows up, so I would set a checkpoint to revisit them. Also, if two teams want conflicting freshness, that is a business decision, and no architecture removes it.
rubricPoints: Turns vague wording into measurable targets such as freshness, query time, volume, and retention
Estimates current volume and growth, since these drive storage and query cost
Matches each measured demand to a pattern such as batch, streaming, warehouse, or archive
States a real limit, such as uncertain estimates or conflicting business priorities that need a decision

suggested.rationale: That design exercise asks you to turn stated needs for vehicle-position data into an ingest and read path, practising the same requirement-to-architecture mapping.

lessons.plain: Portability means you can move your data and applications to a different home without rebuilding them from scratch. Multicloud means running workloads across more than one cloud provider, often to avoid depending on a single vendor or to meet a customer's demands. Data residency means a rule that certain data must stay in a specific country or region. These pressures often pull against each other. The more you lean on one provider's special features, the harder it is to leave, and the fewer places you may legally keep a copy. Good design means choosing deliberately where lock-in is acceptable and where it is not.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company keeps customer order records in one cloud's analytics service. A regulator now says those records must stay in one country, and leadership wants the option to move to another cloud within a year. Which design choice would you expect to matter most for that goal, and why?
lessons.teach:
Portability is the ability to move data or an application to a different platform with limited rewriting. Lock-in is the opposite: the time and money it costs to leave a platform. Lock-in grows when you depend on something only one provider offers, such as a proprietary data format or a managed service with its own query dialect. Data residency is a rule that says where data may be stored or processed, usually a country or region. It limits portability because every copy you create, including backups and replicas, must still obey it.

Why it works: keep the durable copy in an open, widely readable format such as Parquet or Avro, keep transformations in standard SQL or a portable framework, and keep orchestration in a tool you can run elsewhere. The expensive part, the data, can then be read by many engines, and the cheaper part, the code, can be redeployed.

Worked example: a team exports daily orders as Parquet files into object storage in one approved region. Step 1: the files are in an open format, so any query engine can read them. Step 2: the daily transform is standard SQL, so it can run on a second engine. Step 3: the job runs from a container image, so a second cloud can host it. Step 4: before any copy lands in the second cloud, its storage location is checked against the residency rule. If all four hold, the move takes days instead of months.

Common mistake: assuming a multicloud design exists just because two clouds are in use. If the pipeline depends on one vendor's proprietary transform syntax, the second cloud is only a theoretical backup. Another mistake is forgetting that a disaster-recovery replica is still a copy and can break residency.

Consequence: when a residency rule or a price change arrives, a portable design lets you move data in a planned way. A locked-in design forces an emergency rewrite or a non-compliant copy.

questions.prompt: A Spanish clinic-software vendor stores nightly appointment summaries as CSV files in a Madrid-region bucket. The summary is standard SQL that runs from a container image, but it is scheduled by a proprietary workflow service that only one cloud offers. The goal is to restart the job on a second cloud within a few weeks if needed. Work through it: Step 1: the CSV files can be read by most query engines, so the stored data is portable. Step 2: the SQL can run on a second engine. Step 3: the container image can run on a second cloud. Step 4: the proprietary scheduler is the one part that cannot move, so it must be replaced with an orchestration tool the team can run elsewhere. Step 5: [missing]. Which completion fills step 5?
choices: Compress the CSV files before copying them, so the backup takes less time to transfer.
Rewrite the summary in the scheduler's proprietary language so it matches the new cloud.
Assume the backup is exempt from residency because it exists only for disaster recovery.
Before a backup copy of the summaries is written to a second cloud region, confirm its storage location satisfies the Spanish residency rule, since a replica is still a copy.
questions.why: Residency applies to every copy, including backups and replicas, so the backup's storage location must be checked against the rule before it is written.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is vendor lock-in?
choices: A file format that any query engine can read without conversion.
A backup copy kept in a second cloud so that a failed region can be replaced.
The time and money it costs to leave a platform, which grows when you depend on something only one provider offers.
A rule that says where data may be stored, usually a country or region.
questions.why: Lock-in is defined in the teaching text as the cost of leaving a platform, and it rises when a provider-only feature such as a proprietary format is in use.

questions.prompt: A German logistics company wants its nightly shipment report to stay portable. Which design best supports that goal?
choices: Store the raw data in a proprietary database format, and write the report in that database's own query dialect.
Store the raw data in a single region with no copies, and schedule the report with a tool that only runs inside one cloud.
Keep the report code in a vendor-only notebook format, and export the final results to a spreadsheet each day.
Store the raw data as Avro in an approved region, write the report in standard SQL, and run it from a container image.
questions.why: An open format for the durable data, standard SQL for the transform, and a container for the job together keep both the data and the code movable, which is the portable pattern the text describes.

questions.prompt: A team says its pipeline is multicloud because it runs in two clouds. Its transform, however, uses one vendor's proprietary syntax. What is the most accurate assessment?
choices: The design is portable, because running in two clouds guarantees the code can be moved.
The second cloud is effectively a theoretical backup, because the transform cannot run there without rewriting.
The design is multicloud, because the two clouds give the pipeline two places to run.
The design is only partly fixed, because the data format is the only thing that matters.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that using two clouds does not create a multicloud design when the transform depends on one vendor's proprietary syntax, so the second cloud cannot run the job without rewriting.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how you would decide whether a data pipeline is portable enough, and name one limit or tradeoff of pursuing portability.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would check three things. First, where the durable data lives and in what format. An open format that several engines can read keeps the data movable. Second, whether the transformations and orchestration use standard SQL or code that runs anywhere, or whether they depend on one provider's proprietary syntax or features. Third, every copy: primary data, backups, replicas, and logs must sit in regions the residency rule allows, and I would write that into the design rather than trusting people to remember it. The main tradeoff is that full portability costs something. Avoiding a provider's managed features often means more operating work, slower access to newer capabilities, and sometimes higher cost or lower performance. So I would make lock-in a deliberate choice for specific components, not an accident spread across the whole system.
rubricPoints: Identifies sources of lock-in such as proprietary formats, dialects, or managed features.
Explains that open formats and standard code keep data and pipelines movable.
Treats data residency as a limit on every copy, including backups and replicas.
Names a real tradeoff: portability can cost operating effort, feature access, or performance.
Chooses lock-in deliberately per component rather than by accident.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mainly a set of design principles and constraints, and no listed mission or planned engine directly drills portability trade-offs, so reading is the best fit.

lessons.plain: Before anyone can trust or find a pile of data, a team needs four things. Staging is a holding area where raw data lands as it arrived, before it is cleaned or moved on. Cataloging is keeping a searchable index of which datasets exist, who owns them, and what they mean. Profiling is measuring what the data actually looks like: how many values are empty, what range the numbers fall in, and which columns look like personal details. Discovery is how a person finds the right dataset in that index without having to ask around. Together these turn a folder of files into something an organization can govern. Think of a library: staging is the receiving dock, the catalog is the card index, profiling is checking each book's condition and contents, and discovery is the search desk.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has 400 datasets spread across several storage buckets and warehouse projects, and an auditor asks which ones contain customer email addresses. Without any special tooling, what would you need to find out, and what would make it hard?
lessons.teach:
Staging is the zone where raw data is kept in the form it was received, usually in a cheap object storage bucket with a clear name and a retention rule. Keeping it separate lets you reprocess data later and stops unchecked files from mixing with trusted tables. A catalog is a metadata store: it holds facts about datasets, such as name, owner, purpose, schema, and tags, but not the rows themselves. Metadata that describes what the data is called and means is business metadata; metadata about its structure is technical metadata. Profiling is an automated scan that computes statistics over the data, such as the share of empty values, distinct counts, minimum and maximum values, and whether values match a pattern like an email address. Discovery is searching the catalog by name, owner, or tag. On Google Cloud, the catalog and profiling capabilities are provided through Dataplex Universal Catalog, which was formerly Data Catalog; describe them generically as a metadata index and a measurement job. Who may read each dataset is a separate design decision.

Worked example: a raw orders file lands in a staging bucket on Monday. Step one, the team registers it in the catalog with an owner and a purpose. Step two, the field 'contains personal data' is set to unknown. Step three, a profiling scan runs over the table and finds that 97 percent of the email column matches an email pattern. Step four, a tag 'personal data' is attached, so a discovery search for that tag now returns the dataset.

Common mistake: treating the catalog as a one-time spreadsheet. Once nobody re-profiles or updates tags, a dataset tagged 'no personal data' can silently gain a new column, and a search for personal data misses it. In a running system, that gap means a retention or access rule is never applied to the data it was meant to protect. Profiling is evidence about the data at scan time, and the catalog is only as current as its last update.

questions.prompt: A retail chain's loyalty team keeps a copy of each day's member sign-up file, unchanged, in a staging bucket with a 90-day retention rule. Step one: in March the team registers the dataset in the catalog with an owner and a purpose, and attaches the tag 'personal data' after a profiling scan. Step two: in June the vendor adds a new column called date_of_birth to the file, and the file continues to land daily. Step three is missing. What should the team do next so the catalog still describes the data accurately?
choices: Re-run the profiling scan on the updated file and update the catalog entry so the new column is described and tagged.
Delete the staging bucket, since a new column means the raw file can no longer be trusted.
Move the file into the trusted reporting table so the new column is checked during loading.
Nothing, because the existing 'personal data' tag already covers the whole dataset.
questions.why: The catalog only reflects the data as of its last update, so after a schema change the team must re-profile and update the entry so the new column is described and covered by the right tags.

questions.prompt: For a table of hotel room bookings, which item is technical metadata rather than business metadata?
choices: A tag marking the table as containing guest contact details.
A sentence explaining what a 'booking' means to the finance department.
The owning team's name and the stated purpose of the table.
The column data types and the partition key used to organise the table.
questions.why: Technical metadata describes structure, such as data types and keys, while the owner, purpose, meaning, and tags are business-facing descriptions.

questions.prompt: A bank lands a daily file of wire transfers in a staging zone. Which practice best keeps that staging zone useful for reprocessing later?
choices: Delete the raw file as soon as the first successful load finishes.
Keep the file as received, with a clear name and a retention rule.
Overwrite the raw file with cleaned rows so the bucket stays small.
Store the raw files in the same dataset as the trusted reporting tables.
questions.why: Staging keeps data in its received form under a clear name and retention rule so it can be reprocessed, and overwriting or deleting it would remove the ability to reprocess.

questions.prompt: In March a team tagged a customer table 'no personal data' in the catalog. In June a column of email addresses was added to the table, and a discovery search for personal data no longer returns it. What is the root cause?
choices: The search index is faulty and must be rebuilt by the vendor.
The email column should have been kept in staging instead of the customer table.
The tag reflects the data as of its last update, and nobody re-profiled or updated it.
The catalog cannot store tags for tables that have more than one column.
questions.why: A catalog is only as current as its last update, and profiling is evidence about the data at scan time, so an unrefreshed tag silently misses a newly added sensitive column.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how staging, cataloging, profiling, and discovery work together for governance, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on profiling to find sensitive data.
lessons.modelAnswer: Staging keeps raw data exactly as received in a separate landing area with a known retention period, so we can reprocess it later and so unchecked files are not mixed with curated tables. The catalog records each dataset's owner, purpose, and tags, so there is one place that answers what exists and who is responsible. Profiling measures the actual content: null rates, value ranges, and pattern matches such as email formats. That turns a belief like 'this table has no personal data' into a measured fact and lets us attach a tag. Discovery lets people find datasets by those tags, which is how a governance rule gets applied to the right data. The tradeoff is that profiling reflects the data only at scan time, so it can miss a new column that arrived later. Pattern matching can also produce false positives, such as a code that looks like an email. So we schedule re-scans and treat tags as evidence to review, not as proof.
rubricPoints: Staging holds raw data as received, separate from curated data, with a retention period
The catalog records owner, purpose, and tags so datasets can be found and held accountable
Profiling measures actual content such as null rates and pattern matches, turning assumptions into evidence
Profiling is a point-in-time measurement, so it needs scheduled re-scans and can produce false positives

suggested.rationale: An exam-style scenario asking where each governance step belongs in the architecture adds the most value here, and no listed mission covers catalog or profiling work directly.

lessons.plain: Before anyone moves a data system to a new home, someone has to write down what the finished version should do for the people who rely on it. This objective is about gathering that picture: who depends on the data, what work they do with it, which business steps run around it, and what technology is in place today. You turn those answers into a clear description of the desired end state, meaning the target system you intend to reach. Good migration planning starts with people and processes, not with the new tool.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team wants to move its nightly sales reports from an old on-premises database to a cloud platform. Before choosing any new service, what is the first thing you would want to find out, and why?
lessons.teach:
A stakeholder is anyone who has a stake in the outcome: the people who pay for the system, approve changes, or get hurt when it breaks. A user is someone who touches the data directly, such as an analyst running queries or a manager reading a dashboard. A process is a sequence of steps that happens around the data, often on a schedule, such as a nightly load or a month-end close. The technology inventory is the list of what exists today: databases, scripts, file shares, scheduled jobs, and the links between them. The desired end state is the target you plan to reach, described in terms of outcomes like freshness, deadlines, and who can do what, before any product is picked.

Worked example. A fictional company, Lumen Parts, has a nightly stock report. Step 1: list stakeholders. The finance owner needs figures by 6:30 each morning. Step 2: list users. Three analysts query ad hoc, and forty store managers read a dashboard. Step 3: trace processes. A load runs at 1 a.m., finance closes its books at 6 a.m., and a spreadsheet macro reads an export at 6:30. Step 4: inventory technology. An old database, cron scripts, and a file share. Step 5: write the end state: the dashboard refreshes by 6:30, analysts see data no older than the last load, and the macro is replaced by a published export. The macro appears in no documentation; it surfaces only when someone asks what reads the export.

The common mistake is copying the old system one for one, or choosing the end state from the tool the team likes best. Both skip the question of what people need. In a running system, the cost is concrete. If the macro is missed, the first Monday after cutover leaves finance with no 6:30 file, and the close slips for the whole company.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Clinics runs a weekly no-show report. A stakeholder is anyone with a stake in the outcome, such as the people who pay for or depend on the system. Stakeholders: the operations director needs the list of missed appointments by 8 a.m. Monday. Users: 25 scheduling coordinators filter the list in a shared spreadsheet to plan Monday's reminder calls, and two regional managers read a summary. Processes: a Saturday 11 p.m. export pulls appointments from the scheduling server, and on Sunday the billing team reconciles that export against invoices. Technology inventory: a legacy scheduling server, a weekly export script, and a shared folder. Step 5, which is still missing, is to write the desired end state, described as outcomes such as freshness, deadlines, and who can do what, before any product is chosen. Which statement completes step 5?
choices: Move the scheduling server to a new cloud VM with the same export script so the export matches the old one exactly, then pick a warehouse later.
The no-show list is published whenever the export job finishes, with no fixed deadline, since the reconciliation is handled separately by billing.
The call list refreshes by 7 a.m. Monday for the coordinators, the managers keep read access to the summary, and the billing reconciliation gets a published export it can read on Sunday.
Choose a data warehouse because the analytics team prefers it, and let the coordinators decide their own refresh times.
questions.why: The correct end state names the deadline, who sees what, and the billing team's dependency on the export, which is what step 5 requires, while the other options either copy the old system or pick a product or drop the deadline.

questions.prompt: In the sense used for migration planning, which of the following is a process rather than a stakeholder, user, or technology item?
choices: The reporting database and the cron jobs that feed it.
The chief financial officer who approves the budget for the new system.
A weekly sequence in which a load runs, a team reconciles the output, and a reminder list is sent out on a set schedule.
A shared spreadsheet that an analyst opens to filter yesterday's orders.
questions.why: A process is a sequence of steps that happens around the data, often on a schedule, which matches the scheduled load-reconcile-send chain, while the others are a person who has a stake, a user touching data, and inventory items.

questions.prompt: A team migrating a regional insurer's claims reporting copies its old reporting server one for one into the cloud and says the design is done because the output matches. What is the most likely consequence, based on the planning approach of listing stakeholders, users, processes, and technology before picking a product?
choices: The team will be forced to pick the most expensive cloud product, raising costs but keeping all outputs unchanged.
Undocumented readers and processes that depended on the old server can be left out, so a downstream consumer may miss its file and a close or deadline can slip.
The cloud copy will run faster than the old server, so no one will notice the missing deadlines.
Nothing changes, because copying the system one for one is exactly what planning is meant to produce.
questions.why: Copying one for one skips the question of what people need, so a dependency nobody documented, such as a macro or a reconciliation that reads an export, can break without warning and cause a missed deadline.

questions.prompt: Before choosing any cloud product for a migration, a planner finds that a monthly export file is read by a spreadsheet macro that appears in no documentation. Which action best fits the planning approach?
choices: Ignore the macro, because the desired end state should be chosen from the tool the team likes best.
Ask who or what reads the export and when, so the macro is captured as a process or user need and included in the end state.
Wait until after cutover, then fix any complaints as they arrive.
Delete the export, since nothing documented depends on it, and see whether anyone complains.
questions.why: Hidden readers only surface when someone asks what consumes an output, so tracing dependencies before writing the end state is what protects the downstream process.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a migration plan should describe the desired end state from stakeholder needs, users, processes, and technology before choosing a target service, and name one limit or tradeoff of doing this discovery work.
lessons.modelAnswer: We should describe the end state first because the target service only matters in relation to what people need from the data. If we pick a service first, we tend to rebuild the old system in new packaging and miss the jobs and dependencies nobody wrote down. Discovery means asking stakeholders what outcomes they need, listing users and how they access data, mapping the processes that run on a schedule, and inventorying the technology that exists today. The main limit is that discovery takes time and can never be complete. Some dependencies only show up after cutover, so the plan should include a validation period and a way to roll back. Discovery also needs boundaries: we record requirements, but we do not yet choose security controls or disaster-recovery design, which are separate decisions.
rubricPoints: Defines the desired end state as outcomes for stakeholders and users, chosen before the target technology
Names the four inputs: stakeholders, users, processes, and technology inventory
Explains that hidden dependencies are common and why copying the old system is risky
Names a real limit, such as discovery being incomplete until after cutover, and a mitigation

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers migration discovery, and explaining the end state back to a teammate is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: Moving data into Google Cloud is less like copying a folder and more like moving a household. You decide what goes, how fast it moves, how you will prove nothing was lost, and whether the old house keeps running during the move. Google Cloud offers several tools for different parts of that job. Some copy data on a schedule, some keep a database in sync while the original stays live, some ship a physical storage box when the network would take too long, and some connect your environment to Google Cloud privately. Planning means matching each tool to the data's size, how often it changes, and how much downtime the business can tolerate, then checking the result against the source.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company must move 200 TB of old log archives to Google Cloud, and the office internet link is slow. Before reading on, which would you try first, copying over the network or shipping a physical storage device, and what would you need to know to decide?
lessons.teach:
A migration plan answers three questions: how the data gets there, how it stays current until the switch, and how you prove the copy matches the source. Each tool covers a different part.

BigQuery Data Transfer Service is a managed scheduler that loads data into BigQuery from supported sources on a recurring basis, so you do not write and run the loader yourself. Database Migration Service is a managed way to move an operational database such as MySQL or PostgreSQL, keeping a replica continuously synced until you cut over to it. Datastream is a managed change data capture service: it reads the change log of a source database and streams each insert, update and delete onward, typically into BigQuery or Cloud Storage. Transfer Appliance is a physical storage device that Google ships to you; you load it locally and ship it back for upload, which wins when the data is very large and the network is slow. Networking, meaning private connectivity between your on-premises network and your Google Cloud virtual network, decides whether an online transfer is fast enough and whether data crosses the public internet.

Why it works: a continuous tool lets the source keep serving traffic while the copy catches up, so downtime is limited to the final cutover. A bulk tool trades time in transit for bandwidth you do not have.

Worked example: a 40 TB archive over a 1 Gbps link. Step 1: 40 TB is about 320 terabits. Step 2: at 1 Gbps that is about 320,000 seconds, roughly 3.7 days at full speed, and longer in practice. Step 3: estimate shipping and upload time for an appliance. If the appliance route is faster and the data is static, choose it.

Common mistake: declaring the migration complete after the bulk copy finishes, without capturing changes made during the copy and without comparing row counts and checksums between source and target.

Consequence: a cutover that skips this reconciliation can leave the new system missing recent orders, and the gap may not be noticed until customers report it.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm has 25 TB of static shipment logs on premises, reachable over a 200 Mbps link. Step 1: 25 TB is 200 terabits (25 times 8). Step 2: 200 terabits at 200 Mbps is 1,000,000 seconds, about 11.6 days at full speed. Step 3 is missing. The team estimates an appliance round trip, including shipping and upload, at 9 days for this static data. Which conclusion completes step 3?
choices: Choose the appliance, because its 9-day estimate beats the 11.6-day network time for static data.
Split the logs by year and run both routes at once, since step 3 has no single answer.
Keep the network copy, because 11.6 days is always shorter than any appliance trip.
Choose the network copy, because a physical appliance cannot hold logs of this size.
questions.why: The method is to compare the estimated full-speed network time with the appliance's shipping-and-upload estimate, and for static data the faster route is the right choice, which here is the appliance at 9 days.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches Datastream as this course uses the term?
choices: A physical storage device that Google ships to you for offline upload.
A managed service that reads a source database's change log and streams each insert, update and delete onward.
A private connection between an on-premises network and a Google Cloud virtual network.
A scheduler that runs a recurring loader into BigQuery on a fixed timetable.
questions.why: Datastream is a managed change data capture service, meaning it follows the source database's change log and forwards each change, which is different from the device, scheduler, or network link named in the other options.

questions.prompt: A team must keep a MySQL source database serving live traffic while a synced copy is maintained in Google Cloud, so that downtime is limited to the final switch. Which tool fits this requirement best?
choices: A one-time Cloud Storage bulk copy script run over the weekend.
Transfer Appliance, which ships a physical device to Google for upload.
BigQuery Data Transfer Service, which loads data on a recurring schedule into BigQuery.
Database Migration Service, which keeps a managed replica continuously synced until cutover.
questions.why: Only the continuous replication tool keeps the copy current while the source keeps serving traffic, which is what limits downtime to the cutover; the other options are bulk or scheduled loaders that do not keep a live copy in sync.

questions.prompt: A team bulk-copied 12 TB from its source database and then cut over to the new system without comparing row counts or checking changes made during the copy. What is the main risk?
choices: The network link will be too slow for the copy to ever finish.
BigQuery will refuse to load the tables because the copy was not verified.
The shipped appliance will return too late to be used for the cutover.
Changes made during the copy are missing from the new system, and the gap may go unnoticed until users report it.
questions.why: A bulk copy captures only a snapshot, so changes made during the copy are lost unless they are captured and reconciled, and skipping the row count and checksum comparison means nothing flags the gap before cutover.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between a continuous replication tool and a physical transfer for moving a production database to Google Cloud. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the cutover window and the change rate. If the database takes writes all day and downtime is limited to a few minutes, I would use a continuous tool such as Database Migration Service or Datastream. It copies the existing data, then keeps applying changes from the source until we switch over, so the only outage is the final cutover. The tradeoff is that it depends on a steady network path and needs the source change log enabled, and it adds ongoing load while it runs. If the data is a large static archive that would take days to move over the link, I would consider Transfer Appliance instead. Its limit is that the data is only as current as the day the device was loaded, so it cannot keep a live database in sync. Whichever route I pick, I would reconcile row counts and checksums before cutover.
rubricPoints: Matches the tool to whether the data changes during the move and how much downtime is acceptable
Explains that continuous replication captures changes until cutover, limiting downtime to the switch
Names a real limit of the rejected option, such as a physical device being stale on arrival or a network path being slow
Mentions validating the migrated data against the source before switching over

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly product selection and migration facts with no listed mission or planned engine that practises it directly.

lessons.plain: A data pipeline moves data from where it is made to where it is used. The source is the place data comes from, such as an app sending events, a file drop from a partner, or a database. The sink is the place the pipeline finally writes its output, such as a table for analysts or a folder of files kept for later. Naming both ends first tells you what must be read, what must be written, how quickly data arrives, and how it must be stored. Think of a post office: the sender is the source, the letterbox where the letter ends up is the sink, and the sorting in between is the processing.
lessons.guessPrompt: A mobile app sends a rating each time a user taps a star, and a finance team needs a daily total of ratings by region. For each of the two data flows, name the source and the sink, and say whether the data arrives continuously or in periodic batches.
lessons.teach:
A source is the place where a pipeline's data originates, such as an application that emits events, a database table, a partner's file drop, or a sensor feed. A sink is the place where the pipeline finally writes its output, such as a data warehouse table, a set of files in object storage, or a low-latency key-value store. Data is bounded when it has a known end, like yesterday's order file, and unbounded when it never stops, like a live stream of events. The latency requirement states how quickly data must be usable after it is produced, and that number drives the choice of ingestion pattern.

Why it works: once you name the source and the sink, the rest follows. A continuous stream from producers that must not be lost while a consumer is busy is usually pushed into a managed messaging service, which buffers events until they are processed. A sink is chosen by how it will be read. Lookups of one record by key suit a store built for that, questions across millions of rows suit a warehouse, and cheap long-term copies of raw data suit object storage.

Worked example: a bus company receives a GPS ping from each vehicle every five seconds. Step 1: the source is the vehicle tracker publishing pings, so the data is unbounded. Step 2: dispatch needs the current position within seconds, so the pattern is streaming. Step 3: dispatch looks up one vehicle at a time, so one sink is a low-latency key-value store such as Bigtable. Step 4: the company also needs raw history for audits and replays, so a second sink is Cloud Storage files.

Common mistake: choosing a sink because it is familiar, such as loading a live stream into a warehouse designed for nightly batch loads, then discovering that answers arrive hours late. Another is assuming one source needs only one sink, when the same data often serves both live use and archives.

In a running system, a sink that cannot absorb the write rate makes the pipeline fall behind, and the buffer in front of it grows until data is delayed or dropped.

questions.prompt: A wind farm fits each turbine with a vibration sensor that reports a reading every second, with no planned end. Engineers need an alert within 10 seconds if vibration rises past a safe level, and analysts later study months of readings to spot slow wear. Worked example: Step 1: the source is the sensor feed, which never stops, so the data is unbounded. Step 2: alerts must arrive within 10 seconds, so the pattern is streaming. Step 3 (to complete): the analysts run queries that scan many months of readings across all turbines, so the sink for that use is a data warehouse table, meaning a database built for large queries over many rows. Step 4: the farm also keeps a raw copy of every reading in object storage, which holds files cheaply for replay.
choices: A data warehouse table, because the analysts run queries that scan many months of rows
Object storage files, because they are cheap to keep
A key-value store, because the analysts look up one reading at a time
A managed messaging topic, because it keeps the readings until someone reads them
questions.why: Queries that scan large numbers of rows across months suit a warehouse, while a key-value store suits single-record lookups and a messaging topic is a buffer rather than a place to analyse data.

questions.prompt: A university's registrar receives a single file each night containing the complete list of the term's enrolments, and the file is final once it has arrived. How should this source be classified?
choices: Unbounded, because the records arrive over time
It depends on the file size
Unbounded, because it recurs every night
Bounded, because the file has a known end
questions.why: Bounded data has a known end, and a complete nightly file that is final once received is bounded regardless of how often it arrives.

questions.prompt: A ride-share app streams account events into a fraud check. The check must read one account's recent profile by account ID in under 20 milliseconds. Separately, the company must keep every raw event for seven years at low cost. Which sink fits the profile lookups?
choices: A low-latency key-value store, because the lookups are by account ID
A shared spreadsheet export refreshed daily
Object storage files, because they are the cheapest option
A data warehouse table, because it holds the most data
questions.why: A low-latency key-value store is built for fast retrieval of one record by its key, which is exactly the access pattern described, while the seven-year archive belongs in object storage as a separate sink.

questions.prompt: An IoT pipeline writes sensor readings to a sink that can absorb 2,000 writes per second, but the sensors send 6,000 readings per second during peak hours. What happens in the running system?
choices: The sink speeds up automatically to match the incoming rate
The sink rejects the producers' events so they never enter the pipeline
The pipeline switches itself to batch mode and the backlog clears on its own
The buffer in front of the sink grows, so data is delayed or eventually dropped
questions.why: When the sink cannot keep up with the write rate, the buffer ahead of it fills, which delays or drops data, and nothing in this setup adjusts the sink's capacity or switches modes automatically.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide the source and the sink for a new data feed, and name one limit or tradeoff of the sink you would pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by describing the source: who produces the data, whether it arrives as a continuous stream or as bounded files, and how big and how frequent it is. Then I ask how fresh the answer must be, because that sets whether the pipeline is streaming or batch. Next I look at how the output will be read. Lookups of one record by key point to a low-latency store, analytical questions across large tables point to a warehouse, and long-term raw copies point to cheap object storage. Often I pick more than one sink. The tradeoff I would name is cost and consistency: a low-latency store is fast for single-key reads but is not built for ad hoc analysis, so analysts would need a second copy, and that copy can lag behind the first.
rubricPoints: Names the source and states whether its data is bounded or unbounded
Links the latency requirement to a batch or streaming pattern
Chooses each sink by its read pattern, such as key lookups, analytics, or archives
States a concrete tradeoff of the chosen sink, such as cost, query style, or freshness lag

suggested.rationale: Choosing a source and sink from a described feed and a latency target is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario, and no existing mission covers it directly.

lessons.plain: Data transformation is the work that changes raw data into something more useful: dropping bad rows, adding up totals, joining two sources together, or converting units. Orchestration is the coordination around those steps: deciding which step runs first, which steps can run at the same time, what happens when one fails, and when the whole chain should start. Think of a kitchen. Chopping, cooking and plating are transformations, and the order ticket that tells each cook when to start is orchestration. This lesson covers the logic of both, not the specific tools that run them.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job must (1) copy yesterday's raw sales files, (2) remove duplicate orders, and (3) build a daily revenue total that runs only after step 2 finishes successfully. Which of these parts is the transformation, and which part is the orchestration? Say why in one sentence.
lessons.teach:
A transformation is a step that takes records in and produces different records out. Common kinds are filtering (keep only some rows), mapping (change each row, such as converting currency), aggregating (combine many rows into a summary, such as a daily total), and joining (match rows from two sources on a shared key). Orchestration is the logic that decides when each transformation runs, in what order, what it waits for, and what happens when one fails. The two are separate concerns: the transformation says what to do to the data, and the orchestration says when and in which sequence.

Orchestration is usually modelled as a DAG, a directed acyclic graph. Each task is a node, each dependency is an arrow pointing from the task that must finish first to the task that waits, and no arrow may loop back. A task starts only when its upstream tasks succeed, so the graph itself prevents a step from reading half-finished input. Steps with no arrow between them can run in parallel.

Worked example. A nightly job processes 500 raw order rows for one day. Step 1 filters out rows with a missing order ID, leaving 488. Step 2 removes duplicate order IDs, leaving 480. Step 3 sums revenue per store and depends on step 2. Step 4 publishes the totals and depends on step 3. If step 2 fails, steps 3 and 4 never start, and only step 2 is retried.

Common mistake: scheduling each step at a fixed clock time, such as aggregation at 02:00 and deduplication at 01:30. If deduplication runs long, aggregation reads duplicated rows and the totals are inflated. The fix is to express the order as dependencies rather than wall-clock guesses.

In a running system, a wrong dependency fails silently. Nothing crashes, the dashboard simply shows revenue that is too high, and nobody is alerted because every step reported success. Defining the transformation and its ordering together is what keeps results both correct and explainable.

questions.prompt: A regional bike-share company runs a nightly pipeline on 1,200 trip records from yesterday. Task 1 drops trips with a zero or missing duration, leaving 1,140 rows. Task 2 joins the remaining trips to a station table on station_id, and every trip finds a match. Task 3 computes average trip minutes per station and must wait for Task 2. Task 4 emails the report and must wait for Task 3. Task 5 counts bikes returned at each station and has no arrow connecting it to any other task, so it can run alongside the others. Suppose Task 2 fails. Task 3 does not start because ____, and Task 5 keeps running because ____.
choices: Task 3 is a mapping task and mappings cannot run after a failure, and Task 5 keeps running because it reads the raw trip table directly
Task 3 has an arrow from Task 2 and only starts when Task 2 succeeds, and Task 5 keeps running because no arrow links it to the failed Task 2
Task 3 is scheduled for a fixed clock time later in the night, and Task 5 keeps running because it has a retry policy of its own
Task 3 is waiting on Task 1 as well as Task 2, and Task 5 keeps running because Task 1 already finished successfully
questions.why: A task starts only when its upstream tasks succeed, so Task 3 is held back by its arrow from the failed Task 2, while Task 5 has no dependency on Task 2 and so is unaffected.

questions.prompt: In data pipeline design, which statement correctly separates orchestration from transformation?
choices: Transformation and orchestration are the same thing, and the word orchestration only refers to storing the output of a join
Orchestration is only the process of copying files from one storage bucket to another before any filtering begins
Transformation says what to do to the records, such as filtering or joining, while orchestration says when each step runs, in what order, and what happens on failure
Orchestration decides what each record looks like after conversion, and transformation decides which tasks may run in parallel
questions.why: The separation is that transformations define the work on the data while orchestration controls timing, sequence, and failure handling.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company's pipeline has four tasks: Task A joins sales records to event records on event_id, Task B sums revenue per venue after Task A, Task C publishes the venue totals after Task B, and Task D counts refunds per venue with no arrow to any other task. The team sets Task B to start at 03:00 and Task A to start at 02:30, reasoning that 30 minutes is plenty. Task A takes 45 minutes on a busy night. What is the most likely result, and what change fixes it?
choices: Task C publishes before Task B finishes, so the fix is to remove Task C entirely from the pipeline
Nothing goes wrong because the 30-minute gap guarantees Task A finishes first, so no change is needed
Task B reads incomplete join output and produces understated revenue, so the fix is to make Task B depend on Task A instead of relying on the clock
Task A is cancelled automatically by the scheduler, so the fix is to move Task D to run before Task A
questions.why: Fixed clock times do not wait for the upstream task, so a slow Task A lets Task B read incomplete data; expressing the order as a dependency ensures Task B starts only after Task A succeeds.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's pipeline aggregates parcel scans into daily hub totals. One task that filters out test scans fails silently in the sense that it writes an empty file, but the scheduler marks it as succeeded. The downstream aggregation then produces totals with no test scans removed, and those totals are too high. Which statement best explains why this problem is hard to notice?
choices: Because the task reported success, nothing triggers an alert, and the dashboard shows inflated totals that look plausible, so the error stays hidden until someone checks the numbers
Aggregation tasks cannot process files that contain fewer rows, so they crash whenever a filter returns nothing, which alerts the team immediately
Filtering tasks never affect aggregation, so the totals would stay correct even if the filter produced the wrong output
The scheduler automatically reruns any task whose output is empty, so the totals are corrected before anyone sees them
questions.why: A wrong dependency or wrong upstream output fails silently when every step reports success, so the inflated totals appear normal and go unalerted.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between transformation logic and orchestration logic in a data pipeline, and name one limit or tradeoff of modelling the pipeline as a DAG.
lessons.modelAnswer: Transformation logic is what happens to the data: filtering bad rows, deduplicating, aggregating, joining, or enriching. Orchestration logic is when and in what order those steps run, including what each step waits for, how retries work, and what gets skipped when something fails. In a DAG, the orchestrator reads the dependency arrows and starts a task only after its upstream tasks have succeeded, which lets independent branches run in parallel. The main limit is that a DAG does not naturally express loops or branches that depend on data produced during the same run, so a step that must repeat until a condition holds needs a different pattern. Another tradeoff is that the DAG only guarantees ordering between tasks it declares. If a real dependency is missing from the graph, the pipeline runs in the wrong order and the problem only shows up in the output.
rubricPoints: Separates what the transformation does to the data from when and in what order steps run.
Names at least one transformation type such as filter, deduplicate, aggregate, or join.
Explains that a DAG starts a task only after its upstream dependencies succeed.
States a limit, such as loops or data-dependent branching being awkward, or missing dependencies causing wrong ordering.

suggested.rationale: The planned workflow state machine would let the learner trace ordered steps, dependencies, and failure paths, which is the core of orchestration logic.

lessons.plain: A data pipeline is a chain of machines that moves data from where it starts to where it is stored or analyzed. Those machines talk to each other and to outside services over a network, much like your laptop talks to a website. Networking fundamentals are the basic rules that decide which machines can reach which others, what address each one has, and whether traffic can leave the private space to reach services outside it. If these rules are wrong, a pipeline can look healthy on paper and still sit stuck, unable to read its input or write its output. Knowing the basics lets you check the network before blaming the code.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your pipeline's worker machines have no public IP address and sit on a private network. The job needs to read files from a managed cloud storage service run by the provider. Before reading on, what do you think could go wrong, and what would you check first?
lessons.teach:
A virtual private network, or VPC network, is an isolated network you define inside a cloud provider. Within it, a subnet is a range of private IP addresses tied to one region, and every machine in that subnet gets an internal IP address. Internal addresses are reachable only from inside the network. An external IP address is a public address that the internet can reach. A firewall rule allows or blocks traffic based on direction, port, and source. Egress means traffic leaving a machine. Private Google Access is a subnet setting that lets machines with only internal IPs reach the provider's own managed services, such as storage and messaging, without a public address. Cloud NAT is a managed gateway that lets private machines make outbound connections to the internet, without accepting inbound connections from it.

Worked example. A batch pipeline's workers run in a subnet with no external IPs. Step 1: a worker starts and asks the storage service for its input file. Step 2: the request needs an outbound path to the provider's storage address. Step 3: with no external IP, no NAT, and Private Google Access switched off, there is no route, so the request times out. Step 4: the worker retries, and the whole job sits in startup with zero throughput. Turning on Private Google Access for that subnet gives the workers a path to the services they need while they stay private. Workers also need a firewall rule that lets them reach each other on the ports used for shuffling data between them.

Common mistake: assuming that a private subnet cannot reach Google services at all, or assuming that adding public IPs to every worker is the only fix. Public IPs widen the attack surface and cost money, and Private Google Access is usually the cleaner answer.

Consequence: a streaming pipeline in this state stops consuming messages, and backlog grows. A batch job often looks hung rather than failing with a clear error, so checking routes, subnet settings, and firewall rules is the first diagnostic step.

questions.prompt: A retail company runs stream processors on VMs (virtual machines, which are rented computers) in a subnet called checkout-proc. A subnet is a range of private IP addresses tied to one region. These VMs have only internal IP addresses, there is no Cloud NAT gateway (a managed gateway for outbound internet connections), and Private Google Access (a subnet setting that lets private machines reach the provider's own managed services) is switched off. Step 1: a processor starts and needs to publish order events to the messaging service. Step 2: the publish request needs an outbound route to the messaging service's address. Step 3: [missing step: the one setting that gives the request a route to the service without a public address]. Step 4: the publish succeeds and the processor begins consuming events. Which statement fills step 3?
choices: Each processor is given an external IP, which the messaging service requires before it accepts a publish
Cloud NAT is set to accept inbound connections so the messaging service can call back the processor
Private Google Access is on for checkout-proc, so no public address is needed
The subnet's firewall is changed to allow inbound connections from the internet on port 443
questions.why: Private Google Access on the subnet provides the outbound path to the managed messaging service, which is the missing route in step 3, while the other choices either add inbound exposure or public addresses that are not needed.

questions.prompt: A batch team's ingestion VMs in the subnet ledger-ingest have only internal IP addresses (private addresses used inside a network). Which statement about them is true?
choices: Internal addresses are reachable from the internet once a firewall rule allows port 443 to them
Internal addresses are public addresses that the messaging service assigns to each VM
Internal addresses are reachable only from inside the network, so an outside client cannot connect to the VM directly
A subnet's internal range can be shared across several regions to simplify failover
questions.why: Internal addresses belong to a private network and are reachable only from inside it, whereas public addresses are the ones the internet can reach.

questions.prompt: A nightly batch job runs on workers in a subnet with no external IP addresses, no Cloud NAT gateway, and Private Google Access switched off. Workers reading their input bucket hang at startup and show no error. Which change is the cleanest fix?
choices: Double the number of workers so the startup queue drains faster
Turn on Private Google Access for the subnet so workers reach the storage service without a public address
Add a firewall rule allowing inbound traffic from all sources on every port
Give every worker a public IP so each has a direct internet path
questions.why: The workers lack any route to the storage service, and Private Google Access fixes that without adding public exposure, unlike public IPs, inbound rules, or more workers.

questions.prompt: A VM named shuffle-7 must send data to shuffle-9 on port 5050 (a numbered network port), and both sit in the same subnet. A firewall rule allows or blocks traffic based on direction, port, and source. Which rule lets shuffle-9 accept that traffic?
choices: Private Google Access enabled on the subnet, which opens internal ports between peers
An external IP on shuffle-9 so that traffic from shuffle-7 can reach it
An inbound allow rule for port 5050 whose source is shuffle-7's subnet range, applied to shuffle-9
An outbound allow rule for port 5050 applied only to shuffle-9
questions.why: Receiving traffic at shuffle-9 is controlled by an inbound rule matching the port and the sender's source range, while an outbound rule on shuffle-9 governs what it sends and Private Google Access is unrelated to peer traffic.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that putting the pipeline's workers on a private network makes the data safe and needs no other network setup. Explain in your own words what internal addresses and a private subnet do and do not give you, and name one networking limit or tradeoff they should plan for.
lessons.modelAnswer: A private subnet gives the workers only internal addresses, so nothing on the internet can open a connection to them directly. That reduces exposure, but it does not make the pipeline work by itself. The workers still need a route to the managed services they read from and write to, and that route has to be set up on purpose, either with Private Google Access on the subnet or with a NAT gateway for other outbound traffic. Firewall rules also still need to allow traffic between workers. The tradeoff is that privacy and reachability have to be designed together. Each new source or sink can need a new route or rule, and a missing one usually shows up as a stalled job or timeouts rather than a clear error message.
rubricPoints: Internal addresses keep workers unreachable from the internet but do not by themselves grant any outbound access.
