Common mistake: rebuilding the artifact separately for each environment, so the tested version is not the shipped version. Another is testing only the code and ignoring schema and configuration changes.

Consequence: redeploying a streaming job without a tested version and a rollback plan can leave downstream tables incomplete or duplicated, so recovery planning matters as much as the tests.

The rule to remember: test the exact artifact you will ship, and promote that same artifact through each environment.

questions.prompt: A freight company runs a nightly batch load into a warehouse table. A developer changes three things at once: the transform code, the table schema (renaming the column customer_id to cust_id), and the scheduler config (moving the run from 01:00 to 04:00). The team's CI pipeline only runs unit tests on the transform code. Trace what happens. Step 1: the developer pushes all three changes. Step 2: CI runs the transform tests on 12 sample rows and they all pass. Step 3 is missing from this trace and is the one you must supply. Step 4: CI builds one versioned artifact (v2.4.0) that bundles the code, schema, and schedule together. Step 5: that same artifact is deployed to a staging environment. Which step 3 is needed so that a renamed column breaking a downstream query is caught before anything is packaged?
choices: CI rebuilds the artifact separately for production so the new 04:00 schedule takes effect there without affecting staging.
The scheduler change is applied by hand after deployment so the nightly job keeps its old timing while the code is tested.
CI validates the schema and scheduler files against the sample data, so a rename that a downstream query depends on fails the build before packaging.
Nothing is needed, because a schema change is only metadata and cannot break a query that reads the table.
questions.why: Because the teaching text says a pipeline is more than code and that schema and configuration changes must be tested too, validating them in CI before packaging is what catches the broken rename.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines continuous delivery for a data pipeline?
choices: Every change is released to production automatically the moment it is shared with the team.
Every change is built from scratch in each environment so that each copy matches its target.
Every change that passes the automated checks is packaged the same way each time and can be released on demand.
Every change is tested only by the person who wrote it before it is merged into the main branch.
questions.why: The teaching text defines continuous delivery as packaging every change that passes checks the same way each time so it can be released on demand, which matches only the third option.

questions.prompt: A team tests its streaming job's artifact in staging, then rebuilds a fresh copy from the same source for production. Which risk does this create?
choices: The version that was tested may differ from the version that ships, so the tests no longer prove production is safe.
The engine will refuse to run the job because it expects a single environment.
The production job will run more slowly because the build is newer.
The scheduling definition will be deleted from the project during the rebuild.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that rebuilding per environment means the tested version is not the shipped version, which is exactly the gap the first option describes.

questions.prompt: A developer changes only a partition setting in a pipeline's job configuration and leaves the transform code untouched. Which approach follows the rule of testing what you will ship?
choices: Include the configuration in the versioned artifact and in the automated checks, then promote that same artifact through each environment.
Deploy the configuration change directly to production and test the code only in the next release.
Skip the tests, since no code changed and the configuration is not part of the pipeline.
Run only the transform unit tests, because configuration is set by the platform and cannot affect results.
questions.why: The teaching text says a pipeline includes job configuration and scheduling definitions, so these must be tested and packaged in the same versioned artifact that is promoted unchanged.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how continuous integration and continuous delivery apply to a data pipeline, and name one limit of automated testing for pipelines.
lessons.modelAnswer: CI means that every change to the pipeline code, its table definitions and its job configuration is built and tested automatically when it is shared, so problems show up within minutes. CD means the checked change is packaged once as a versioned artifact and then moved through environments, a test environment first and production after, without being rebuilt by hand. For a data pipeline, the tests usually run the transformation on a small sample with expected output, and the staging run uses production-shaped data. The main limit is that tests only cover the cases someone thought of. A pipeline can pass every unit test and still fail on real data with unexpected nulls, late records or a changed upstream schema. That is why staging runs, schema checks and monitoring after release are still needed. Rollback also needs a plan, because a streaming job that has already written bad rows may need cleanup, not just a redeploy.
rubricPoints: Explains CI as automatic build and testing of every change
Explains CD as promoting the same versioned artifact through environments rather than rebuilding it
Notes that a data pipeline's schema and configuration are part of what is tested and shipped
Names a limit: tests cover known cases, so data-dependent failures need staging, monitoring and rollback planning

suggested.rationale: Repairing a failing CI pipeline practises the build-test-gate loop this objective depends on, though the mission targets general software rather than data pipelines.

lessons.plain: Before choosing where to keep data, look at how the data will be used: how often it is written and read, how much each read needs, how fast answers must arrive, whether reads fetch one record or scan millions, and whether changes must succeed together. A library shelves books one way if readers browse by subject and another way if they look up one title. Storage works the same way. Describing these habits in plain terms first lets you match a system to them, instead of picking the one you know best.
lessons.guessPrompt: A fleet app writes one GPS position per vehicle every five seconds. Dispatchers constantly ask for the latest position of a single vehicle, while analysts once a month want total distance driven per region across three years. Without naming any products, what kind of storage would you expect to suit each need, and do you think one system could suit both?
lessons.teach:
An access pattern is the shape of how data is read and written: how often, how much at once, how quickly answers are needed, and what kind of question is asked. Useful dimensions include the ratio of reads to writes, whether reads fetch one record by its key or scan and summarize many rows, the latency target, whether a change must succeed across several records together, and how fast the data grows. Storage systems are each built around a particular shape. An analytical warehouse reads only the few columns a question needs across huge tables, so it suits totals and aggregates but is slow and costly for many tiny lookups. A wide-column key store serves single-key reads and writes at high volume with low latency, but it does not join tables for open-ended questions. A relational database gives multi-row transactions. Object storage holds files cheaply and durably. Each design gives up some abilities to be good at others, so the match has to be made on purpose.

Worked example: a fleet sends a position for each of 2,000 vehicles every five seconds, which is 400 writes per second, always on. Dispatchers fetch the latest position of one vehicle and need an answer in milliseconds. Analysts total distance per region per month over three years. Step one: the writes are constant, keyed by vehicle and time, and need fast single-key access, so a wide-column key store fits. Step two: the dispatcher reads are single-key lookups, which the same store serves. Step three: the monthly totals scan years of history, so an analytical warehouse fed by exports fits that workload.

Common mistake: choosing by what the team already knows, or by data size alone. Putting dispatch reads on the warehouse would make each lookup slow and expensive, and the dispatch screen would lag behind the vehicles it tracks.

A mismatched store shows up as latency and cost in production rather than as a wrong answer, so the access pattern must be written down before any product is chosen.

questions.prompt: A regional bank records each transfer between two accounts. Requirements: (a) a transfer must debit one account and credit the other as one all-or-nothing change; (b) branch staff fetch the current balance of a single account by account number; (c) the compliance team totals transaction counts per branch per month over seven years. Worked so far: step one, the transfer writes need multi-row transactions, so a relational database fits. Step two, the balance lookups are single-row reads by account number, which the same relational database handles. Step three is the only step left for you: choose the store for the compliance totals and give the reason for that choice.
choices: A wide-column key store, because it handles high write volume well
The same relational database, because it already contains every transaction
Object storage, because seven years of records can be held most cheaply there
An analytical warehouse fed by exports, because the totals read a few columns across many years of rows
questions.why: Totals over long history read only a few columns across huge tables, which is the shape an analytical warehouse is built for, while the other options are weak at open-ended aggregation.

questions.prompt: A parcel company tracks each shipment in a record and must move a parcel between two hubs as one change that either fully succeeds or fully fails across several linked rows. Which storage shape fits this requirement?
choices: An analytical warehouse that scans columns across all shipments
An object store that keeps each shipment as a file
A wide-column key store that serves single-key reads quickly
A relational database that provides multi-row transactions
questions.why: Only a relational database gives multi-row transactions, which is the requirement that the parcel move must succeed or fail as a whole.

questions.prompt: A team stores its orders in a wide-column key store because it is fast for single-key reads. They now want a report of total orders per country for last year, which they run by reading every row. What is the most likely problem?
choices: The key store cannot scale to a single year of orders
Object storage would have been cheaper for the same totals
The key store does not join tables or summarize many rows for open-ended questions, so the report will be slow and costly there
The team should add more writes per second to speed up the report
questions.why: A wide-column key store is built for single-key access and does not handle open-ended summaries over many rows well, so the report is a mismatch that shows up as latency and cost.

questions.prompt: A mobile app receives about 5,000 small device events per second and must return the latest event for one device ID within 10 milliseconds. No multi-row transactions are needed. Which store fits best, and why is an analytical warehouse a near miss?
choices: A relational database, because it is always the safest default; a warehouse cannot store events
A wide-column key store, because it serves single-key reads and writes at high volume with low latency; a warehouse is slow and costly for many tiny lookups
An analytical warehouse, because it is the fastest store for any lookup
Object storage, because files are durable; a warehouse would lose events
questions.why: The access pattern is high-volume single-key reads and writes with a low latency target, which a wide-column key store is built to serve, while a warehouse is slow and costly for many tiny lookups.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate proposes putting all vehicle telemetry into one analytical data warehouse because it is the most powerful option. Explain to them, in your own words, how you would analyze the access pattern before choosing storage, and name one limit or tradeoff of the warehouse option for the live dispatch reads.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by writing down the access pattern before naming a product: how many writes per second, how often each record is read, whether reads fetch one record by key or scan many, the latency the dispatch screen needs, and whether writes must be atomic across records. For this telemetry, the live dispatch reads are single-vehicle lookups that need millisecond responses against a constant high write rate, which a key-based wide-column store handles well. The analyst monthly totals are large scans and aggregates, which an analytical warehouse handles well. The tradeoff of putting everything in the warehouse is that per-row lookups are slower and cost more per query, so dispatch would feel the delay. The warehouse can still be the right home for history, fed from the operational store.
rubricPoints: Describe the access pattern dimensions (read/write ratio, lookup vs scan, latency, transactions) before choosing a product
Match the live dispatch reads to a key-based low-latency store
Match the monthly aggregates to an analytical warehouse
State a concrete tradeoff of using the warehouse for per-row lookups

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises choosing storage from access patterns, so reasoning through an exam-style scenario adds the most.

lessons.plain: Google Cloud offers many managed places to keep data, and each is built for a different kind of work. Choosing one means asking how the data will be read and written: by a single record lookup, by a scan that adds up millions of rows, by a bank-style transaction, or simply as stored files. Think of a filing cabinet, a warehouse of boxes, a locked safe, and a sticky note on your desk. Each has a best job, and using the wrong one makes work slow or expensive. This objective is about matching the access pattern to the right product and being able to say why the nearest alternative would fit worse.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a shop's website records every product view, and analysts will later ask questions like 'total views per category last quarter' across several years of data. Would you store these events as plain files in a bucket, in a key-value store looked up by one id, or in a system built to add up huge numbers of rows, and why?
lessons.teach:
Start with the access pattern: how the data is written, how it is read, and how much of it each question touches. Google Cloud's managed storage products are services Google operates for you, so you choose the shape of the data and the access rules, not the servers. Several named products cover different shapes. A relational database stores data in tables of rows and columns, speaks SQL, and supports transactions, which means a group of changes either all apply or none do. Cloud SQL runs familiar engines such as MySQL and PostgreSQL for conventional application databases. AlloyDB is a PostgreSQL-compatible database built for heavier transactional load. Spanner is a relational database that scales horizontally across regions while keeping transactions consistent. BigQuery is a data warehouse built to scan and summarize enormous volumes of data for analysis, not to update single rows quickly. BigLake lets that kind of query reach data kept as files in a data lake without copying it. Cloud Storage holds whole files, called objects, addressed by name, with no query engine on top. Bigtable is a wide-column store that fetches rows by key at very high volume. Firestore is a document database for application records. Memorystore is an in-memory cache, very fast but normally not the permanent record.

Why it works: each product trades features for one strength. BigQuery stores data by column, so a query that sums one field across billions of rows reads only that column.

Worked example: a site records one billion page views a year, and analysts ask ad hoc questions such as total views per category for last quarter. Step one: the work is aggregation over many rows, which rules out a key lookup store and a single-row transactional database. Step two: the questions are ad hoc SQL, which favours the warehouse. Step three: keep the raw files in Cloud Storage as cheap long-term copies. Choose BigQuery.

Common mistake: choosing the product you already know. A team that runs analytics on its checkout database finds the reports slow down the payments that share it.

Consequence: in a running system, a report scan competes with live transactions, and customers see timeouts at checkout.

questions.prompt: A ride-share company records a GPS ping from each vehicle every second. Dispatch asks one question many times a second: where is vehicle 4417 right now? Separately, analysts want daily totals of miles driven, but that is a different job. Work through the choice. Step one: the dispatch read is a single-key lookup repeated at very high volume, not a scan across many rows, so a data warehouse is a poor fit. Step two: a row-based transactional database with multi-row transactions is more machinery than this lookup needs. Step three is missing. Which choice completes the reasoning?
choices: Choose Bigtable, keyed by vehicle ID, because it fetches rows by key at very high volume.
Choose Spanner, because it scales across regions while keeping transactions consistent.
Store the pings in Memorystore as the permanent record, since it is the fastest option available.
Keep the pings in Cloud Storage and query them with BigLake, since that avoids copying the data.
questions.why: Bigtable is a wide-column store built to fetch rows by key at very high volume, which matches the per-vehicle lookup, while the other options either suit scans, cache data, or solve a problem the dispatch read does not have.

questions.prompt: A startup must keep customer invoices as PDF files. Each file is retrieved by its name, and nobody runs queries across the contents. Which managed product fits best?
choices: Cloud Storage, which holds whole files addressed by name with no query engine on top.
Firestore, because it is a document database for application records.
BigQuery, because it is the best place for any data that must be kept long term.
Memorystore, because it is the fastest place to read a file by name.
questions.why: Cloud Storage holds whole objects addressed by name, which is exactly the retrieve-by-name pattern described, while the other products each add a feature the invoices do not need.

questions.prompt: A team stores payment records in BigQuery and must move money between two accounts so that both updates apply or neither does. What is the main problem with this choice?
choices: BigQuery is a warehouse built to scan and summarize, not to update single rows quickly in transactions; Cloud SQL or Spanner fits better.
The data must first be copied into Cloud Storage before any update can run.
BigQuery is too slow to read one row at all.
BigQuery can hold only one table per project.
questions.why: BigQuery is designed for large scans and summaries rather than quick transactional single-row updates, so a relational database that supports transactions is the better fit for an all-or-nothing transfer.

questions.prompt: A game studio keeps the only copy of each player's inventory in Memorystore so that reads are fast. What is the main risk of this design?
choices: Memorystore cannot hold more than a few megabytes of data in any configuration.
Memorystore is an in-memory cache and is normally not the permanent record, so data held only there is at risk; a durable store should hold the source of truth.
Memorystore automatically writes every change to BigQuery, which slows reads down.
Memorystore cannot be read by an application using SQL queries, so inventory checks will fail.
questions.why: Memorystore is a fast in-memory cache that is normally not the permanent record, so keeping the only copy there risks losing player data, and a durable product should be the source of truth.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate wants to move our order-history reads, which look up one customer's orders by id thousands of times a second, into BigQuery because it is 'the fast database'. Explain to them in your own words why that choice is a poor fit, name one limit of the option you would recommend instead, and state the tradeoff you are accepting.
lessons.modelAnswer: BigQuery is built to scan and summarize huge amounts of data, so it does well at questions that touch millions of rows and poorly at fetching one customer's records. Each lookup pays for analytics machinery, and its response time is typically seconds rather than the milliseconds a web page expects, so the order page would feel slow and the cost of many small queries adds up. I would keep order history in a transactional database such as Cloud SQL or AlloyDB, indexed by customer id, where a single-row lookup is cheap and quick. The limit of that choice is that such a database is not built for large cross-customer analysis, so I would copy orders into BigQuery on a regular schedule for reporting. The tradeoff is running two stores and keeping the copy reasonably current, which is worth it because each store does one job well.
rubricPoints: BigQuery is optimized for scanning and aggregating many rows, not for frequent single-record lookups.
Per-lookup latency and cost make the analytics warehouse a poor fit for a customer-facing read path.
A transactional database indexed by customer id is the better home for the live reads.
Naming the tradeoff, such as keeping a reporting copy in sync, shows the choice is deliberate.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a product from an access pattern is best practised by reasoning through exam-style scenarios where near-miss options must be rejected.

lessons.plain: Planning for storage cost and performance means deciding, before you load data, how much it will cost to keep and how quickly you can read and write it. Storage is billed in more than one way: you pay to hold data, you pay each time a service reads or moves it, and some cheap storage tiers charge extra to read it back. Speed depends on how the data is laid out and how the system is asked to find things. A good data engineer estimates these costs from the expected access pattern, such as how often reports run and how much each one reads, and checks the design against both budget and speed. It is like choosing where to keep files in a warehouse: the cheapest shelf is useless if every pick takes an hour.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team stores ten years of sales records, and a dashboard scans the whole table every few minutes to show today's total. Before any teaching, which do you expect to drive the monthly bill most: how much data is stored, or how much is read each time the dashboard runs? Say why.
lessons.teach: Storage cost is what you pay to hold bytes over time, usually per gigabyte per month. Query cost, sometimes called scan cost, is what you pay each time a service reads data to answer a question; in BigQuery on-demand pricing, this is driven by the bytes scanned. Storage class means the tier a file or table sits in: colder tiers cost less to hold but may charge more to read and require data to stay for a minimum time. Partitioning splits a table into pieces by a column such as date, so a query that filters on that column reads only the matching pieces. Clustering sorts rows inside those pieces by other columns so filters can skip whole blocks. Egress means data leaving a region or the cloud, which is billed separately. Why it works: you pay for what a system reads and moves, so the cheapest design is the one that reads the least for the questions you actually ask. Worked example: a sales table holds 2 TB across ten years, and a dashboard refreshes every 5 minutes with a query for today's total. Step 1: unpartitioned, each refresh scans all 2 TB. Step 2: 288 refreshes a day scan 576 TB daily. Step 3: partitioned by sale date, each refresh reads only today's partition, roughly 2 GB. Step 4: 288 refreshes now scan about 576 GB daily, a thousandfold drop, while storage cost stays the same. Common mistake: tuning the per-gigabyte storage price while ignoring how often and how much is read, or partitioning on a column that no query filters by. Consequence: a dashboard that refreshes in a loop can quietly multiply a scan bill after launch, so estimate bytes read per query times queries per day before you pick a design.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm keeps a 4 TB table of GPS location records, split into 1,000 equal daily partitions by ping date. An hourly job totals the last 7 days of records. Because the job filters on ping date, each run reads only 7 partitions, about 28 GB. Step 1 is done: the date filter limits reads to those 7 partitions. Step 2 is missing: which completes the estimate of bytes scanned in a day, given the job runs 24 times a day?
choices: Divide 4 TB by 24 runs to get the bytes each run reads
Add the per-gigabyte storage price to the 28 GB scan size
Multiply 4 TB by 24 runs, since a filtered job still reads the whole table
Multiply 28 GB per run by 24 runs to get about 672 GB scanned per day
questions.why: Daily scan volume is the bytes read per run multiplied by the number of runs per day, so 28 GB times 24 is about 672 GB.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does clustering do to a partitioned table?
choices: It moves older rows to a colder storage class to lower the monthly bill
It copies the table to a second region so reads are billed as egress
It sorts rows inside each piece by other columns so filters can skip blocks of rows
It splits the table into date pieces so queries can skip whole pieces
questions.why: Clustering orders rows within each partition by chosen columns so a filter can skip blocks, whereas partitioning is the step that splits the table into pieces.

questions.prompt: A 3 TB events table is partitioned by ingest date, but every report filters on customer_id and most reports span the full history. Which change best reduces bytes scanned?
choices: Export the table to a file bucket and query it there with the same filters
Add clustering on customer_id inside the existing partitions
Keep the ingest-date partitions and move the table to a colder storage class
Increase the number of partitions by splitting each day in two
questions.why: Partitioning on a column no query filters by gives no pruning, so clustering on the column that is actually filtered lets the engine skip blocks, while a colder storage class only changes the holding price.

questions.prompt: A team's nightly job copies a 1 TB dataset from a region in Europe to a region in the US so a dashboard there can read it. Which cost is most likely overlooked in their estimate?
choices: Per-gigabyte monthly storage in the US region
Egress charges for data leaving the source region
Query scan charges on the dashboard
Storage class minimum duration fees
questions.why: Data leaving a region is billed separately as egress, a charge that is distinct from the cost of holding the bytes or scanning them in a query.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would estimate the cost and speed of a new event table before loading it. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach, such as the estimate being only as good as your assumptions about how the data will be queried.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the questions the table must answer and how often each runs, because those set the read volume that drives the bill. For each query, I estimate how many bytes it would scan with no partitioning, then with partitioning on the column the queries filter by, and multiply by runs per day. I add storage cost from the expected data size and retention, and check whether any data is in a colder tier with read fees or minimum storage times. For speed, I look at whether the layout lets queries skip most of the data. The main limit is that the estimate is only as good as the access pattern I assumed. If real users filter on different columns or run queries far more often than planned, the cost and speed will differ, so I would recheck after launch using the actual query logs.
rubricPoints: Storage cost and query or scan cost are separate and both must be estimated
Estimate reads per query times queries per day, not just data size
Partitioning or clustering reduces scanned data only when queries filter on those columns
The estimate depends on the assumed access pattern, so it needs checking against real usage

suggested.rationale: Estimating storage and scan costs from access frequency in fictional credits is exactly what the planned cost-model engine would let the learner practise.

lessons.plain: Data does not stay useful at the same level forever. Lifecycle management means deciding what happens to stored data over time: how long you keep it, when it moves to cheaper and slower storage because nobody reads it often, and when it is deleted or protected from deletion because a rule requires it. Think of a filing room: recent files stay on the desk, older ones go to a basement archive, and some boxes are destroyed on a set date unless a lawyer says otherwise. The goal is to pay for storage that matches how the data is actually used, and to keep only what you are allowed and needed to keep.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company stores application logs in a bucket. Engineers read logs from the last week every day, almost never read logs from last year, and must keep all logs for seven years. What would you do with the logs as they age, and why might keeping everything on the fastest storage be a poor choice?
lessons.teach:
Lifecycle management is the set of rules that govern stored data from the moment it is written until the moment it is removed. It has three common parts. Tiering moves data to cheaper storage classes as it gets older, trading lower monthly cost for slower or fee-bearing reads. Expiration deletes data automatically after a set age. Retention holds data for at least a minimum period, and a retention lock prevents anyone, including administrators, from deleting it before that period ends.

Why it works: most stored data is written once and read rarely after its first days or weeks. Storage is billed per gigabyte per month, and colder classes are cheaper per gigabyte but charge more to read and often impose a minimum storage duration. Rules let the platform apply the right price to each age band without someone remembering to do it by hand.

Worked example: a bucket holds application logs. Rule one says objects older than 30 days move to a colder class. Rule two says objects older than 365 days are deleted. Rule three, set by a compliance team, is a seven-year retention period on the bucket. Trace an object written on day 0. On day 30 it moves to the colder class and costs less each month. On day 365 the expiration rule is due, but the retention period still blocks deletion, so the object is kept until seven years have passed, and only then can it be removed.

Common mistake: assuming an expiration rule overrides a retention requirement. When both apply, the longer protection wins, so a deletion that someone expected to happen is silently blocked, which surprises people who wanted cleanup.

Consequence in a running system: a service that reads old data from a cold tier pays retrieval fees and waits longer, so a tiering rule that is too aggressive can make a dashboard slow and expensive. Rules apply to existing data as well as new data, so one mistaken rule can affect a large amount of data quickly.

questions.prompt: A film archive stores raw camera files in a bucket, which is a container for stored objects. Its lifecycle rules are: objects older than 60 days move to a colder, cheaper storage class (tiering), and objects older than 400 days are scheduled for deletion (expiration). A separate retention period of 500 days is set on the bucket, and it blocks deletion until it ends. Trace a file written on day 0. On day 60 it moves to the colder class and costs less each month. On day 400 the expiration rule comes due, and this is the step to complete: ______. The file is removed on day 500, when the retention period ends.
choices: The file moves back to the standard class on day 400, because expiration always reverses tiering.
The file is deleted on day 400 because expiration applies to the file and retention applies only to files written after the rule was set.
The expiration rule is more specific than retention, so the file is deleted on day 400 and the retention period is ignored.
The retention period still blocks deletion on day 400, so the file is kept until day 500 and removed only after that.
questions.why: When expiration and retention both apply, the longer protection wins, so the file stays until the 500-day retention period ends.

questions.prompt: In lifecycle management, what does a retention lock do?
choices: It prevents anyone, including administrators, from deleting the data before the retention period ends.
It automatically deletes data as soon as its retention period is over.
It encrypts stored data so that only the original writer can read it.
It moves data to the cheapest storage class once the retention period starts.
questions.why: A retention lock stops deletion, including by administrators, until the minimum retention period has passed, while expiration and tiering are separate rules.

questions.prompt: A weather-sensor company stores readings in a bucket. Rule one moves objects older than 14 days to a colder class. Rule two deletes objects older than 90 days. A retention period of 30 days is set on the bucket. An object is written on day 0. On which day is it first eligible for deletion?
choices: Day 30, because the retention period is the only rule that controls deletion.
Day 90, because the expiration rule is later than the 30-day retention minimum, so the longer protection is not the deciding factor here and the object is removed then.
Day 60, because the retention period and expiration rule add together.
Day 14, because the tiering rule removes objects from the bucket.
questions.why: Both rules agree that deletion cannot happen before day 30, and the expiration rule is due on day 90, so the object first becomes eligible for deletion on day 90.

questions.prompt: A marketing team has 4 TB of product images in a bucket, most of them several years old. On Monday they add a rule that moves objects older than 7 days to a colder class. A dashboard that reads these images starts running more slowly and costs more. What best explains this?
choices: The rule also applies to existing images, so the older ones were moved to the colder class and reads now incur retrieval fees and delays.
Colder classes make reads faster because the data is compressed, so the cost increase is caused by something else.
The rule only affects images uploaded after Monday, so the dashboard slowdown must come from a different cause.
The expiration rule was triggered on Monday, deleting the images that the dashboard needed.
questions.why: Lifecycle rules apply to existing data as well as new data, so already-old images become eligible to move at once, and reading from a colder tier costs more and takes longer.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to cloud storage how lifecycle rules decide when data moves or is deleted, and name one limit or tradeoff the team should weigh before turning on automatic deletion.
lessons.modelAnswer: Lifecycle rules act on the age of each piece of data. A rule can say that after a set number of days the data moves to a cheaper, slower class, or that after a set number it is deleted. The cheaper classes are not free to use: they charge for reads and often require data to stay a minimum time, so moving data that is read often can cost more, not less. The tradeoff with automatic deletion is that it is permanent. If a rule removes data that a later audit or investigation needs, nothing brings it back unless versioning or a copy exists elsewhere. Before enabling a deletion rule, a team should confirm the retention requirement, check exactly which data the rule touches, and test the rule on a non-production copy first.
rubricPoints: Lifecycle rules act on data based on its age or similar conditions.
Tiering trades lower storage cost against retrieval fees and minimum storage durations.
Retention requirements can block deletion even when an expiration rule is due.
Automatic deletion is permanent, so it must be checked against audit and recovery needs.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly rules, price tiers and retention concepts that are best learned by reading how the behaviour is defined and then explaining it back.

lessons.plain: A data warehouse is a large store built for asking questions about history, such as how many rides ran last month and which city earned the most. The data model is the plan for how that stored data is laid out: which tables hold the things being counted, which hold the descriptions around them, and how the two connect. A good plan makes questions quick and clear to write. A poor plan forces every question to untangle messy records first. Think of it like organising a shop's receipts so the owner can total sales by week, product, or store without re-reading every slip.
lessons.guessPrompt: A fleet company wants to report total fuel used by vehicle type and by month. Would you store every trip as one wide table with the vehicle type and month repeated on each row, or keep the vehicle details in their own table and link to them? Which one is easier to change later, and why?
lessons.teach:
A data warehouse model usually arranges data as a fact table surrounded by dimension tables, which is called a star schema. A fact table holds measurements of events, such as one row per completed trip with its distance and fuel used. A dimension table holds the descriptive context used to slice those measurements, such as the vehicle, the driver, or the calendar date. Each fact row links to dimension rows through keys.

The most important decision is the grain, meaning exactly what one fact row represents. Settle it first, in plain words, such as one row per completed trip. Every column in the fact table must fit that sentence. Dimension keys are often surrogate keys, which are simple numbers the warehouse generates itself, so a changed attribute in the source system does not break history.

The star layout works because warehouse questions are mostly totals grouped by descriptive attributes. The big measurement table stays narrow, and each question joins through one dimension at a time.

Worked example. The fact table trips has grain one row per completed trip, with columns vehicle_key, date_key, fuel_litres and distance_km. The dimension table vehicles has vehicle_key and vehicle_type. The question is total fuel for diesel vans in March. Step 1: join trips to vehicles on vehicle_key. Step 2: join to the date dimension and keep only March. Step 3: keep only vehicle_type equal to diesel van. Step 4: sum fuel_litres.

Common mistake: mixing grains in one fact table, such as putting trip rows and a monthly total row side by side. Sums then count the same fuel twice.

Consequence in a running system: if a nightly load appends a monthly summary into the trips table, the fuel dashboard jumps the next morning and no error is raised.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain stores one row per item sold at the till in a fact table called sales_items, with columns store_key, product_key, date_key, units and revenue_gbp. The question is: what was total revenue from bread products in Leeds shops during week 14? Step 1: join sales_items to products on product_key and keep only rows where category is bread. Step 2: join to stores on store_key and keep only rows where city is Leeds. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: sum revenue_gbp.
choices: Group the result by product_key before summing
Join the stores table a second time on city
Join to the date dimension on date_key and keep only week 14
Divide revenue_gbp by units to get an average price
questions.why: The date filter for week 14 needs a join from the fact table's date_key to the date dimension, and only then can rows be kept by week, so that join is the missing step.

questions.prompt: In a star schema, what does a dimension table hold?
choices: A running total of every measurement since the warehouse was built
One row per measured event, with the numbers to be totalled
Descriptive context, such as who, what or when, used to slice the measurements in the fact table
The grain statement that says what one fact row represents
questions.why: A dimension table holds the descriptive attributes that questions group and filter by, while the fact table holds the measurements themselves.

questions.prompt: A telecom company wants a fact table of call records for analysing network usage. Which grain statement fits the design principle that every column must fit one sentence?
choices: One row per call, plus a monthly total row for each customer
One row per customer, holding the total of all their calls
One row per completed call, with its duration and cost
One row per mobile tower, with a count of calls and the customer postcode
questions.why: Setting the grain as one row per completed call lets every column (duration, cost, keys) describe that single call, whereas the other options mix grains or change the unit being counted.

questions.prompt: A retailer's source system changes a supplier's name, and its warehouse dimension table uses the source system's own supplier name as the key. Why is using a warehouse-generated surrogate key instead the safer design?
choices: It removes the need for a dimension table, so no joins are required
It speeds up the nightly load by skipping the dimension table entirely
Existing fact rows keep pointing at the same dimension row, so the name change does not break historical totals
It makes the fact table grain change automatically whenever a name changes
questions.why: A surrogate key is a stable number the warehouse generates, so a changed descriptive attribute in the source does not sever the links from historical fact rows.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we fix the grain of a warehouse fact table before choosing its columns, and name one tradeoff of the star layout compared with keeping everything in one wide table.
lessons.modelAnswer: We fix the grain first because it is the single sentence that says what one fact row means, such as one completed trip. Every column has to describe that same thing. If we pick columns first, we end up mixing trip-level numbers with monthly totals or driver-level figures, and then any sum we run double counts or mixes levels. Once the grain is written down, the rest of the model follows: measurements go in the fact table and descriptions go in dimensions. The tradeoff of the star layout is that answering a question needs joins across several tables, which costs some query work and needs clean keys. A single wide table avoids joins and is simple to read, but it repeats descriptive text on every row, makes changes to a vehicle's details touch millions of rows, and makes history harder to keep straight when attributes change.
rubricPoints: The grain is one exact sentence about what a fact row represents, and it is set before columns.
Fact tables hold measurements; dimension tables hold descriptive context used for grouping and filtering.
Mixing grains in one table makes totals wrong, often by double counting.
The star layout trades extra joins for narrower tables and easier handling of changing descriptions.

suggested.rationale: Writing join and aggregate queries against a small star schema is the practice that makes the grain and dimension choices concrete.

lessons.plain: Normalization is the habit of storing each fact in one place only. Instead of writing a customer's address on every order they place, you keep the address in one customer record and have each order point to that record. This makes data easier to keep correct, because a change happens once and every report sees it. The opposite choice, copying data so that reads need fewer lookups, is called denormalization. Deciding how far to go in either direction depends on whether the system is mostly recording changes or mostly reading and summarizing large amounts of data.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop stores each order with the customer's full name and street address repeated on every order row. If a customer moves house, what could go wrong, and how would you change the storage to prevent it?
lessons.teach:
Normalization is the process of splitting data into related tables so that each fact is stored once. The normal forms are rules of increasing strictness. First normal form means each cell holds a single value and there are no repeating groups. Second normal form means every non-key column depends on the whole key, not part of it. Third normal form means non-key columns depend only on the key, not on each other. A key is the column or columns that uniquely identify a row.

Why it works: when a fact lives in one place, an update changes it once, and nothing can contradict it. Denormalization is the deliberate reverse, copying data so that a read needs fewer joins, which are operations that combine rows from two tables.

Worked example. An orders table holds the customer's city on every order row. Step 1: Alice moves from Leeds to York and has 40 orders. Step 2: an update changes 39 of those rows and misses one, so reports show Alice in both cities. Step 3: in a normalized design, city lives in a customers table and each order stores only a customer_id. The move is a single row update, and every order sees York.

Common mistake: denormalizing an operational system because joins feel slow, before measuring, and then writing the same fact in several places. Consequence: in a running order service, duplicated addresses mean some invoices still print the old address after a correction. Analytical warehouses reverse this trade-off, because they scan wide tables in bulk and rarely update single facts, so some controlled duplication is often the right design there.

questions.prompt: A ticketing service stores venue_name and venue_postcode on every ticket row, so a venue with 1,200 sold tickets holds 1,200 copies of its postcode. Step 1: the venue moves to a new postcode, and the team creates a venues table with one row per venue, keyed by venue_id. Step 2: the tickets table is changed so each ticket stores only venue_id. Step 3: the venue's postcode is updated in the venues table, and nothing else is edited. What does a ticket read for its venue postcode now?
choices: The new postcode, read through its venue_id, so all 1,200 tickets see the change from one row update
Nothing, because a ticket cannot show a postcode without the venue_name column
The new postcode only for tickets sold after step 3, since older rows were not rewritten
The old postcode, because each ticket row froze its value when it was created
questions.why: Once the postcode lives in one venues row and each ticket stores only the venue_id, every ticket reads the current value through that link, so a single update is enough.

questions.prompt: A clinic's appointments table has the columns appointment_id, patient_id, and patient_phone. Which change most directly applies the idea of storing each fact once?
choices: Delete patient_id so that each appointment row is unique by its phone number
Move patient_phone to a patients table keyed by patient_id, and leave only patient_id on each appointment
Keep patient_phone on each appointment and add a second copy in a reminders table so reads need no join
Store patient_phone as a comma-separated list of every number the patient has ever used in one cell
questions.why: Moving the phone to a table keyed by patient_id means a phone change is one row update and cannot contradict copies sitting on appointment rows.

questions.prompt: A staff table has columns employee_id (the key), department_id, and department_floor. Every row for a department repeats its floor. Which statement about this table is correct?
choices: It breaks first normal form because employee_id is a number
It is in third normal form because every column depends on employee_id
It is fine because a floor is a fixed fact and cannot change
It breaks third normal form because department_floor depends on department_id, which is another non-key column, so the floor belongs in a departments table
questions.why: Third normal form forbids a non-key column depending on another non-key column, and here the floor depends on department_id rather than on the key employee_id.

questions.prompt: A data warehouse holds a table of 400 million event rows, where each row is one recorded event. A daily report scans most columns across many rows, and individual facts are rarely updated. Which design fits best?
choices: Split every descriptive attribute into its own table and join all of them at query time
Keep one row per event but store the whole event history inside a single text cell
Store a few frequently read descriptive columns directly in the wide table as controlled duplication
Keep the table fully normalized, since warehouses should always match operational design
questions.why: Bulk scans and rare updates mean duplicated columns cost little to maintain while removing joins speeds reads, which is the trade-off warehouses are built around.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would keep data split into many related tables and when you would deliberately copy it into fewer, wider ones. Name one limit or trade-off of each choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would keep data normalized when the system records many small changes, such as orders, payments or account updates, and when wrong or inconsistent copies would cause real harm. Each fact lives in one table, so an update touches one row and reports agree. The cost is that reads need joins, which can slow down large queries and make the schema harder for new people to follow. I would denormalize when the workload is mostly reads over large data, such as dashboards or analytics, and the source data changes in batches. Copying facts into wider tables avoids repeated joins and speeds scans. The trade-off is that every copy must be refreshed, and a missed refresh produces figures that look plausible but disagree. So I would only denormalize where I can say how each copy is kept current, and I would measure first rather than assume joins are the bottleneck.
rubricPoints: Normalization stores each fact once, so updates stay consistent
Denormalization trades write-time consistency work for faster reads and fewer joins
Choice depends on read versus write pattern and the cost of inconsistency
Every denormalized copy needs a plan for how it is refreshed

suggested.rationale: Designing tables and comparing a normalized schema with a denormalized one in SQL is the hands-on way to see the trade-off.

lessons.plain: A data warehouse is the place a company keeps its data so people can ask questions of it, such as totals by region or trends over months. Designing one well starts from what the business needs rather than from the data you happen to have: how fresh the answers must be, who asks questions, what kinds of questions they ask, how long records must be kept, which parts are sensitive, and how much money can be spent. Each requirement pushes a design choice, such as how tables are split, which columns are grouped together, and who can see what. It is like laying out a library around how readers actually borrow books, not just how the books arrived in delivery boxes.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team copies its application's transaction tables straight into a warehouse and points its dashboards at them. Without any further detail, what problem do you expect as the data grows, and what would you change first?
lessons.teach:
A warehouse design is the set of choices about tables, grouping, access, location, and retention that let a set of business requirements be met. Start by turning each requirement into a measurable statement: freshness (data no more than one hour old), query shape (most questions filter by date and store), concurrency (200 dashboard viewers at 9 am), retention (seven years), sensitivity (customer contact details restricted), and budget (a monthly ceiling on spend). Each statement should point to a specific design decision. The logic works because a warehouse typically charges for and slows down according to how much data a query reads, so any choice that lets queries skip unneeded data serves cost and speed at once.

Worked example. A retailer wants a sales dashboard refreshed hourly, analysts querying by date and store, and finance keeping seven years of history. Step one: one-hour freshness means a scheduled load every hour, not a nightly job. Step two: most queries filter on sale date, so the sales table is partitioned by sale date, meaning it is split into segments by that column so a query can skip the segments it does not need. Step three: store is the next most common filter, so rows are clustered by store identifier, meaning rows with the same store are stored close together. Step four: contact details are sensitive, so they go in a separate restricted table, not the sales table. Step five: seven-year retention means no automatic expiration is set on the sales table.

Common mistake: copying the source system's schema and calling the job finished. Application databases are built for writing individual transactions quickly, not for answering broad questions, so a straight copy keeps a shape that forces every dashboard refresh to scan years of rows.

Consequence: an unpartitioned sales table means every hourly refresh reads the full history, so the bill climbs each month and dashboards slow as the data grows. A design that maps each requirement to one concrete choice keeps both under control.

questions.prompt: A logistics company stores shipment scan events and wants its operations dashboard refreshed every 15 minutes. Analysts mostly filter scans by event date and warehouse region. Regulators require ten years of scan history, and driver licence numbers are sensitive and must be restricted. Step one: 15-minute freshness means a scheduled load every 15 minutes, not a nightly job. Step two: most queries filter on event date, so the scans table is partitioned by event date, meaning it is split into segments by that column so a query can skip segments it does not need. Step three: [missing]. Step four: driver licence numbers go in a separate restricted table, not the scans table. Step five: ten-year retention means no automatic expiration is set on the scans table. Which choice correctly completes the missing step three?
choices: Partition the scans table by warehouse region as well as by event date
Cluster rows by warehouse region, meaning rows from the same region are stored close together so queries can skip the others
Copy the source scanning system's table layout unchanged so the load is simpler
Set an automatic expiration of ten years on the scans table so old rows are removed
questions.why: Region is the next most common filter after event date, so the design clusters rows by region, which keeps same-region rows close together, while the other options either misapply partitioning, copy the source schema, or delete data that retention requires keeping.

questions.prompt: In a warehouse table design, what does partitioning mean?
choices: Storing rows with the same store identifier close together on disk
Limiting which users can read particular columns of a table
Splitting a table into segments by a column so queries can skip segments they do not need
Keeping a second copy of the table so a failed load can be recovered
questions.why: Partitioning splits a table into segments by a chosen column, usually a date, so queries that filter on that column read less data; the other options describe backup, clustering, or access control.

questions.prompt: A design brief says billing postcodes are sensitive and only two staff may see them. Three hundred analysts query watch time by content genre and day from a watch-events table. Which design best meets both requirements?
choices: Store postcode in the watch-events table and partition that table by postcode so the restriction is automatic
Set a 30-day automatic expiration on the watch-events table so postcode data does not persist
Keep postcode in a separate restricted table and leave the watch-events table free of it
Store postcode in the watch-events table and rely on analysts not querying that column
questions.why: Sensitive fields belong in a separate restricted table so the broad analyst table never holds them, which is the design the requirement points to; the other options either expose the data, rely on behaviour instead of design, or delete data the analysts need.

questions.prompt: A payments table holds four years of transactions. Analysts filter every query by transaction date, but the table was built by copying the source application's schema and was never partitioned. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: Each refresh reads the full history, so cost and query time grow as data accumulates
Adding an automatic expiration to the table will fix the slowdown while keeping all history
Queries stay fast because the table's size does not affect how much data is read
The monthly cost stays fixed no matter how many years of rows are stored
questions.why: Without partitioning on the filter column, every query reads the whole table, so cost and latency rise as history grows, which is the consequence of copying an application schema rather than designing for queries.

lessons.explainPrompt: A product manager asks why you cannot just load everything into one large table and call it the warehouse. Explain to a teammate how the business requirements should shape the design, and name one limit or tradeoff of the design choices you would make.
lessons.modelAnswer: Everything in one large table makes every question read everything, so cost and speed get worse as data grows. I would start by writing down the requirements as checkable statements: how fresh the data must be, which filters people use most, how long records are kept, which columns are sensitive, and what budget applies. Then each statement maps to a choice. Frequent date filters suggest partitioning the table by date so queries skip old segments. Frequent store filters suggest clustering rows by store. Sensitive columns go into a restricted table or get column-level access rules. The tradeoff is that partitioning and clustering only help for the filters we predicted. If analysts start filtering on something else, the queries get no benefit, so the design needs review as usage changes.
rubricPoints: Map each business requirement to a specific, checkable design decision rather than choosing a design first.
Explain that partitioning limits how much data a query reads, which affects both cost and speed.
Name a tradeoff: design choices favor the access patterns that were predicted and can stop helping when usage changes.
Mention that sensitive data is separated or restricted to meet access requirements.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a requirements-to-design scenario adds the most here, and no listed mission or engine directly covers warehouse design.

lessons.plain: Designing a warehouse architecture means deciding how data is laid out and loaded before anyone writes a report, so the most common questions are cheap and fast to answer. Start by listing how the data will really be read: which filters people use, how often, how fresh the answers must be, and how many people query at once. Then shape the storage around those reads, such as splitting large tables into time-based pieces and keeping a separate summary ready for dashboards. A good design makes the usual question touch a small slice of data. A poor one makes every question read everything.
lessons.guessPrompt: A dashboard always shows one day of sales for one store, but the sales table holds five years of rows. Without knowing any product details, what would you change about how the table is stored so each dashboard load reads less data?
lessons.teach:
Start with the access pattern: the set of questions people ask of the data, including their filters, how fresh the answers must be, and how often they run. The architecture is the set of storage choices that makes those questions cheap. A warehouse is a system built for large scans and aggregates over many rows, and it usually stores data by column, so a query reads only the columns it names.

Partitioning means splitting one logical table into segments keyed by a column, most often a date. A query that filters on that column skips every segment it does not need. This skipping is called pruning. Clustering means keeping rows physically sorted within each partition by a few other columns, so a filter on those columns can skip blocks of rows as well.

Worked example: a sales table holds five years of rows, and the dashboard filters on sale date and store. Step 1: partition by sale date, so a one-day query touches roughly 1 in 1825 of the data. Step 2: cluster by store, so within that day only the blocks for that store are read. Step 3: the dashboard now scans one day's partition instead of the whole table, so it costs less and returns sooner.

Common mistake: partitioning on a column nobody filters on, or on a key with so many distinct values that it creates a huge number of tiny pieces. The table looks organized, but every query still reads everything.

Consequence: in a running system, unpruned scans make dashboards slow under load, multiply the bill, and compete with other queries for capacity. A refresh that works in testing can time out at 9am on a busy day.

The architecture is correct only when it matches the measured access pattern.

questions.prompt: A ride-sharing company keeps two years of trip rows in one table. Its city dashboard filters on trip date and pickup city. Step 1: partition the table by trip date, so a one-week report touches only seven daily segments. Step 2: this step is missing. Step 3: the dashboard now reads only the matching city's blocks within those seven days, so it returns sooner. Which choice fills Step 2?
choices: Cluster by fare_amount, because the dashboard sorts results by fare
Partition by rider_id, which gives one segment for each rider
Copy the table to a second location so queries no longer scan the original
Cluster by pickup_city, so within each day's segments only that city's blocks are read
questions.why: Clustering keeps rows sorted within each partition by a filter column, so the pickup_city filter can skip blocks inside the already-pruned date segments.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does pruning mean in a partitioned warehouse table?
choices: Sorting rows inside each partition by several columns to speed up joins
Compressing each column so a query reads fewer bytes from disk
Deleting old rows so the table takes up less storage space
Skipping whole partitions that a query's filter rules out, so they are never read
questions.why: Pruning is the skipping of partitions (segments keyed by a column such as date) that a query's filter shows it does not need.

questions.prompt: A factory logs one sensor reading per machine every second for three years. Its monitoring query always asks for one machine_id over a two-hour window. Which table layout fits this access pattern best?
choices: No partitioning at all, because one table holding three years of rows is always the fastest layout
Partition by the minute of each reading, so every minute becomes its own segment
Partition by reading date, then cluster by machine_id, so a two-hour query skips other days and reads only that machine's blocks
Partition by machine_id and cluster by reading timestamp, since each machine then gets its own partition
questions.why: Partitioning on the date skips the days outside the window, and clustering on machine_id skips the rows of other machines within the remaining partition.

questions.prompt: A team partitions an orders table on order_id, which is unique for every row. Their daily report filters on order_date. What is the most likely result?
choices: Each order becomes its own tiny piece, and the date-filtered report has no useful partition to skip, so it still scans most of the table
The warehouse rejects the table, since partitions are only allowed to use dates
The report becomes faster, because each order can now be found directly by its ID
The report reads only the newest partition, because order_id always increases
questions.why: Partitioning on a high-cardinality key that the queries never filter on creates many tiny pieces and leaves the date filter with nothing to prune, so queries still read nearly everything.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would shape a warehouse table for a dashboard that always filters by day and customer, and name one limit or tradeoff of the design you chose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would first confirm the access pattern from the query logs. The dashboard filters by day and customer, and the team needs answers within seconds. I would partition the table by day, since every query names a date range, so most of the five years of data is skipped without being read. Within each day, I would cluster by customer, so a customer filter reads only the blocks holding that customer's rows. The tradeoff is that this only helps when a query filters on the partition column. An ad hoc query by product with no date filter will read everything again. Partitioning also adds management work, such as setting an expiry for old days and keeping the load job aligned to the date. So I would tell the team the design fits this dashboard, and that other questions need their own table or a pre-aggregated summary.
rubricPoints: Partitioning by the date column lets queries skip data they do not need.
Clustering by customer orders rows so customer filters read fewer blocks.
The design only helps when queries filter on the partition or cluster columns.
Other access patterns may need a separate table or summary, so the design must be tied to measured use.

suggested.rationale: A planned SQL lab would let the learner write queries against partitioned and clustered tables and watch how much data each query scans.

lessons.plain: A data lake is a large, inexpensive place to keep raw files of many kinds, such as logs, CSV exports and images, before anyone has decided exactly how they will be used. Running one involves three everyday jobs. Discovery means finding out what files exist and recording a short description of each so people can locate them. Access means deciding who may read or change which parts of the lake, and keeping those decisions organised rather than scattered. Cost means making sure you pay for the right kind of storage and that nobody runs up large bills by scanning everything. Google Cloud offers a service called Dataplex that arranges storage into a lake with zones and assets, which gives you levers for all three jobs. The same thinking applies to any data lake.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a company stores ten years of raw web logs in one big shared folder, which of the following worries you most, and why: nobody can find what is in it, too many people can read it, or the storage bill is too high?
lessons.teach:
A data lake is a storage area that holds data in its original file form, such as logs, exports and images, and adds structure later. Dataplex is the Google Cloud service that wraps this storage into a managed lake. Inside a lake, a zone is a grouping for one stage of data, commonly a raw zone for untouched input and a curated zone for cleaned data. An asset is an existing storage location, such as a bucket of files or a BigQuery dataset, attached to a zone. Discovery means the service automatically scans assets and records metadata, which is information about the data such as file format, table names and columns, so people can find it in a catalog without someone writing it down by hand. Access is controlled with IAM, the identity and permission system, granted at the level of the lake, zone or asset. Where one table must serve readers differently, BigLake lets you apply row or column restrictions so each reader sees only what they are allowed to see. Cost controls include choosing a storage class suited to how often data is read, setting budget alerts that notify you when spending passes a limit, adding labels so spending can be split by team, and limiting how much data each query scans.

Worked example: a raw zone holds web-server logs in a bucket. Step one: attach the bucket to the raw zone as an asset with discovery turned on, so the log format is registered. Step two: grant analysts read access on the curated zone only, not the raw zone. Step three: set a monthly budget alert on the project and label the bucket with its owning team. Step four: when analysts query a curated table, filter on the date column so the engine reads only recent partitions rather than the whole history.

Common mistake: granting a broad role across the whole project to clear an access error quickly. That gives readers access to raw personal data they should never see, and the grant is hard to audit later.

Consequence: in a running system, an unscoped grant exposes data quietly, and unfiltered scans appear as a bill nobody expected until the month closes. Access and cost are therefore configuration that must be reviewed like code, not settings made once and forgotten.

questions.prompt: A city transit agency keeps GPS pings from its buses as raw JSON files in a bucket named bus-pings-raw. That bucket is attached to the raw zone as an asset with discovery turned on, so the format is registered. Step one: the planning team gets read access on the curated zone only, not the raw zone. Step two: a 2,000 dollar monthly budget alert is set on the project. Step three is blank. It must let the finance team see what this bucket costs, separately from the rest of the project. Which choice fills step three?
choices: Turn off discovery on the raw zone so the JSON format is no longer registered in the catalog.
Move bus-pings-raw into the curated zone so that finance can read its billing records.
Grant the planning team the Owner role on the whole project so they can also query the raw bucket.
Label bus-pings-raw with its owning team so its spending can be split out by team.
questions.why: Labels are the mechanism for splitting spending by team, while the budget alert only tracks the project total and the other choices either widen access or change discovery, which does not address cost.

questions.prompt: A clinic stores lab results as CSV exports in a bucket, and the team wants that bucket registered inside its managed data lake under a zone. In the teaching terms, what is the bucket called once it is attached to that zone?
choices: An IAM permission granted at the lake, zone or asset level that controls who may read the data
A budget alert that notifies the finance lead when monthly spend passes a chosen limit
An asset: an existing storage location attached to a zone
A label key-value pair attached to a resource so that spending can be grouped by team
questions.why: In the course's terms an asset is an existing storage location, such as a bucket or dataset, attached to a zone, while the other choices describe cost alerts, access permissions, and labels.

questions.prompt: A payments company keeps one BigQuery transactions table. Fraud analysts need every column, but customer support agents must not see card numbers and may only see rows from their own region. Which approach fits this, according to the teaching text?
choices: Give the support agents a read-only role across the whole project so they can reach every table they need.
Set a budget alert on the transactions table so that any unusual reads trigger a notification.
Apply BigLake row and column restrictions on the table so each reader sees only what they are allowed to see.
Add a label per region to the table so that support agents are shown only rows that carry their region label.
questions.why: BigLake row and column restrictions are the teaching text's answer to letting one table serve readers differently, while a project-wide role would expose the sensitive columns and labels do not restrict what a reader can see.

questions.prompt: A startup's hourly job reads its 4 TB event table with no date condition, and every run scans the full history, so the monthly bill jumps. The table already has a date column. Which single change most directly reduces how much data each run scans?
choices: Raise the budget alert threshold so the job is not interrupted when spending rises.
Grant the job's service account a broader project role so it stops hitting access retries.
Filter the query on the date column so the engine reads only the recent partitions.
Add a label naming the team that owns the event table, so the cost can be attributed to it.
questions.why: Limiting the scan with a filter on the date column is the teaching text's cost control for reducing how much data a query reads, while labels only attribute cost, alert thresholds only notify, and broader grants widen access without reducing the scan.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would set up access and cost controls for a new data lake, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would split the lake into a raw zone and a curated zone, and attach each storage location as an asset with discovery turned on so the files are registered and searchable. Access would be granted per zone: engineers write to raw, analysts read only curated, and nobody gets a project-wide role, because broad roles are hard to audit and expose raw personal data. For cost, I would pick a storage class that matches how often each zone is read, add team labels so spending can be attributed, set a budget alert, and ask analysts to filter queries on partition columns so scans stay small. The tradeoff is that discovery and fine-grained rules add setup and ongoing overhead, and the curated zone is only as current as the pipeline feeding it, so a stale copy can mislead readers even when access is correct.
rubricPoints: Explains zones and assets and how discovery records metadata so data can be found
Scopes access per zone or asset using least privilege, avoiding broad project-wide roles
Names concrete cost controls such as storage class choice, budget alerts, labels, and limiting bytes scanned
States a real limit or tradeoff, such as setup overhead or stale curated data

suggested.rationale: A situation where a lake's access and cost settings conflict forces the learner to reason through which controls to apply, which adds more than reading the console steps alone.

lessons.plain: A data lake is a large store of raw data files, such as logs, exports, and sensor readings, kept in their original format in cheap object storage. Processing data in a lake means running computations directly on those files where they sit, instead of first copying everything into a database. Think of a warehouse as a tidy filing cabinet where every drawer is labeled before anything goes in, and a lake as a big storage room where you open boxes and sort them when you need an answer. The skill is choosing when to clean, convert, and summarize the files, and how to run that work again safely.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has ten years of raw CSV exports sitting in cheap file storage, and a new report needs only last month's rows. Without any prior knowledge, what would you change about how the files are organized and read so the job does not scan everything every time?
lessons.teach:
A data lake is a store of files kept in their original form, usually in object storage such as Google Cloud Storage, where each file is an object found by its bucket (a top-level container) and its path. Processing data in a lake means running a job that reads those files, transforms them, and writes results back, using an engine such as Apache Spark, which is an open engine that splits one large job across many workers. Schema-on-read means the structure of a file is interpreted when it is read, not enforced when it is stored, so a bad row does not block the upload but may break a job later. A partition is a way of organizing files into folders by a key such as date. Parquet is a columnar file format, meaning it stores each column together so an engine can read only the columns a query needs.

Why it works: files are cheap to keep and many can be read in parallel, so you can store everything first and decide later what to build. The main lever for speed and cost is partitioning, because a job can skip folders it does not need.

Worked example: daily click files live under events/dt=2024-05-01/, events/dt=2024-05-02/, and so on. A job that builds the May summary first lists only the folders whose date starts with 2024-05, then reads just those files, counts events per day, and writes Parquet output to curated/summary/month=2024-05/. A rerun overwrites that one output partition instead of adding to it.

Common mistake: appending each run's output to the same folder. A retry then doubles every count, and the dashboard shows inflated numbers with no error raised.

In a running system, an unpartitioned lake forces every job to scan all history, so cost and runtime grow with total data rather than with the slice you actually need.

questions.prompt: A ride-share company stores trip files as objects in a data lake, one folder per day, such as trips/dt=2024-06-14/. A job builds a weekly fare summary for 2024-06-10 through 2024-06-16. Step 1: it lists only the folders dated 2024-06-10 through 2024-06-16 and skips the rest. Step 2: it reads those files and sums fares per city. Step 3 is missing and must be filled in: the job writes its Parquet result to a folder named for the week, and the rule is that a rerun must replace that week's result rather than add to it. Which step 3 is correct?
choices: Append the new result to the same week folder so earlier runs are kept alongside it, which means each rerun adds another copy of the totals.
Write the result to a new folder with a random name on every run, then have the dashboard pick the newest one by its timestamp.
Read every daily folder in the lake again before writing, so the output is always rebuilt from complete history.
Overwrite the week=2024-06-10 output partition so a rerun replaces that week's result in place.
questions.why: Overwriting the one output partition makes a rerun replace that week's result, which keeps the totals correct, whereas appending or writing to new random folders would double or scatter the counts.

questions.prompt: A vendor drops sensor readings into a data lake as raw files without checking them first. One file has the text n/a in a column that should hold a number. Under schema-on-read, at what point does this bad value most likely cause a problem?
