choices: When the file is written to Parquet, because the format silently converts every bad value to zero.
When a job later reads and parses that column, because the structure is interpreted only at read time.
When the upload finishes, because the storage service rejects any object that contains text in a numeric column.
When the bucket is created, because the lake checks every future file against a schema before accepting it.
questions.why: Schema-on-read means the file's structure is interpreted when it is read, so a bad value passes the upload and only causes trouble when a job parses it.

questions.prompt: A parking authority keeps three years of meter payments as Parquet files partitioned by month. A report needs only the revenue column for one city in March. Which design choice does the most to reduce the work the job does, and why?
choices: Convert the files to one large CSV so the job opens a single object, since fewer objects always means less work.
Keep the Parquet layout and month partitions, so the job skips other months' folders and reads only the revenue column.
Keep all files in one flat folder and filter by city inside the job after every file has been fully read.
Add more Spark workers only, since extra workers are the main way to cut the amount of data the job scans.
questions.why: Partitioning lets the job skip folders outside March and the columnar Parquet layout lets it read only the revenue column, so both reduce the data scanned.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm has two years of shipment files in one flat folder with no date folders. Its monthly report takes longer every month even though the report covers the same length of time each run. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Spark has fewer workers each month, so each job has less capacity to finish the same work.
The job cannot skip any files, so it must scan all history, and runtime grows with total data.
The files are stored as Parquet, which gets slower as the number of columns in the folder grows.
The lake enforces a fixed schema, so bad rows accumulate in the folder and slow every read.
questions.why: Without partitions the job has no way to skip folders it does not need, so its cost and runtime grow with the total size of the history rather than the slice it needs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only used a relational database why processing in a data lake is different, and name one limit or tradeoff they should expect when they run jobs directly on lake files.
lessons.modelAnswer: In a relational database, the data is structured and checked when it is written, and queries run against that managed copy. In a data lake, the files are stored as they arrived and the structure is only interpreted when a job reads them, which is schema-on-read. That makes ingestion cheap and flexible, because nothing is rejected at upload time. The tradeoff is that bad or inconsistent rows only surface during processing, so jobs need validation and clear rules for what counts as a valid file. A second limit is performance: a job that cannot skip data has to read everything, so partitioning the files by a key such as date and writing results in a columnar format are what keep cost and runtime proportional to the slice you need. Teams should also make reruns safe by overwriting a partition rather than appending to it.
rubricPoints: Data lake stores raw files as they arrived; structure is applied when read (schema-on-read), not when written
Contrast with a database that validates and structures data at write time
Names a real tradeoff, such as late discovery of bad data or full scans without partitioning
Notes that reruns should overwrite partitions to avoid duplicate results

suggested.rationale: The objective is mostly about recognizing lake processing patterns and product roles, which a clear reading and worked example teach better than any listed mission or planned engine.

lessons.plain: A data lake is a large store where you keep data in its original form, such as log files, exports, and images, without first shaping it into tables. Monitoring a data lake means keeping watch on that store so you notice problems early: a pipeline that stopped delivering files, a folder that quietly grew far beyond normal, an unexpected spike in who is reading sensitive data, or a dataset nobody can find. It is like a warehouse manager who checks the loading dock log and shelf counts every morning, instead of waiting for a customer to report a missing order.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job that writes files into a data lake crashes at midnight and writes nothing. The storage service itself reports no error. How would you find out it happened, and what would you measure to catch it?
lessons.teach:
A data lake is a storage area, usually object storage such as Google Cloud Storage, that holds raw files of many kinds. Each file is an object, identified by the bucket (a top-level container) it sits in and its path name. Monitoring a data lake means continuously measuring the lake and acting when a measurement drifts from what you expect. Three kinds of signal matter. Metrics are numbers sampled over time, such as bytes stored per bucket or the count of objects that arrived in the last hour. Logs are records of events, such as who read or wrote an object; audit logs record administrative and data-access actions. Metadata is data about data, such as the schema, owner, and last update time of each dataset, usually kept in a catalog such as Dataplex.

Why it works: a lake has no table engine checking each write, so failures hide quietly. A job can die and leave an empty folder, and nothing errors. Monitoring turns silence into a signal by comparing expected behaviour with measured behaviour, and an alert fires when the gap crosses a threshold you chose.

Worked example: a nightly job should land files under a landing prefix by 02:00. Step 1: a metric counts new objects under that prefix each day. Step 2: an alert rule says that if the count is zero by 03:00, the on-call team is notified. Step 3: on a night when the upstream export fails, the count stays at zero, the rule fires at 03:00, and the team learns of the failure before analysts open their dashboards at 08:00.

Common mistake: alerting only on storage size or cost. Those numbers say little about whether data is correct or current. A lake can keep growing from other writes while the pipeline that feeds a key dataset has been dead for a week.

Consequence: a silently stale lake feeds reports and models with old data. The error is usually found late, by a downstream user, and is hard to trace back to its source. Freshness monitoring therefore belongs next to the pipeline itself.

questions.prompt: A logistics company receives sensor readings from trucks. Each hour, a loader writes new files under the prefix hourly/ inside the bucket freight-telemetry. The team wants an alert if the data goes stale. Step 1: a metric records the timestamp of the most recently written object under hourly/. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: at 14:20 the newest timestamp is 12:30, so the gap is 110 minutes, and the alert fires. Which choice correctly fills Step 2?
choices: Read the audit log to find which service account wrote each file, then alert if that account is not the loader
Compare the total bytes stored in freight-telemetry against last month's total and alert on any increase
Delete every object under hourly/ that is older than 90 minutes so the prefix stays small
Compare the age of the newest object against a chosen limit of 90 minutes and notify the on-call team when the age exceeds it
questions.why: The freshness rule compares the measured age of the newest object with a threshold the team chose, and notifies someone when that threshold is crossed, which is the same measure-compare-alert pattern the lake needs.

questions.prompt: A data team wants to know which owner is responsible for each dataset in their lake, what columns each dataset has, and when each dataset was last updated. Which kind of signal provides this information?
choices: Metrics, because they are numbers sampled over time
Metadata, usually kept in a catalog, because it describes the datasets themselves
Bucket size reports, because they show how much each dataset holds
Event logs, because they record who wrote each object
questions.why: Metadata is data about data, such as schema, owner, and last update time, and it is typically held in a catalog, so it answers these questions directly.

questions.prompt: A lake's only alert fires when the bucket total grows by more than 40 percent in a week. Over the same period, the pipeline that feeds a key sales table has been failing for three days, but no alert has fired. What is the most accurate explanation?
choices: Audit logs were turned off, so the failing writes were never recorded anywhere
Storage growth from other writes means the sales pipeline must be running correctly
The bucket total is a size measure, and a size alert says little about whether one dataset is current, so a freshness signal for that dataset is needed
The alert threshold should have been set to 10 percent instead of 40 percent
questions.why: The lake can keep growing from other writes while one dataset goes stale, so monitoring only size cannot reveal the failure; a freshness metric on that dataset's path is the right signal.

questions.prompt: A compliance team needs to know which external account read each object in a sensitive dataset during last month. Which signal should they use to answer this?
choices: A catalog entry showing the dataset's owner and schema
A metric counting the total number of reads per bucket per day
Audit or event logs, which record who performed data-access actions on each object
A bytes-stored metric broken down by prefix
questions.why: Logs are event records that capture who did what, and audit logs specifically record data-access actions, so they can identify each reader; a metric gives only counts and a catalog gives descriptive data.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would monitor a data lake that a nightly pipeline feeds. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would watch three things. First, freshness and volume: a metric that counts new objects under each expected prefix per day, with an alert if the count is zero or far below normal by the deadline. Second, access events: audit logs showing who reads or writes sensitive prefixes, with an alert when an unexpected identity appears. Third, catalog health: whether each dataset still has an owner and a recent update recorded in its metadata. The main limit is that these checks prove the files arrived, not that their contents are correct. A file can land on time and still be malformed, so I would add a content check inside the pipeline as well. The tradeoff is alert noise: thresholds set too tight will page people for normal variation, so I would tune them against several weeks of history before relying on them.
rubricPoints: Monitoring compares measured behaviour, such as object counts and arrival times, against expectations and alerts when the gap is too large.
Useful signals include metrics for freshness and volume, logs of reads and writes, and metadata about ownership and schema.
Freshness checks catch silent pipeline failures that the storage service itself never reports.
Volume or cost alone does not prove the data is correct or current.
Thresholds that are too tight create alert noise, so they need tuning against historical behaviour.

suggested.rationale: Setting a threshold on a freshness metric and checking when it fires is the core skill, and the planned alarm builder engine would let a learner practise it.

lessons.plain: A data platform is the set of places an organization keeps its data, plus the rules for finding, trusting, and using it. Think of a large warehouse building: some shelves hold raw crates as they arrive, other shelves hold cleaned and labelled goods, and a directory at the entrance says what exists and who may take it. On Google Cloud, Dataplex is a governance layer that organizes storage into groups and zones, Dataplex Catalog is the searchable directory describing each dataset, Cloud Storage holds files cheaply, and BigQuery is the place where fast SQL analysis runs. This lesson shows how these pieces fit together into one platform.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has millions of raw log files sitting in cheap file storage, and analysts need to answer questions across them with SQL. Besides the files themselves, what would you need so that people can find the right data and trust it?
lessons.teach:
A data lake is a large store of data kept mostly as files in their original or lightly processed form. A data warehouse is a system built for running fast analytical SQL queries over structured tables. Cloud Storage is object storage: it keeps files in containers called buckets, cheaply and at large scale, but it does not understand what the files mean. BigQuery is a managed analytics warehouse. Dataplex organizes storage into lakes and zones, where a zone is a labelled area such as raw or curated. Dataplex Catalog holds metadata, which is information about data: its schema, owner, description, and location. Metadata is what lets a person search for a dataset without opening every file.

Worked example. A ride-telemetry team lands raw JSON position messages in a raw-zone bucket. A discovery scan registers those files as tables with inferred schemas. A cleaning job removes malformed records and writes the result to a curated-zone bucket in a columnar format. Owners add descriptions and owners to each entry in the catalog. Analysts search for vehicle positions, find the curated table, and query it in BigQuery. Each step adds meaning without changing the stored bytes.

Common mistake: treating the catalog or the lake as the security boundary. Discovery and governance describe data; access still has to be granted on the buckets and datasets that hold it. A running consequence: if analysts are pointed at the raw zone, malformed records flow into dashboards and the reported numbers are wrong. Keep raw and curated data separate, and direct analysts to the curated tables.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm lands carrier scan files in a raw-zone bucket. A discovery scan registers those files as tables with inferred schemas. A cleaning job drops rows that fail validation and writes the remaining rows to a curated-zone bucket as columnar files. The data owner then adds a description and an owner to the catalog entry, so analysts can find the table by search. One step is still missing before analysts should be able to query the curated table: which step is it?
choices: Re-run the discovery scan on the raw zone and confirm every inferred column type by hand before anyone searches
Convert the curated columnar files back into raw JSON so BigQuery can read them
Grant analysts read access on the curated bucket, since the catalog describes the data but does not enforce who can read it
Nothing else is needed, because the catalog entry already controls who can read the files
questions.why: The catalog holds metadata that describes data, so read access has to be granted separately on the bucket or dataset that stores the files.

questions.prompt: A team needs to keep original vendor PDFs and scanned images cheaply, at large scale, with no need to run SQL over their contents. Which Google Cloud product fits best?
choices: A Dataplex Catalog entry, because it holds the files themselves
A Cloud Storage bucket, which holds files cheaply at scale
A data warehouse query, because the files must be analysed with SQL straight away
A BigQuery table, because it stores the original files directly
questions.why: Cloud Storage is object storage that keeps files cheaply in buckets without understanding their meaning, which suits files that need no SQL analysis.

questions.prompt: A payroll dataset has a catalog entry with a clear owner and a good description. An intern nonetheless can read the underlying payroll files in their bucket. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The owner's description is too short for the catalog to enforce any limits
Access was never restricted on the bucket holding the files, because the catalog only describes data
The catalog entry lacks a schema, so the system falls back to granting open read access on the files
Discovery registered the files, which opened them to every catalog reader
questions.why: Catalog metadata describes data and does not act as a security boundary, so access must be set on the bucket or dataset itself.

questions.prompt: A retailer wants staff to find a store-footfall dataset through search without opening each file. Which information should go into its catalog entry?
choices: A description, the schema, the owner, and the location of the data
The compression codec, byte size, and creation time of each individual file
The storage class label only, so searches can filter by cost
The number of buckets the team has created in the project
questions.why: Metadata such as description, schema, owner, and location is what lets a person find and understand a dataset without opening its files.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would split a new data platform into raw and curated storage, where the catalog fits, and name one limit or tradeoff of loading everything straight into one warehouse table instead.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would land incoming data unchanged in a raw zone, usually Cloud Storage buckets grouped under a Dataplex lake, so we always keep the original records. A cleaning step then writes validated, consistently structured data to a curated zone, and that is what analysts query in BigQuery. Dataplex Catalog holds the descriptions, owners, and schemas, so people can find the right table. The tradeoff of loading everything into one warehouse table is that bad or changing source records land directly in the table people trust, and you lose the original copy to compare against when something goes wrong. Keeping a raw zone costs storage, and the catalog must be maintained or it goes stale, but that is cheaper than wrong numbers in reports.
rubricPoints: Raw data is kept unchanged in a separate zone so it can be replayed or audited.
Curated data is validated and is the layer analysts query.
The catalog stores metadata such as schema, owner, and description so data can be found.
Loading everything into one table loses the original copy and exposes bad records to consumers.

suggested.rationale: Choosing where raw and curated data live under a lake and warehouse is a scenario-reasoning skill that an exam-style situation builds better than a single existing mission.

lessons.plain: Imagine a large company where many teams each keep their own data: sales, logistics, finance. Some rules must be the same everywhere, such as who may see personal details or how long records are kept. Other choices are better made by the team that knows the data best. A federated governance model splits the work this way. A central group sets the shared standards and safety rails, and each team owns and manages its own datasets within them. The result is one common set of rules without making one team a bottleneck for every change.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has ten data teams, and one central group must decide who can see customer addresses across all of them. Would you have that central group approve every single access request, or let each team decide everything on its own? Why might neither extreme work well, and what would you split between the two groups?
lessons.teach:
Data governance means the rules for who owns a dataset, who may read or change it, how sensitive fields are labelled, how long data is kept, and how quality is checked. A federated governance model divides this work. A central group defines the shared policies, vocabulary, and guardrails. Distributed domain teams, each owning a dataset or group of related datasets, apply those policies to their own data and make the day-to-day decisions. Metadata is data about data: descriptions, owners, and sensitivity labels. A catalog is a searchable inventory of metadata, so people can find a dataset and see who owns it. Google Cloud's Dataplex is a governance layer that organises data spread across storage systems into lakes and zones and applies these shared rules across them. A policy tag is a classification label attached to a column, which can then drive who may read that column.

Worked example. The central group defines a label called sensitive-personal and a rule that only approved roles may read labelled columns. The customer-service team owns the customers table and tags its phone-number column with that label. An analytics team asks to query the table. The rule applies automatically, the owning team approves the analysts' group, and only that group receives read access to the phone column. The catalog shows the table, its owner, and its labels, so anyone can see where the data came from and who to ask.

Common mistake: making the central group own every dataset, which turns it into a bottleneck, or letting each team invent its own labels, so sensitive means something different in each place and cross-team queries and audits silently miss columns.

Consequence: when a label is applied inconsistently, a dashboard built by another team can read a personal-data column that nobody reviewed, and the audit report looks clean because it searches for a label that was never used.

Federation works only when the shared standards are small, clear, and enforced, and the owners are named.

questions.prompt: A hotel group runs a central data governance group, which defines a shared label called government-id and a rule that only approved roles may read columns carrying it. The reservations team owns a bookings table. In a migration, the team adds a new column, guest_passport_number, to that table. Before any analyst queries the table, the reservations team applies the government-id label to the new column. The rule then limits reads of that column to approved roles, and the catalog entry for the table lists the label so auditors can find it. Which step is missing from the account above?
choices: Each analyst must request a new label name for the passport column so that it does not clash with existing labels.
The reservations team must verify that the new column's label is recorded in the catalog before an analyst queries it, so the rule and the catalog both reflect the change.
Nothing else is needed, because the rule covers every column in the table automatically once the table exists.
The central group must reassign ownership of the bookings table to itself before the column can be labelled.
questions.why: A federated model relies on the owning domain team applying the shared labels to its own columns, and the rule only restricts a column once it carries the label, so the owner must confirm the label is in place and visible in the catalog.

questions.prompt: In a federated governance model, which of the following is an example of metadata?
choices: The raw rows of a customer orders table, including each order amount.
The compiled binary of a nightly job that loads sales data into a warehouse.
The text message a support agent sends to a customer about a late delivery.
A record stating that the ledger_2024 dataset is owned by the treasury team and carries the confidential sensitivity label.
questions.why: Metadata is data about data, such as descriptions, owners, and sensitivity labels, and only the ownership and label record describes a dataset rather than holding its contents.

questions.prompt: A university has forty research groups, each with its own datasets. Which arrangement best matches a federated governance model?
choices: Each research group chooses its own label names and keeps them private, so groups can work independently of one another.
A central office personally approves every dataset before any group may create a table, so no group makes its own decisions.
A central group defines a small shared set of labels and rules, and each research group owns its datasets and applies those rules to them.
Datasets are stored without named owners, because the central IT group is responsible for everything in the university.
questions.why: Federation splits the work: the central group sets small shared standards and each domain team owns and applies them to its own datasets, with owners named.

questions.prompt: A mobile game studio's central governance group defines the label sensitive-personal and an audit that searches the catalog for that label. One team, however, has been tagging its player email and device-ID columns with the label PII instead. What is the most likely result?
choices: The audit reports those columns as protected, because PII and sensitive-personal are treated as synonyms by the catalog.
The audit searches only for sensitive-personal, so the PII-tagged columns are never found and the audit report looks clean even though personal data is unreviewed.
The audit fails with an error, which alerts the central group to the problem so it can fix the labels.
The team's columns are automatically converted to the sensitive-personal label by the catalog when the table is saved.
questions.why: When teams invent their own labels, the audit searches for one term and silently misses columns tagged with another, producing a clean-looking report that hides unreviewed personal data.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only ever managed one team's database what a federated governance model is, and name one tradeoff it creates that a fully centralized model would not have.
lessons.modelAnswer: A federated governance model means one central group sets the shared rules and each domain team applies them to the data it owns. The central group decides things that must be consistent everywhere, such as what counts as personal data, the label names, the minimum rules for who may read sensitive columns, and how datasets are catalogued. Domain teams decide the details for their own data, like which analysts need access and how their tables are structured. The main tradeoff is consistency versus speed: because each domain team makes local decisions, two teams can interpret a rule differently unless the standards are small, clear, and checked automatically. A fully centralized model avoids that drift but makes one team a queue for every access change. So the federated design only works if the shared standards are actually enforced and every dataset has a named owner.
rubricPoints: Central group sets shared standards, labels, and guardrails
Domain teams own and apply the rules to their own datasets
A catalog or shared metadata makes ownership and labels discoverable
Names a real tradeoff, such as inconsistent interpretation versus bottleneck risk
Notes that enforcement and named owners are required for it to work

suggested.rationale: The core skill here is reasoning about who decides what and the tradeoffs involved, which is best practised by explaining the model back in your own words.

lessons.plain: A chart or dashboard tool does not do the analysis itself. It asks a storage system for numbers, draws them as charts, and refreshes them on a schedule. Connecting data to a visualization tool means giving that tool a safe path to the data: the address of the store, a login it can use, and permission to read only the tables it should show. Someone must decide which tables are clean enough to display, who may see them, and how fresh the numbers need to be. The engineer who sets up the connection makes those choices concrete, and a wrong choice shows up as a wrong chart or an unexpected bill.
lessons.guessPrompt: A product manager wants a live sales dashboard in a chart tool, but the raw sales table contains duplicate rows caused by a retry bug. Before any teaching, what do you think should happen between the raw table and the chart, and who should be responsible for it?
lessons.teach:
A visualization tool, also called a BI tool, is a program that sends questions to a data warehouse and turns the answers into charts. A warehouse is a managed database built for large analytical queries. A connection is the saved setup that lets the tool reach the warehouse: an address, a credential, and a choice of which dataset or table to read. A service account is a non-human identity that a program uses to log in, and an IAM role is a bundle of permissions granted to an identity on a resource. A curated view is a saved query that presents a clean, filtered version of raw data under a stable name. Tools often keep a cached copy of results, and the schedule that updates that copy is the refresh.

The tool works because every chart refresh is really a query run under the connection's credential. The tool never understands the business meaning of the data; it only shows what the query returns. So the data must be prepared before the tool sees it.

Worked example. A dashboard shows daily revenue from a raw orders table. Step 1: the data engineer creates a view called orders_clean that keeps only the latest row for each order ID. Step 2: the engineer creates a service account for the dashboard and grants it read-only access to the curated dataset only. Step 3: the tool connects with that account and points at orders_clean, not at the raw table. Step 4: the refresh runs hourly, and each run executes the view query.

Common mistake: connecting the tool with a personal owner login, or pointing it at the raw table so duplicates appear on the chart. A dashboard that refreshes every minute against a large unfiltered table can raise query costs and slow the warehouse for other teams, so refresh frequency is a decision, not a default.

Prepared, narrowly permitted data is what makes a connection both correct and safe.

questions.prompt: A customer-support team at a bike-rental company wants a dashboard of currently open tickets. The raw tickets table stores one row per status change, so a ticket that was opened and later closed has two rows. Step 1: the data engineer creates a view called tickets_current that keeps only the newest row for each ticket ID. Step 2: the engineer creates a service account named support-dash and grants it read-only access to the curated dataset only. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: the refresh is set to run every six hours. Which action completes Step 3?
choices: Create the connection using the support-dash service account and point it at tickets_current rather than the raw table.
Set the refresh to run every minute so the open-ticket count is always as current as possible.
Point the tool at the raw tickets table so that every status change appears as its own bar on the chart.
Connect the tool with the team lead's personal owner login so the lead can edit the charts later.
questions.why: The connection must use the read-only service account and read the curated view, so each ticket is counted once and the tool holds only the permission it needs.

questions.prompt: In a dashboard connection, what does the refresh control?
choices: The name of the curated view that the chart reads from when someone opens the dashboard.
Which IAM role the service account holds on the warehouse project, so the tool can read the data at all.
How often the tool's cached copy of results is updated by running the underlying query again, and the setting that schedules those runs.
Whether the chart colours change when a user switches the dashboard to a dark theme.
questions.why: A refresh is the schedule that updates the tool's cached copy, and each refresh run executes the query behind the chart.

questions.prompt: Northwind Freight, a logistics firm, wants a dashboard of late deliveries. Which setup best fits the idea in this objective?
choices: Give the tool an owner role on the whole project so it never runs into a permission error when a new table is added later.
Share the raw deliveries table so anyone with the link can read it, which lets the tool connect without any credential.
Connect the tool with the senior analyst's personal login, since that login already has access to every dataset in the project and removes any permission questions.
Create a read-only service account for the curated late-deliveries view and connect the tool with it.
questions.why: The tool should use a non-human service account with read-only access to a prepared view, which is both correct for the chart and limited in what it can touch.

questions.prompt: A regional sales dashboard shows about 30 percent more orders than the finance report. The tool points at a raw table where an order can appear in several rows after edits. What is the most likely cause, and the fix?
choices: The warehouse is corrupt, so restore the warehouse from last month's backup and the counts will match finance again.
The chart colours are wrong, so change the dashboard theme so that duplicate bars are hidden from view.
The tool counts duplicate rows from the raw table, so point it at a curated view that keeps one row per order.
The refresh runs too rarely, so set it to every minute to catch orders that the earlier refresh missed.
questions.why: The tool only shows what the query returns, so counting several rows for one order inflates the chart, and a curated view with one row per order fixes it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never set up a dashboard why connecting a visualization tool to a warehouse is not just pasting in a table name. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you would choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: Pointing a dashboard at a table name skips the work that makes the numbers trustworthy. The tool runs a query every time it refreshes, under whatever credential it was given, so the connection decides both what people see and what it costs. I would point the dashboard at a curated view that removes duplicates and filters out test data, and I would give the tool a dedicated read-only service account with access to that one dataset. The tradeoff is that the view adds a layer someone must maintain: if the raw schema changes, the view can break and the dashboard goes stale. Refresh frequency is another tradeoff. Hourly refreshes keep load and cost predictable but mean the numbers can be an hour old, so I would confirm with the consumer how fresh the figures really need to be.
rubricPoints: A connection needs an address, a credential, and a limited choice of data to read.
The tool runs queries on each refresh, so the data must be prepared before the tool sees it.
Use a curated view and a read-only service account rather than raw tables or personal logins.
Refresh frequency trades freshness against cost and load on the shared warehouse.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly console steps, product options, and access settings that are best learned by reading the product's catalogue of connection methods.

lessons.plain: Precalculating fields means working out a value once, ahead of time, and storing it alongside the raw data, instead of recalculating it every time someone asks a question. Think of a shop that writes each receipt's total on the receipt when it is printed, rather than adding up the items every time a manager asks. A dashboard that needs the same result thousands of times a day gets fast, consistent answers. The person who usually sets this up is the data engineer who builds the pipeline feeding the reports.
lessons.guessPrompt: A report shows average trip speed across 50 million trips, and it takes forty seconds each time someone opens it. Without looking anything up, name two different places where you could do the speed calculation, and say which you would pick if hundreds of people open this dashboard every day.
lessons.teach:
A derived field is a column whose value is calculated from other columns, such as speed being distance divided by duration. Precalculating a field means computing that derived value once, during the data pipeline when rows are loaded or transformed, and saving it as a real column in the table. The alternative is computing it inside every query, so the arithmetic runs again each time a report reads the rows.

Why this helps: analytical stores are built to scan many rows quickly, but a query still pays for every row it reads and every calculation it performs. If a dashboard repeatedly groups by a complicated expression across billions of rows, precomputing that expression means the report reads a plain column and does far less work. Precalculation also gives everyone one agreed definition, so two dashboards do not compute speed in slightly different ways.

Worked example. A pipeline receives trip records with distance_km and duration_minutes. Step 1: during loading, the transform computes speed_kmh as distance_km divided by (duration_minutes divided by 60). Step 2: the result is written into the table as the speed_kmh column. Step 3: the dashboard averages speed_kmh grouped by day, reading one column instead of dividing on every row each time. Step 4: when a zero duration arrives, the transform must handle it, for example by storing null, otherwise the division fails or produces an infinite value.

Common mistake: precalculating a field that depends on rules which later change, then never recomputing it. The stored value goes stale silently. In a running system, if the upstream duration changes from minutes to seconds and the stored speed column is not rebuilt, every report shows wrong numbers while the query code looks perfectly correct.

Stored fields cost storage and must be rebuilt whenever their rules change, so precalculate the expensive, stable, heavily reused values and leave rarely used or fast-changing calculations inside the query.

questions.prompt: A grocery chain loads daily store sales into its warehouse with two source columns, revenue_usd and units_sold. The team decides to precalculate avg_price_per_unit. Step 1: during loading, the transform computes avg_price_per_unit as revenue_usd divided by units_sold. Step 2: the result is written into the table as a real column. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the store-performance dashboard reads avg_price_per_unit directly instead of dividing on every row. Which choice correctly fills the missing Step 3, given that from 1 March finance changes revenue_usd to include sales tax?
choices: Leave earlier rows alone, because only newly loaded rows need the tax-inclusive rule and the column is recalculated at query time anyway
Replace units_sold with a count of transactions so that the average price is always a whole number
Store the sales tax in a separate column and have every dashboard add it back when it reads the average price
Rebuild the stored avg_price_per_unit for rows loaded before 1 March so that old and new rows use the same revenue definition
questions.why: A stored derived column does not update itself when its rule changes, so rows written under the old rule must be recomputed to match the new definition.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches what it means to precalculate a field?
choices: Deleting derived columns from the table after each report so that storage costs stay low
Running the same arithmetic inside every query so that each report always uses the latest source values
Computing a derived value once during the data pipeline and saving it as a real column in the table
Storing the raw source columns in a separate system so that derived values can be added later by analysts
questions.why: Precalculating means the derived value is computed during loading or transformation and persisted as an ordinary column, rather than recalculated each time a query runs.

questions.prompt: A warehouse stores a precalculated margin_pct column computed from cost_per_unit. On 1 June the finance team changes how cost_per_unit is valued, and the pipeline is updated, but the stored margin_pct column is left as it was. What is the most likely result?
choices: Dashboards show margins that look plausible but are based on the old cost rule, and nothing signals the error
The warehouse automatically recomputes margin_pct the next time any dashboard reads it
Queries fail with a syntax error until the column is dropped and recreated
Only rows loaded after 1 June are affected, so older margins remain correct under the new rule
questions.why: A stored column keeps its old values silently when its rule changes, so reports keep working and display numbers that are quietly out of date.

questions.prompt: A fleet operator has a daily dashboard that reads fuel_km_per_litre, a value equal to km_driven divided by litres_used. The formula has not changed in three years, the value is read by fifteen dashboards and forty analysts, and the raw columns are very large. Which approach best fits the precalculation objective?
choices: Precalculate fuel_km_per_litre during loading, since the rule is stable and the value is read often
Precalculate it only for the dashboard that runs monthly, and let the other dashboards keep dividing
Store the division result as text so that analysts can read it without any arithmetic
Leave the division inside each query, because precalculation always makes reports slower
questions.why: A stable, heavily reused, expensive calculation is the kind of value the objective recommends precalculating, because the stored column saves repeated work and gives everyone one definition.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would precalculate a field for a reporting table and when you would leave the calculation inside the query, and name one limit or tradeoff of precalculating.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would precalculate a field when the same expensive calculation is used by many reports, the formula is stable, and the dashboards are slow because they repeat the work on every row. Trip speed is a good example: it is derived from two columns, the formula rarely changes, and many people read it, so computing it once during loading saves time for every reader and gives everyone the same definition. I would leave a calculation inside the query when it is rarely used, depends on parameters the user chooses at runtime, or changes often. The main tradeoff is staleness. The stored column is only as correct as the last time it was rebuilt, so if the upstream units or business rules change, the pipeline must recompute the field, or every report silently shows wrong numbers. We also pay for extra storage and must keep the transform logic in one place.
rubricPoints: Defines a precalculated field as a derived value computed once and stored in the table
Explains the benefit: reports read a plain column and avoid repeated computation across many rows
Gives a criterion for choosing precalculation versus computing in the query
Names the tradeoff: stale values when rules change, plus extra storage and rebuild effort

suggested.rationale: Writing transforms that store derived columns and comparing query cost is SQL practice, which the planned SQL lab would provide.

lessons.plain: BigQuery is Google's data warehouse, a place where large amounts of data are stored and queried with SQL. Some reports are requested over and over, such as a dashboard that refreshes the same totals every few minutes. Two features make that repeated work cheaper and faster. One keeps a copy of frequently used data in fast memory close to the query engine, like a whiteboard kept at the front of the room instead of walking to the archive each time. The other saves the answer to a query ahead of time and keeps it up to date, so the dashboard reads a small finished table instead of scanning raw rows. Knowing which one fits, and what freshness or cost it brings, is the skill.
lessons.guessPrompt: A dashboard runs the same summary query every five minutes over a table of a billion rows, and the answer changes only when new rows arrive. Before you learn the feature, what would you try in order to avoid rescanning the raw rows every time, and why?
lessons.teach:
A materialized view is a stored table whose contents are the result of a query over one or more base tables. A base table is the ordinary table where your raw data lives. Because the result is stored and BigQuery keeps it current as base data changes, a dashboard asking for daily totals can read a few hundred summary rows instead of scanning billions of raw events. BigQuery usually refreshes the view incrementally, folding in only new data rather than recomputing everything. Materialized views support only a restricted set of query shapes, so the query you want must fit those rules.

BI Engine is an in-memory acceleration layer. You reserve a fixed amount of memory for a project and region, and BigQuery keeps frequently queried table data there. Eligible queries from business intelligence tools read from that memory, which lowers latency. You do not rewrite the SQL, and you pay for the reserved capacity rather than per query. A reservation that is too small does not break anything; some queries simply are not accelerated and still run.

Worked example: a fleet table holds one billion position pings, and a dashboard shows average speed per depot per hour. Step 1: define a materialized view that groups pings by depot and hour. Step 2: BigQuery stores roughly one row per depot per hour. Step 3: the dashboard queries the view and reads that small table. Step 4: a new batch of pings arrives, and BigQuery merges it into the stored result instead of rereading history.

Common mistake: assuming a materialized view is always fresh or is always used. Freshness depends on refresh timing, and BigQuery decides when a query can be answered from the view. Another mistake is buying BI Engine capacity for a workload that is really slowed by an unrelated, poorly joined query.

Consequence in a running system: a view that has not refreshed yet shows older numbers as if they were current, which can mislead operators during an incident. Confirm the data age before trusting a live figure.

questions.prompt: A bike-share company keeps one row per ride in a base table. An analyst defines a materialized view that counts rides per station per day, so the dashboard reads a small summary table. Step 1: the view is defined over the ride table, grouped by station and day, with a count of rides. Step 2: BigQuery stores roughly one row per station per day. Step 3: the dashboard queries the view. Step 4 is missing. At 9 a.m. the dashboard shows yesterday's counts, and the analyst must decide whether that figure includes rides loaded at 2 a.m. before reporting it as current. What should the analyst do?
choices: Check the view's data age, meaning when it last refreshed, against the 2 a.m. load before trusting the count.
Assume the count is current, because a materialized view is refreshed every time a query runs against it.
Rewrite the dashboard query to read the base ride table directly, so it sees the latest rows.
Increase the BI Engine reservation so the view refreshes faster.
questions.why: A materialized view can lag behind its base table, so the analyst must confirm its refresh time covers the 2 a.m. load before treating the figure as current.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines a materialized view in BigQuery?
choices: A copy of a raw table made once per day and never changed afterward.
A memory reservation that keeps frequently queried table data available for fast reads.
A saved query that is rerun from raw data each time someone opens the dashboard.
A stored table holding the result of a query over base tables, kept updated as base data changes.
questions.why: A materialized view stores the result of its defining query and is refreshed as the base tables change, which is different from a saved query that reruns from raw data, a one-time copy, or an in-memory reservation.

questions.prompt: A team's BI dashboard is slow. They have a BI Engine reservation, and the slow query joins two large tables with a poorly written join condition that is not related to the dashboard's summary metric. What is the most likely right move?
choices: Rewrite or fix the poorly joined query, because BI Engine speeds up eligible reads but does not repair an unrelated slow query.
Delete the materialized view so BigQuery stops refreshing it.
Pay for per-query billing instead of the fixed reservation to speed the join.
Increase the BI Engine reservation until the slow join becomes fast.
questions.why: BI Engine accelerates eligible reads from memory but cannot fix a query whose slowness comes from its own join logic, so the query itself needs correcting.

questions.prompt: A project reserves a small amount of BI Engine memory for a region, and the reservation is smaller than the working set of its dashboards. What happens to the dashboard queries?
choices: All dashboard queries fail until the reservation is increased.
Queries that do not fit are not accelerated, but they still run and return correct results.
BigQuery automatically rewrites the SQL to a smaller dataset so it fits in memory.
The base tables are deleted to free memory for the reservation.
questions.why: An undersized BI Engine reservation only means some queries are not accelerated; they still run normally and return the same results.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate wants to make the operations dashboard faster. Explain to them, in your own words, when you would reach for a materialized view and when BI Engine would help instead, and name one limit or tradeoff of the option you pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: A materialized view fits when many dashboard queries ask the same aggregate question, such as average speed per depot per hour. I would define the view over the raw pings so BigQuery stores the summarized result and updates it incrementally, and the dashboard reads a small table. BI Engine fits when the query is already reasonable but a BI tool hits the same hot data constantly and latency matters, because it keeps that data in reserved memory without changing the SQL. The tradeoff I would name for the view is freshness: the stored result can lag the raw table until the next refresh, and not every query shape is allowed, so an incident dashboard may need a note showing data age. For BI Engine the tradeoff is cost, since I pay for reserved memory whether or not it is busy, and a too-small reservation only speeds up part of the workload.
rubricPoints: A materialized view stores a precomputed query result that BigQuery keeps refreshed from base tables.
BI Engine keeps frequently used data in reserved in-memory capacity to speed up eligible BI queries without SQL changes.
The main limit of a materialized view is freshness lag and a restricted set of supported query shapes.
The main tradeoff of BI Engine is paying for reserved capacity, and an undersized reservation accelerates only part of the workload.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between these features under a realistic dashboard situation with latency and freshness constraints teaches the reasoning better than a fact list.

lessons.plain: A slow query is a question put to a data warehouse that takes far longer than it should or costs more than it should. Troubleshooting it means finding where the time and the scanned data go, much like tracing a slow commute by checking each stop. Before rewriting anything, you look at how much data the query read, how the engine split the work into steps, and which step took the longest. The fix usually comes from reading less data or moving less data between machines, and you only know it worked after measuring before and after.
lessons.guessPrompt: A dashboard query over a year of sales takes four minutes, but it only needs last week's totals. Before opening any tool, what would you suspect first, and why?
lessons.teach:
BigQuery is Google Cloud's serverless data warehouse, where you pay for the bytes a query scans under on-demand pricing or for slots under capacity pricing. A slot is one unit of processing capacity. A partitioned table is split into segments by a date or integer column, so a filter on that column lets the engine skip whole segments; this is called partition pruning. Clustering sorts rows inside a table by chosen columns so filters on those columns read fewer blocks. A query is run as stages, and a shuffle moves rows between workers so they can be joined or grouped.

Why this works: most slow queries read more data than the answer needs, or move a huge number of rows between workers. So troubleshooting starts with measurement: bytes processed, the execution details that show each stage's time and rows in and out, and the query plan. You look for a stage where row counts explode, a stage where one worker holds most of a key (skew), or a full scan where a filter should have pruned partitions.

Worked example: a table is partitioned by order_date, and a query filters on order_ts, a separate timestamp column, wrapped in a calculation such as DATE(order_ts) equals '2024-05-01'. Step one: bytes processed equals the whole table. Step two: the plan shows every partition being read. Step three: rewrite the filter directly on order_date, and bytes processed drops to one day's worth.

Common mistake: guessing at a fix, such as rewriting joins or adding indexes, before measuring. Consequence: in a shared project, a query that scans the whole table multiplies cost and slows other teams' jobs, so one corrected filter can help the entire project.

questions.prompt: A finance team's table of card payments, 8 TB in total, is partitioned by payment_date, meaning it is split into segments by that date, and clustered by merchant_id, meaning rows are sorted inside the table by that column. An analyst wants the total for one day, 2024-06-14, and writes WHERE CAST(payment_ts AS DATE) = '2024-06-14' on a separate timestamp column. Step one: the job reports 8 TB processed for a one-day answer. Step two: the plan shows every partition being read, because the engine cannot match a filter on payment_ts to the partition column payment_date. Step three, which is missing: what should the analyst change?
choices: Move the job to capacity pricing so the 8 TB scan costs less.
Rewrite the filter directly on payment_date, for example WHERE payment_date = '2024-06-14', so the engine can skip the other partitions.
Add a clustering column on payment_ts so the engine sorts rows by time.
Replace the total with an approximate count so fewer bytes are read.
questions.why: The filter must reference the partition column directly so partition pruning, which is skipping segments for other days, can happen.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is clustering in BigQuery, and how does it differ from partitioning?
choices: It caches the last query result for 24 hours so repeat runs cost nothing.
It sorts rows inside a table by chosen columns so filters on those columns read fewer blocks.
It splits the table into segments by a date or integer column so whole segments can be skipped.
It copies the table to every worker so joins need no shuffle.
questions.why: Clustering sorts rows inside a table by chosen columns, while partitioning is the separate act of splitting the table into date or integer segments.

questions.prompt: A job on a 3 TB clickstream table partitioned by event_date has a correct date filter, and bytes processed are one day's worth. However, the execution details show one join stage going from 40 million rows in to 6 billion rows out. Which explanation fits best?
choices: The partition filter failed, so the whole table is being scanned again.
The join key repeats heavily on both sides, so each matching pair multiplies the output rows.
The table needs a clustering column on user_id so the join reads fewer blocks.
Slots have run out, so the job is queuing for capacity.
questions.why: A stage whose output rows explode points to the join multiplying matches, and the byte count already shows that pruning worked, so the scan is not the cause.

questions.prompt: A colleague's report query is slow. Before measuring anything, they plan to add an index and rewrite two joins. What is the main problem with this plan?
choices: The fix is correct, but it should wait until a new billing month begins.
It is guessing at a fix before measuring bytes processed and the plan, so the real cause may be elsewhere.
Joins are never worth rewriting in a data warehouse.
Indexes are only useful for tables under one gigabyte.
questions.why: Troubleshooting starts with measurement, so changing joins or adding indexes before reading the bytes processed and the plan risks fixing the wrong thing.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would troubleshoot a dashboard query that has become slow. Name the first thing you measure, one specific cause you would check for, and one limit of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by measuring, not guessing. In BigQuery, the first thing I check is bytes processed for the job, because a query that scans the whole table is the most common reason a dashboard is slow and expensive. Next I open the execution details and the query plan to see which stage takes the longest and whether row counts jump sharply at a join or aggregation. If the scan is full, I check whether the filter uses the partition column directly, since wrapping it in a calculation can stop pruning. The limit of this approach is that the plan shows what happened on one run, so I rerun the query and compare bytes and timing before and after a change. Some slowness also comes from the data itself, such as skew, and that may need a different table design rather than a query edit.
rubricPoints: Measure bytes scanned and stage timings before changing the query
Check whether partition pruning or clustering is actually applied
Look for row explosion or skew at joins and aggregations
Compare before and after results, since one run's plan can mislead

suggested.rationale: Reading execution details and plans in a hands-on SQL lab builds the measuring habit that this objective depends on.

lessons.plain: Before a dashboard, analyst, or machine-learning model can use a dataset, someone has to decide who may see which parts of it and hide the parts that should stay private. Think of a shared spreadsheet where some columns are locked for most readers, some values are replaced with stars, and sensitive names are found and scrubbed before the file leaves the building. On Google Cloud this comes from three layers: permissions on who can reach the data, rules on which columns and rows each person sees, and tools that scan and mask personal information. The skill is naming the consumer, then naming the layer that protects what they need to see and nothing more.
lessons.guessPrompt: A marketing analyst needs a table of customer orders to count sales by city, but the table also contains customers' email addresses. Without any technical knowledge, what are two different ways you could keep the emails away from the analyst while still letting the city counts work?
lessons.teach:
Three ideas do most of the work here. Access control decides which people or service accounts, called principals, may use a resource. It is granted through IAM, Identity and Access Management, which attaches a role to a principal on a resource such as a project, dataset, or table. Column-level security goes further: a column can be tagged as sensitive, and only principals granted access to that tag can read it. Other readers either get an access error or see a masked value. Row-level security limits which rows a reader sees, using a filter rule. Sensitive Data Protection, formerly known as Cloud DLP (Data Loss Prevention), inspects data for patterns such as email addresses, card numbers, or national ID formats. These patterns are called infoTypes. It can then de-identify matches by masking them, replacing them with a token, or removing them.

Why this works: each layer answers a different question. IAM answers whether this person can touch this dataset at all. Column and row rules answer which parts of it they may see. Inspection answers what sensitive content is hiding in data nobody has labelled yet.

Worked example. An orders table has columns city, amount, and email, and the email column carries a sensitive tag. Step 1: the analyst holds a role that allows querying the dataset, so the table is reachable. Step 2: the analyst runs a query selecting city and amount, which succeeds. Step 3: the same analyst selects email, and the sensitive-column rule denies it or returns a masked value, because their principal lacks the reader grant for that tag. Step 4: a scan with Sensitive Data Protection over a new upload finds email-like text in a notes column nobody tagged, and flags it for review.

Common mistake: assuming that because a dashboard hides a column, the data is protected. The raw table is still readable by anyone with dataset-level read rights, and an export or copied table carries the values with it. Consequence: a masked report can sit on top of an unmasked table that a sandbox job copies to a wider audience, so the leak happens where nobody was looking.

questions.prompt: Harbor Fitness keeps a check_ins table with columns gym_id, member_id, and check_in_time. Coach Ana holds a role that lets her query the dataset, and a row filter limits her to gym 17. Step 1: Ana can reach the table, so her query runs. Step 2: her row filter returns only gym 17 rows to her. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the wider staff group reads the exports dataset and sees check-ins for every gym. Which statement fills the missing step?
choices: The nightly export job is bound by Ana's row filter, so it copies only gym 17 rows.
The nightly export job runs under its own service account, which is not bound by Ana's row filter, so it copies every gym's rows.
Sensitive Data Protection tags every check-in row as sensitive, which removes the rows from the export.
Ana's row filter is copied along with the data, so the export also holds only gym 17 rows.
questions.why: Row filters attach to the principal they were granted to, so a job running under a different service account with no such filter copies all rows, and copies carry the values with them.

questions.prompt: A billing team has a payments table where the card_number column carries a sensitive tag. Which control decides whether a specific analyst sees the real card number or a masked value?
choices: A project-level owner role, which lets the analyst change anything in the project.
A row-level filter that limits which payment rows the analyst can see.
Column-level security tied to the sensitive tag, with a reader grant for that tag.
A Sensitive Data Protection scan that reports where card numbers appear.
questions.why: Column-level security governs which columns a principal may read, and the tag grant is what lets one analyst see the real value while others get an error or a masked value.

questions.prompt: A retailer's loyalty table has a free-text feedback column that nobody has tagged. A team needs to find phone-number patterns hiding in it. Which layer does this job?
choices: Column tags, because they mark columns that are already known to be sensitive.
IAM role grants, because they name which principals may query the dataset.
Sensitive Data Protection inspection, which scans content for infoType patterns such as phone numbers.
Row-level filters, because they choose which rows a reader is allowed to see.
questions.why: Inspection finds sensitive content in data nobody has labelled, using infoType patterns, while the other three controls only grant or limit access to data already in place.

questions.prompt: A company hides the salary column in a dashboard built on a staff table, then shares the raw table with a partner group that has dataset read rights. What is the main risk?
choices: Partners can see salaries only if a row-level filter is missing, so the column hiding has no effect either way.
Partners cannot read the table at all, since any shared table is locked to the dashboard owner by default.
Partners with dataset read rights can read the raw salary values, because the dashboard's hiding does not change the stored table.
Nothing is at risk, because the dashboard's hiding is written back into the table and applies to all readers.
questions.why: A masked report does not protect the underlying table, which stays readable by anyone with dataset-level read rights, so the leak sits where nobody is looking.

lessons.explainPrompt: You are about to give an analyst team access to a sales dataset that contains customer phone numbers. Explain to a teammate how you would decide what they can see, naming the protection layer you would use for each part and one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing what the team needs: order counts and totals by region, not individual contacts. I would grant them a read role on the dataset through IAM, since that only lets them reach the dataset. Then I would tag the phone column as sensitive and keep that tag's reader grant with a small group, so everyone else gets a denial or a masked value when they select it. If the data came from a source I do not fully trust, I would run Sensitive Data Protection over it to find phone numbers in columns nobody labelled. The tradeoff is that fine-grained rules add setup and upkeep, and the scan only finds patterns it knows, so it can miss unusual formats. I would also tell the team that copying the table into another dataset brings the raw numbers along, so the protection has to travel with the data.
rubricPoints: Separates dataset-level access through IAM from column and row restrictions.
Explains that sensitive-data scanning finds known patterns, such as phone numbers, and can de-identify them.
Names a real limit: scans miss unusual formats, and fine-grained rules need ongoing upkeep.
Notes that copies or exports can carry unmasked values, so protection must travel with the data.

suggested.rationale: Deciding which principal sees which columns in a realistic data-sharing situation is best learned by reasoning through a scenario rather than memorising settings.

lessons.plain: Before a computer can learn to predict something, someone has to turn raw records into a clean table where each row is one example and each column is one piece of information about it. Imagine a delivery company that wants to guess which orders will arrive late. The raw order log has timestamps, addresses, and courier IDs in messy forms. Someone must decide which details help, convert them into useful numbers, and make sure the answer being predicted is recorded for past orders. The same cleaning must happen again each time the model is asked about a new order. This lesson covers that preparation work and how BigQuery, Google's data warehouse, can run both the preparation and a simple model using SQL.
lessons.guessPrompt: A model will learn to predict whether an order arrives late. Would you feed it the raw departure timestamp exactly as stored, or build something from it first? Explain your reasoning in a few sentences.
lessons.teach:
A feature is an input column the model uses to make a guess, such as distance in kilometres or the hour an order was placed. A label is the answer the model is trained to predict, such as a flag saying the order arrived late. Feature engineering means building those input columns from raw data, for example turning a full timestamp into an hour of day, or turning a long address into a region. Training is the step where the model learns patterns linking features to labels using past rows where the answer is known. Serving is the step where the trained model scores new rows that have no label yet.

BigQuery ML lets you create and train a model with SQL inside the warehouse, so the data does not have to be exported to a separate tool. The preparation is usually a query that selects the feature columns and the label, and that query defines exactly what the model sees.

Worked example: suppose an orders table has departure_time, distance_km, courier_id, and late_flag. Step one, a feature query derives hour_of_day from departure_time and keeps distance_km. Step two, training uses only past orders where late_flag is already known. Step three, the model learns the pattern from those rows. Step four, for a new order, the same hour_of_day and distance_km calculation runs before the model scores it.

Common mistake: leakage. If the training query includes delivery_minutes, a column filled in only after the courier arrives, the model looks accurate in testing but performs poorly in production, because that value is unknown at the moment a prediction is needed.

Consequence in a running system: if the serving path computes features differently from training, predictions drift silently over time, a problem often called training-serving skew. The remedy is one shared, versioned definition of each feature used in both places.

questions.prompt: A bike-share company called Harbor Bikes keeps a table named rides. Its columns are start_ts (a timestamp of when the ride began), station_id, rider_group, minutes_ridden, and long_ride. The long_ride column is a flag set to 1 when minutes_ridden is over 30, and it is only filled in after a ride ends. The analyst wants a model that predicts long_ride for rides that have not started yet. Step one: a feature query derives weekday from start_ts and keeps station_id. Step two: training uses only past rides where long_ride is already known. Step three: the model learns the pattern from those rows. Step four: ___ . Which step completes the process correctly?
choices: Retrain the model on the new ride's long_ride flag before scoring it
Export the rides table to a spreadsheet so weekday can be worked out by hand
Score the new ride using minutes_ridden, which is filled in once the ride ends
Apply the same weekday calculation from start_ts to the new ride before the model scores it
questions.why: At serving time, a new ride has no label and no end-of-ride data yet, so the same feature calculation used in training must run on its start_ts and station_id before the model scores it.

questions.prompt: A library wants a model that predicts whether a book loan will be returned late. Each loan row has loan_length_days, branch_id, member_since_year, and returned_late_flag, which is 1 if the book came back after its due date. In this setup, which column is the label?
choices: branch_id
loan_length_days
member_since_year
returned_late_flag
questions.why: The label is the answer the model is trained to predict, and here that answer is the returned_late_flag column; the other columns are inputs the model can use to make its guess.

questions.prompt: A support desk trains a model at ticket creation to predict whether a ticket will breach its 24-hour response target. The training query includes closed_by_agent_id, a column filled in only when an agent closes the ticket, which can be days later. What is the main risk, and what should happen?
choices: The model will run out of memory, so the column should be cast to a smaller type
The model will refuse to train because labels must be text, so the column should be converted to text
The model will look accurate in testing but perform poorly when scoring new tickets, so the column should be removed from the feature query
The model will learn faster, so the column should be kept and the training window shortened
questions.why: That column is unknown when a prediction is needed, so including it is leakage: test results look good but production predictions are poor, and the fix is to drop it from the features.

questions.prompt: A coffee chain's training query computes hour_of_day in UTC, but its serving path computes hour_of_day in local store time. The model keeps running without errors. What happens over time, and what is the standard remedy?
choices: Predictions get more accurate because the serving data is fresher, so the team should do nothing
Predictions drift silently because the same feature name means different values in training and serving, so one shared, versioned feature definition should be used in both places
Training fails with a schema mismatch, so the team should delete the serving path
BigQuery ML converts time zones automatically, so nothing changes and no remedy is needed
questions.why: This is training-serving skew: the mismatched feature calculations cause quiet degradation with no error, and the remedy is one shared, versioned definition of each feature used in both training and serving.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who will build the next prediction feature why the same feature logic must run at training time and at serving time. Then name one tradeoff of training the model inside the warehouse with SQL rather than in a separate tool.
lessons.modelAnswer: The model only learns what the training data shows it, so if a feature is computed one way during training and another way when serving, the model receives inputs it never learned from and its predictions get worse without any error message. That is why the cleaning and derivation logic should be defined once and reused in both places, ideally as a shared, versioned query or view. The tradeoff of doing this in BigQuery ML is that the data stays in the warehouse, which removes copying and keeps governance simple, but the model types and tuning options are more limited than in a dedicated machine learning framework. So for a simple, well-understood prediction over tabular data it is a good fit, while complex models may need a different tool.
rubricPoints: Features must be computed identically at training and serving time to avoid skew.
Defining feature logic once, in a shared versioned query or view, prevents drift.
Training inside the warehouse keeps data in place and simplifies access control.
The tradeoff is fewer model types and tuning options than a dedicated ML framework.

suggested.rationale: Writing the feature query and checking for leakage in SQL is the core practice here, and the planned SQL lab would let the learner do that directly.

lessons.plain: Unstructured data is material with no fixed columns, such as PDF manuals, emails, support tickets, scanned pages, or call transcripts. Before an AI system can search it by meaning, the material has to be turned into readable text, cut into passages of sensible size, and each passage turned into an embedding: a list of numbers that places its meaning near similar text. Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, is a pattern where a language model first looks up the most relevant passages and then writes its answer using them. The preparation work largely decides how good those lookups are.
lessons.guessPrompt: A support team wants a chatbot to answer questions from 400 PDF manuals. Before any AI model is involved, what do you think must happen to those PDFs so that a search for 'how do I reset the router' can find the right paragraph?
lessons.teach:
An embedding is a list of numbers, called a vector, that a model produces from a piece of text so that texts with similar meaning get vectors that sit close together. A vector index is a store that can quickly find the stored vectors nearest to a query vector. Retrieval is the step of fetching the passages whose vectors are closest to the question's vector. RAG places that step in front of a language model: the retrieved passages are pasted into the prompt, and the model answers from them.

The model can only represent what it is given. A scanned PDF gives you pixels, not words, so text extraction comes first, often using optical character recognition (OCR), which reads text out of images. Next, the text is split into chunks: passages small enough to be specific but large enough to carry their context. Each chunk keeps metadata, meaning facts about where it came from, such as the document name, section, page, and version date, so an answer can cite its source.

Worked example with a 60-page router manual. Step 1: extract text from every page. Step 2: split the text at section headings, aiming for roughly 300 to 500 words per chunk, with a small overlap so a sentence at a boundary is not lost. Step 3: attach metadata to each chunk. Step 4: send each chunk to an embedding model and store the vector beside its text and metadata. Step 5: at question time, embed 'how do I reset the router' the same way, retrieve the closest few chunks, and pass them to the language model.

Common mistake: chunking by a fixed character count that splits a procedure in half, so the retrieved chunk contains step 1 but not the warning that applies to step 3. Another is embedding a whole 60-page document as one vector, which blurs its meaning until it matches almost nothing well.

In a running system, when the manual is revised, the old chunks must be replaced, or the assistant keeps quoting a superseded procedure. Refreshing the chunks and vectors has to be part of the pipeline, not a one-off task.

questions.prompt: A small bakery-equipment maker has 85 scanned service bulletins, each a single-page image. Its team runs this pipeline: (1) run optical character recognition (OCR, which reads text out of images) on each bulletin to get its words; (2) split each bulletin into one chunk per numbered fix, since each fix is a self-contained procedure; (3) [missing step]; (4) send each chunk to an embedding model and store the resulting vector beside its text. A support bot will later answer customer questions using these chunks. Which step belongs in the blank?
choices: Skip OCR for later bulletins and embed the raw image pixels directly, because the embedding model can read images without any text extraction step
Remove any chunk under 300 words so that the stored vectors represent only substantial passages of text
Embed all 85 bulletins as one combined vector so the search covers the whole collection in a single lookup at question time
Attach metadata such as bulletin number, machine model, and revision date to each chunk
questions.why: Each chunk should keep metadata about its source so that the bot can cite where an answer came from, and this is added after chunking and before embedding.

questions.prompt: In a retrieval system, what is the job of a vector index?
choices: It stores the original text files so that people can read them in their source format
It translates a question into a different human language before the model reads it
It deletes vectors that have not been retrieved for thirty days to save storage
It quickly finds the stored vectors that are nearest to a query vector
questions.why: A vector index is a store built to find the nearest stored vectors to a query vector quickly, which is the core of retrieval.

questions.prompt: A team embeds a 120-page employee policy handbook as one single vector. When staff ask specific questions, the assistant rarely retrieves the right passage. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The vector index was not given the document's version date, so it ranks the passages randomly
One vector averages the meaning of many topics, so it matches almost nothing well; the handbook should be split into chunks first
Retrieval only works on questions that are written as full sentences, and staff use keywords
The embedding model cannot process any document longer than ten pages, so the vector is empty
questions.why: Embedding a whole long document as one vector blurs its meaning across topics, so it fails to match specific questions; splitting into focused chunks fixes this.

questions.prompt: A company updates its benefits guide every January. Its support assistant has begun quoting last year's superseded rules. Which change to the pipeline best prevents this?
