choices: Replace the old chunks and their vectors whenever the guide is revised, as a standing part of the refresh pipeline
Keep the old vectors and add the new ones beside them, so the assistant can choose the newer answer
Ask the language model to ignore any passage that mentions a year earlier than the current one
Increase the number of retrieved passages from three to thirty so the correct answer is more likely included
questions.why: Stale chunks and vectors must be replaced when the source changes, and the refresh has to be part of the pipeline rather than a one-off task.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only used spreadsheets how a RAG assistant gets from a folder of scanned PDFs to a grounded answer. Name one limit or tradeoff of the chunk size you would choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: A scanned PDF has no searchable text, so first we extract text, using OCR for the scanned pages. We then split the text into chunks, typically a few hundred words each, with a small overlap so ideas at the edges survive. Each chunk gets metadata: document name, section, page, and version date. An embedding model turns each chunk into a vector, and we store the vector with its text and metadata. When a user asks a question, we embed the question the same way, find the nearest chunks, and give those to the language model, which answers from them and can cite the page. The tradeoff with chunk size is precision against context. Small chunks match a question tightly but can lose the surrounding steps or warnings. Large chunks keep context but dilute the meaning of each vector and use more of the model's prompt space.
rubricPoints: Scanned or non-text files must be turned into text first, for example with OCR.
Text is split into chunks sized to keep meaning and context, often with a small overlap.
Each chunk keeps metadata such as source, section, page, and version for citation and refresh.
An embedding model converts each chunk and the question into vectors, so retrieval finds passages with similar meaning.
Chunk size is a tradeoff between precise matching and preserved context.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a realistic document-to-answer situation adds more here than any listed mission, since none currently covers embeddings or retrieval.

lessons.plain: Before one team hands its data to another, someone has to set the ground rules: what the data means, how fresh it must be, how good it must be, who may see it, and what happens when its format changes. Think of a shared kitchen with a sign-up sheet and cleaning rules. Without those rules, the people downstream cannot trust what they receive, and the people upstream cannot safely change anything. Defining the rules is the step that turns a pile of data into something a dashboard, a model, or another team can depend on.
lessons.guessPrompt: A marketing team wants to build a weekly dashboard from a table that the product team updates whenever they like. Name three things the two teams should agree on before the dashboard goes live, and say why each one matters.
lessons.teach:
A sharing rule is a written agreement between the team that produces a dataset and the teams that consume it. It states what the data means, how it is shaped, how fresh it is, how good it must be, who may read it, and how changes will be announced. The producer is the team that creates and owns the data. A consumer is anything that reads it, such as a dashboard, a model training job, or another team's pipeline. The schema is the list of fields with their names and types. Freshness is how old the newest data may be. Data quality means checks such as no missing keys and values inside an agreed range. Deprecation is the planned removal of a field, announced ahead of time with a date.

These rules matter because consumers build logic on assumptions. If a field silently changes meaning, every downstream number changes with it, and nothing fails loudly.

Worked example. A ride platform publishes a daily trips table. Its agreement says: fare_usd is a decimal in US dollars and is never null; the table is complete by 06:00 UTC; at most 0.5 percent of rows may fail validation; and driver_id is restricted to finance. Now the producer wants to store fares in cents. Step one: they do not simply change the column. Step two: they publish a new field, fare_cents, and announce that fare_usd will be deprecated on a stated date 30 days out. Step three: consumers migrate during that window. Step four: after the date, fare_usd is removed and the agreement moves to version 2.

Common mistake: treating a table that can be read as a table that can be shared. Access without written rules forces consumers to guess at meaning and freshness.

Consequence: if fare_usd quietly switched to cents, revenue dashboards would show values a hundred times too large, and nobody would see an error until someone noticed a strange chart. Rules only protect anyone when someone enforces them, which is why the producer's validation checks belong inside the agreement.

questions.prompt: A food delivery company publishes a daily orders table. Its sharing rule says eta_minutes is a whole number of minutes and is never null. The producer now wants to store delivery estimates in seconds, so they follow these steps. Step one: they do not change eta_minutes in place. Step two: they publish a new field, eta_seconds, and announce that eta_minutes will be deprecated on a stated date 45 days out. Step three: [missing step to complete]. Step four: after the date, eta_minutes is removed and the agreement moves to version 2. Which choice correctly fills in step three?
choices: The producer silently converts the stored eta_minutes values to seconds so old readers keep working without changes.
The producer deletes eta_minutes on the announced date without any further notice to consumers.
Consumers move their logic to read eta_seconds during the announced 45-day window.
The producer keeps eta_minutes indefinitely and never mentions eta_seconds in the agreement.
questions.why: Step three is the window in which consumers migrate to the new field before the announced removal date, which is the purpose of announcing a deprecation ahead of time.

questions.prompt: A logistics team's sharing agreement says the shipments table will be complete by 05:30 UTC each day. A dashboard that refreshes at 05:45 UTC shows a shipment whose newest status row is from the previous day, and the team's validation checks show no failed rows. Which clause of the agreement has been missed?
choices: The deprecation rule, because a field has been announced for removal.
The freshness rule, because the newest data is older than the agreed limit.
The consumer rule, because the dashboard is reading the table too early.
The schema, because the field names and types have changed.
questions.why: Freshness is defined as how old the newest data may be, and here the data is older than the agreed completion time while the quality checks are passing, so the freshness clause is what has been missed.

questions.prompt: A weather data producer renames the column cust_id to customer_id in a shared table and announces the change on the same day it goes live, with no deprecation window. The values in the column are unchanged. What is the main problem with this approach?
choices: Renaming a column is always safe as long as the values stay the same.
The only team affected is the producer, since consumers do not read column names.
The problem is that customer_id is longer, which slows down dashboards that sort by column name.
The change alters the schema without the planned notice that lets consumers migrate, so their queries can break with no warning period.
questions.why: Deprecation exists so that schema changes are announced ahead of time with a date, and an immediate rename removes that window, leaving consumers who depend on the old name without time to adapt.

questions.prompt: A data science team trains a churn prediction model by reading a sessions table that another team produces. In the sharing rules, which term describes the data science team's role?
choices: Consumer, because it is anything that reads the dataset, including a model training job.
Deprecation, because the team decides when old fields are removed.
Producer, because the team uses the data to create something new.
Schema, because the team defines the list of fields the model needs.
questions.why: A consumer is defined as anything that reads the dataset, and a model training job reading the sessions table fits that definition, while the producer is the team that creates and owns the data.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a data sharing rule is, using one example from a team you know, and name one limit or tradeoff of writing these rules up front.
lessons.modelAnswer: A data sharing rule is a written agreement between the team that produces a dataset and the teams that read it. It covers what each field means, its type, how fresh the data must be, which quality checks must pass, who may access it, and how changes are announced. For example, if our order service publishes a daily orders table, the rule might say the total column is in dollars with no nulls, and the table is ready by seven each morning. The main tradeoff is time. Writing rules and agreeing on versioning and deprecation dates slows the producer down, and the rules go stale if nobody owns them. Still, without them, a silent change such as switching units can corrupt every downstream report before anyone notices. So I would keep the rules short, back them with validation checks, and review them whenever the schema changes.
rubricPoints: A sharing rule is a written agreement between a data producer and its consumers.
It covers meaning and schema, freshness, quality checks, access, and how changes are announced.
A concrete example shows the rule protecting consumers from a silent change.
Naming a tradeoff, such as the upfront time cost or rules going stale, shows understanding of limits.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the agreement back to a teammate, including its tradeoff, is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine practises writing these rules.

lessons.plain: Publishing a dataset means turning data that a pipeline produced into something other people can safely rely on. Raw data is often messy: duplicates, late records, mixed time zones, and columns nobody has explained. Publishing is the step where someone cleans it into a defined shape, writes down what each column means, states how fresh it is and who to ask when it breaks, and then gives consumers access to that stable version instead of the working copy. Think of a restaurant menu: the kitchen can change anything behind the counter, but the menu promises a fixed set of dishes with clear descriptions.
lessons.guessPrompt: A dashboard team reads a table your pipeline rewrites every hour. Last week the pipeline renamed one column, and nobody told the dashboard team, so the dashboard broke. What single change to how the data is handed over would have prevented this, and why?
lessons.teach:
Publishing a dataset means making a deliberately prepared version of data available to named consumers under a promise. A consumer is any person or system that reads the data, such as a dashboard, a machine learning training job, or another team. A schema is the list of columns and their types. Freshness is how recent the data is, for example refreshed by 06:00 UTC, where UTC is the standard world time zone used for scheduling. The contract of a published dataset is the combination of its schema, the meaning of each column, its freshness target, a named owner who answers questions, and a rule for how changes are announced. A staging table is a working copy that the pipeline writes into and may change at any time.

Why it works: consumers couple themselves to whatever they read. If they read a staging table, every upstream change reaches them immediately. If they read a published object, the owner can rebuild internals behind it while keeping the contract stable, and can announce breaking changes before they happen.

Worked example. A ride-events pipeline lands raw events in a staging table. Step 1: remove exact duplicate rows that arrive from retried uploads. Step 2: convert all timestamps to UTC and rename trip_ts to trip_time_utc. Step 3: drop rows with no driver id and record how many were dropped. Step 4: write the result to a dataset called rides_published with a documented schema, an owner set to the fleet analytics team, and a freshness target of 06:00 UTC daily. Step 5: grant read access to the reporting group.

Common mistake: publishing the raw staging table because it is already built, then letting consumers query it directly. The first upstream rename silently breaks every report built on it.

Consequence in a running system: a broken published dataset stops dashboards, and a model trained on duplicated rows can quietly give wrong answers. That is why the owner must be reachable and changes must be versioned. Publishing fixes the contract, but the data is only as trustworthy as the checks run before each release.

questions.prompt: A city air-quality agency collects hourly readings from 340 sensors. Its pipeline runs these steps in order: (1) drop rows where the sensor id is blank, (2) remove exact duplicate rows left by a retried upload, (3) convert measurement times to UTC, the standard world time zone used for scheduling, and rename meas_ts to measured_at_utc, (4) [step not shown], (5) write the result to a dataset called aq_hourly with an owner set to the environmental health unit and a freshness target of 07:00 UTC daily. Which choice correctly fills step 4?
choices: Document what each column means, including its unit, and agree in advance how schema changes will be announced
Copy the staging table's schema unchanged so that consumers notice no difference
Give the dashboard's service account write access to aq_hourly so it can fix bad rows itself
Rename the sensor id column to match the dashboard tool's naming so the join works
questions.why: Step 4 is where the column meanings and the change-announcement rule are set, which are parts of the published contract, while the other choices either skip that work or weaken the owner's control.

questions.prompt: A dataset's contract includes a freshness target of 09:30 UTC. Which statement describes that target correctly?
choices: It is the time the owner must be reached by phone if a query fails
It is the promise of how recent the data will be by that time, such as refreshed by 09:30 UTC
It is the list of columns and their types that consumers may rely on
It is the timestamp of the newest row in the staging table at all times
questions.why: A freshness target is a promise about how recent the published data will be, which is different from the schema, the owner's contact role, or the staging table's contents.

questions.prompt: A fraud-scoring training job reads the internal staging table of a pipeline directly. A teammate renames a column in that staging table during a cleanup. What is the most likely outcome and root cause?
choices: Nothing happens, because staging tables are backed up every night
The owner should have edited the job's code instead of the staging table
The job breaks or misreads, because it coupled itself to a table the pipeline may change at any time instead of reading a published object
The job adopts the new name by itself, since training jobs detect schema changes
questions.why: Consumers that read a staging table inherit every upstream change immediately, which is why the job breaks or silently misreads the renamed column rather than being protected by a published, versioned contract.

questions.prompt: A team publishes a dataset with a documented schema, a freshness target and a named owner, but it has no rule for announcing changes. What is the main risk?
choices: Breaking changes can reach consumers without warning
The owner stops being responsible for the data
Consumers cannot read the dataset until a rule exists
The dataset will stop refreshing on its freshness target
questions.why: Without an announcement rule the owner has no agreed way to give consumers notice before a breaking change, so reports and models can break unexpectedly.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what it means to publish a dataset, and name one limit or tradeoff of publishing a curated copy instead of letting consumers read the raw pipeline output.
lessons.modelAnswer: Publishing a dataset means the pipeline's output is cleaned into a defined shape, documented, given an owner and a freshness target, and exposed to consumers as a stable object. The point is that consumers depend on a contract rather than on internal working tables, so the owner can fix or reshape the pipeline without breaking reports. The tradeoff is cost and lag: maintaining a curated copy means extra storage, extra compute to rebuild it, and a delay between raw arrival and publication, so consumers who need the newest records may have to accept a slightly older, cleaner view. Publishing also does not make the data correct by itself. It only makes the promises visible, so quality checks have to run before each release, or a published dataset just presents bad data with a nicer label.
rubricPoints: Defines publishing as a curated, documented, stable version that consumers depend on.
Names what a contract includes, such as schema, column meaning, freshness, and an owner.
Explains why consumers should not read raw staging tables directly.
States a tradeoff such as extra cost, delay to publication, or staleness versus cleanliness.
Notes that publishing does not by itself guarantee data quality.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is articulating a dataset contract and its tradeoffs to a teammate, and no listed mission or planned engine practises that directly.

lessons.plain: Publishing a report means turning a one-off analysis into something other people can rely on without redoing the work. Think of a restaurant: a chef can cook each dish from raw ingredients every time someone orders, but a printed menu with fixed recipes lets every guest get the same dish with no surprises. In data work, publishing gives a dashboard, chart, or summary a stable home, a clear name, a known refresh time, and an owner who answers questions when the numbers look wrong. The goal is that a reader can trust the figure they see today the same way they trusted it yesterday.
lessons.guessPrompt: A dispatch manager and a finance analyst both open on-time rate dashboards built from the same trip table, and the numbers differ by 8 points. What do you think is the most likely cause, and what would you change before anyone sees either number again?
lessons.teach:
A published report is a shared, named result that a defined audience reads on a known schedule. It has four parts: the data it draws on, the logic that turns raw rows into metrics, a refresh schedule that says when the numbers update, and an owner who is responsible when they are wrong. A query someone ran once in an editor is an analysis. It becomes a report when other people depend on it.

Why it works: the metric definition is written down once and computed in one place, so every chart that reads it shows the same figure. Consumers read results instead of reconstructing the logic, and a change to the definition is made in one place and reaches every reader.

Worked example. A dispatch manager wants a weekly on-time delivery rate. The raw trip events table has three problems: a retried upload wrote some trips twice, timestamps are stored in UTC while the manager reads local time, and some trips have no promised window. Step 1: keep one row per trip ID. Step 2: convert arrival times to the local time zone. Step 3: define on-time as arrival at or before the end of the promised window, and state explicitly that trips with no window are excluded. Step 4: save this logic as a named view, set it to refresh every Monday at 06:00, and record the operations data team as owner. The dashboard reads that view and nothing else.

Common mistake: publishing the raw query and letting each dashboard reimplement the filters. Two dashboards then disagree by several points and nobody can say which is right.

Consequence: if the source column is renamed, the scheduled refresh fails. Without a freshness check or an owner watching it, the dashboard keeps showing last week's number under this week's date, which is worse than showing an error.

A published report is only as trustworthy as its definition, its refresh, and its owner.

questions.prompt: A retail chain wants a weekly return rate for its online orders, defined as returned units divided by shipped units. The raw order-lines table has three problems. Step 1: keep one row per order-line ID, because a sync job wrote some lines twice. Step 2: drop lines flagged as test orders from the staging store. Step 3: define the rate using shipped units only as the denominator, and state explicitly that units cancelled before shipping are excluded from both the numerator and the denominator. Step 4 has not been written yet. Step 4 is the step that makes this a published report, meaning the step that saves the logic as a named view (a saved query that other tools read like a table), sets how often it recalculates, and names who is responsible for it. Which option completes Step 4?
choices: Export the cleaned rows to a spreadsheet and email it to managers on the first working day of the month
Ask an analyst to re-run the query by hand each Friday and paste the result into a slide deck
Save the logic as a named view, set it to refresh daily at 05:00, and record the store operations team as owner
Let each regional dashboard copy the three filters so that each team can adjust them locally
questions.why: Step 4 turns the logic into a shared, named result with a refresh schedule and an accountable owner, which is what the teaching text defines as a published report.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the four parts the teaching text says a published report has?
choices: A color scheme chosen separately for each dashboard
An owner who is responsible when the numbers are wrong
A refresh schedule that says when the numbers update
The data the report draws on
questions.why: The four parts are the data, the logic that turns rows into metrics, the refresh schedule, and the owner; a color scheme is a visual choice and is not one of them.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm publishes a weekly average pallet dwell time. One dashboard excludes pallets on hold and another includes them, so the two show figures several points apart. Which change addresses the root cause?
choices: Define the metric once as a named view and have both dashboards read only that view
Rename the two dashboards so readers can tell which figure to trust
Ask each team to add its own hold filter and note the difference in a footnote
Refresh both dashboards more often so the gap closes sooner
questions.why: The teaching text says the metric definition should be written once and computed in one place so every chart reading it shows the same figure; each dashboard reimplementing filters is the common mistake.

questions.prompt: A warehouse publishes a weekly cycle-count accuracy report. The engineer who built it has left the company, the report name is still listed, and the scheduled refresh still runs without errors. What is the most serious risk?
choices: Query costs drop because nobody is re-running the logic by hand
Figures can go wrong with no one accountable for noticing or fixing them
Charts load more slowly once the refresh runs unattended
Other teams stop reading the report, so the numbers stop being used
questions.why: The teaching text says a published report depends on its owner, and without one, a wrong figure can keep being shown with no one responsible for catching it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what makes a report published rather than just a query someone ran, and name one tradeoff of publishing it as a shared, scheduled artifact.
lessons.modelAnswer: A query someone runs once is an analysis. It becomes a published report when the metric definition is fixed in one place, the input is cleaned and deduplicated, the numbers refresh on a known schedule, and a named owner answers when they look wrong. Readers then use the published result instead of rebuilding the logic, so two dashboards show the same figure. The tradeoff is maintenance. When the source changes, the refresh can break, and the owner has to notice. A shared definition is also slower to change, because editing it changes every chart at once, so the team needs a process for definition changes. Without a freshness check, a stale number can look current, so I would always show the as-of time next to the figure.
rubricPoints: Says publishing means a fixed, named result with one agreed metric definition, not an ad hoc query.
Mentions a refresh schedule and a freshness signal so readers know how current the numbers are.
Names an owner responsible for errors, changes, and questions.
Names a real tradeoff such as maintenance burden or slower definition changes.

suggested.rationale: Deciding what to publish and who owns it is best learned by reasoning through a realistic stakeholder disagreement, which an exam-style scenario supports better than any single listed mission.

lessons.plain: Sometimes one team has data that another team needs, such as sales figures, weather readings, or product details. The old way was to export a file and send it, which creates copies that quickly go out of date. Analytics Hub is a Google Cloud feature that lets a team offer its data to others so they can read the live version without receiving a copy. The data stays with its owner, and the people who need it can find it, subscribe to it, and query it. This lesson covers the sharing mechanism only, not the rules governing who may share what.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a supplier needs this week's sales figures from a retailer, is it better for the retailer to email a weekly copy, or to let the supplier read one live table? Explain why in a sentence or two.
lessons.teach: Analytics Hub is a feature of BigQuery, Google Cloud's data warehouse (a database built for scanning large amounts of data with analytical queries). It lets one team share datasets with other teams or organizations without copying them. The core idea is publish once and read in place. Four terms matter. A data exchange is a named catalog that holds listings, like a shelf in a shared library. A listing is an entry in an exchange that points to a dataset the owner wants to share, with a description so others can find it. A subscriber is a consumer who subscribes to a listing. Subscribing creates a linked dataset in the subscriber's own project, which is a read-only reference to the publisher's underlying tables. Because the subscriber queries the live tables, not a stale copy, there is one source of truth. When the publisher updates a table, every subscriber sees the change on their next query, and nobody maintains separate exports. Worked example: a retailer creates an exchange called partner-data and adds a listing for its daily store sales dataset. A supplier browses the exchange and subscribes to that listing. BigQuery creates a linked dataset in the supplier's project. The supplier runs a query on the linked dataset and sees the same rows the retailer sees. Common mistake: assuming a subscription gives the subscriber a writable copy they can change or keep forever. The linked dataset is read-only, and if the publisher removes the listing or revokes access, the subscriber loses it. Consequence: a dashboard built on a linked dataset breaks when the publisher unpublishes the listing, so the consuming team needs to know who owns the source and how it can change.

questions.prompt: A city transit agency creates an exchange called metro-open and adds a listing for its bus route ridership table. A university transport lab browses the exchange and subscribes to that listing. Step 1: the lab's project gets a linked dataset that refers to the agency's table. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: the lab runs a query and sees the same rows the agency sees. Which choice correctly fills the missing step?
choices: The agency copies the ridership table into the lab's project, and the lab then owns and edits that copy.
The lab gets write access to the agency's dataset so it can add its own survey rows alongside the transit counts.
The agency exports a CSV of the table each month, and the lab loads it into a new table in its own project.
The lab's project gets a read-only linked dataset that points to the agency's live tables, so the lab queries the source directly.
questions.why: The linked dataset is a read-only reference to the publisher's live tables, which is why the lab sees the same rows as the agency and not a separate copy.

questions.prompt: A pharmacy chain publishes a listing for its inventory table in an exchange. A distributor subscribes. On Thursday the pharmacy corrects a stock count in that table. What does the distributor's query return on Friday?
choices: The distributor sees a copy that the pharmacy must re-export by hand each week.
The distributor sees Monday's count, because a subscription keeps a copy from the day it was created.
The query fails until the distributor manually refreshes the subscription.
The distributor sees the corrected count, because the linked dataset reads the publisher's live table.
questions.why: A subscriber queries the publisher's live tables through the linked dataset, so a correction made by the publisher appears on the next query with no extra step.

questions.prompt: A museum publishes a listing for its visitor counts. A research group subscribes and builds a dashboard on its linked dataset. The museum then removes the listing from the exchange. What happens to the dashboard?
choices: The dashboard keeps working by using the research group's own saved copy of the data.
The linked dataset becomes writable, so the group can keep it and continue the dashboard.
BigQuery automatically sends the group a new copy of the counts so the dashboard keeps running.
The dashboard's queries fail, because the group loses access to the listing and its linked dataset.
questions.why: Subscribers hold only a read-only reference that depends on the publisher's listing, so removing the listing removes their access and breaks anything built on it.

questions.prompt: A water utility publishes a listing for its meter readings in an exchange called aqua-share. A regional planner subscribes, then tries to insert a corrected reading directly into the linked dataset. What is the result?
choices: The insert succeeds but only in the planner's project, and it is removed when the subscription renews.
The insert succeeds and overwrites the utility's table on the next sync.
The insert is rejected because the linked dataset is read-only, so the correction must go through the utility, which owns the source.
The insert succeeds, and the planner's correction also appears in the utility's table.
questions.why: A linked dataset is read-only, so a subscriber cannot change the publisher's data and must ask the owner of the source to make the correction.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Analytics Hub lets another team use our BigQuery data, and name one limit or tradeoff of sharing this way compared with exporting a file.
lessons.modelAnswer: Analytics Hub works through an exchange, which is a catalog, and listings inside it that point to datasets we choose to share. When another team subscribes, BigQuery creates a linked dataset in their project. That dataset is a read-only reference to our tables, so they query the live data and we don't have to ship exports. The main tradeoff is dependency. Their reports only work while our listing exists and access stays in place. If we unpublish or change the source, their queries fail or change without warning. An exported file keeps working after we stop sending updates, but it goes stale and can be copied and changed. So sharing live is better for a single source of truth, but the consumers need to treat our data as something they depend on.
rubricPoints: Defines an exchange as a catalog and a listing as a published entry pointing to a dataset
Explains that subscribing creates a read-only linked dataset that reads the live tables, not a copy
Names a limit: consumers depend on the publisher, and removing the listing or access breaks their queries
Contrasts this with file exports, which go stale but keep working independently

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practices BigQuery sharing, so the core facts and console steps are best learned by reading.

lessons.plain: Minimizing cost against actual business need means paying only for the data work the business really asks for. Every pipeline run, stored byte, query scan, and always-on machine costs money, so the question is not how cheap can we be but how much does each part of the platform need to deliver. A report read once a week does not need the same fresh, expensive setup as a live fraud check. Good cost work starts by writing down what the business needs (how fresh the data must be, how long to keep it, how fast answers must arrive, how often it is read) and then removing spending that serves nobody. It is like heating a house: you heat the rooms people use, at the temperature they need, rather than the whole building at full power all night.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team keeps every raw event forever in fast, expensive storage, but the only reader is a monthly report that uses just last quarter's data. Name two things you would change first and say why, using your own reasoning.
lessons.teach:
A business need is the written requirement a data system must meet: how fresh the data must be, how long it must be kept, how quickly answers must come back, and how often it is read. A cost driver is something you are billed for. In data platforms the main drivers are how much data you store and in which storage class, how long compute machines or pipelines run, how many bytes each query scans, and data moved between regions. Right-sizing means matching capacity to measured use rather than to a guess. A storage class is a price tier: rarely read data can sit in a cheaper tier, but retrieving it often costs extra and takes longer. Partitioning splits a large table into slices, usually by date, so a query can read only the slices it needs. A lifecycle rule automatically moves or deletes data after a set age. Cost falls without changing what users receive, because you stop paying for units nobody consumes.

Worked example: a table holds 1,000 daily slices of events, 10 TB in total. A dashboard needs only yesterday's counts. Unpartitioned, each query scans all 10 TB. Step 1: write the need: yesterday only, refreshed hourly. Step 2: partition the table by event date, so one query reads one slice, about 10 GB, roughly a thousand times less. Step 3: add a lifecycle rule that moves data older than 90 days to a cheaper archive tier, because the audit requirement is seven years but nobody queries the old rows often. The dashboard cost drops sharply and old storage gets cheaper, with no change to what the business sees.

Common mistake: cutting cost by deleting or downgrading data the business still needs, such as records kept for audit, or by putting daily-read data in the cheapest archive tier and paying retrieval fees that exceed the savings.

In a running system, a deletion rule set too early shows up only later, when a quarterly audit finds missing rows. A cheap archive tier on hot data makes dashboards slow and more expensive than before.

Every cost you keep should trace back to a written business need, and every need should be checked against how the data is actually read.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm stores 2 TB of parcel scan events in one unpartitioned table. Its weekly carrier report needs only the last 7 days. Customs rules require scan records kept for five years, and almost nobody reads records older than 60 days. Step 1 is done: the need is written as last 7 days, refreshed weekly, five-year retention. Step 2 is done: the table is partitioned by scan date, so each weekly run reads only about 7 slices. The firm still needs step 3, the step that handles the old records without breaking the retention need. Which step is it?
choices: Add a lifecycle rule that moves scans older than 60 days to a cheaper tier automatically, and keeps them for the full five years.
Move all records older than 7 days into the cheapest archive tier so the weekly report reads them there.
Delete scan records older than 60 days to cut storage, since few people read them.
Turn off partitioning so the table is stored as one object and no slices need managing.
questions.why: A lifecycle rule moves old records to a cheaper tier automatically, which cuts cost while the five-year retention need is still met, unlike deleting them or putting weekly-read data in archive.

questions.prompt: In the sense used in this course, what is a storage class?
choices: A price tier: rarely read data costs less to hold, but getting it back can cost extra and take longer.
The number of machines that run a pipeline at the same time.
A rule that deletes data automatically once it reaches a set age.
A folder naming convention that groups tables by the team that owns them.
questions.why: A storage class is a price tier, and the trade-off is lower holding cost against retrieval fees and slower access for rarely read data.

questions.prompt: A team runs a cluster of eight machines around the clock, but their nightly job runs for only 2 hours and nothing else uses the cluster. Which change best matches the cost to actual use?
choices: Keep the cluster running and add more machines so the nightly job finishes faster.
Partition the cluster by night so each machine handles one hour of work.
Start the cluster for the nightly job, shut it down when the job ends, and size it to the measured load.
Move the cluster's disks into the archive tier so the idle hours cost less.
questions.why: Compute is billed for how long it runs, so right-sizing and running only for the measured 2-hour window removes the cost of idle hours without changing the output.

questions.prompt: A fraud team's review table of 80 GB is queried every few minutes all day. Someone moves it to the cheapest archive tier to save money. What is the likely result?
choices: Each query scans fewer bytes, so the monthly bill drops sharply.
Retrieval fees and slower reads can make the table cost more and respond more slowly than before.
Costs stay the same, because archive tiers only change where bytes are physically stored.
The table is deleted automatically, because archive tiers expire data after a fixed period.
questions.why: Archive tiers suit rarely read data; for a table read every few minutes, retrieval fees and delays outweigh the lower storage price.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a data platform is spending more than it needs to, and name one cost cut that could hurt the business and how you would avoid it.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing the business needs for each dataset: how fresh it must be, how long it must be kept, and who reads it and how often. Then I would compare those needs with what we actually pay for: storage by tier, data scanned per query, and how long pipelines and machines run. Anything paid for but not needed is a candidate for cutting. The risk is cutting something the business still depends on. For example, moving old data to an archive tier looks cheap, but if an audit or a rarely run report needs it, retrieval fees or a missing dataset will cost more than we saved. So before any cut, I would confirm the requirement with its owner, test the change on a copy, and keep a rollback path. I would also record the decision so the next person knows why the data is kept.
rubricPoints: Ties each cost to a written business need such as freshness, retention, or read frequency
Names concrete cost drivers like storage tier, bytes scanned, and compute run time
Gives one specific cut and the business risk it could create
Describes a check before cutting, such as confirming with the owner or testing on a copy

suggested.rationale: A planned cost model in fictional credits would let the learner compare spend against a stated need and see how each cut changes the bill.

lessons.plain: Some data jobs matter far more than others. A nightly job that calculates what customers are billed must finish on time, while an analyst's exploratory query can wait. Ensuring enough resources are available means setting aside enough computing power, memory, and other capacity so the critical jobs can always start and finish, even when other work piles up. It is less about buying more machines and more about deciding who gets capacity first when there is not enough for everyone. A good answer names which jobs are critical, how much room they need at their busiest, and what happens when demand spikes.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company runs a nightly billing job and also lets many analysts run heavy queries at any time on the same shared pool of computing power. One afternoon the analysts start a large batch of queries and the billing job begins running late. What single change would most protect the billing job, and why might that change not be enough on its own?
lessons.teach:
Capacity is the computing power a data platform can use at a given moment, such as processing slots, workers, CPU, memory, and disk throughput. A business-critical process is one whose delay or failure has a direct business cost, such as a billing run, a fraud-score refresh, or a report a regulator expects by a deadline. Ensuring enough resources means making sure such a process can get the capacity it needs when it needs it.

It works by separating guaranteed capacity from shared capacity. A guarantee, sometimes called a reservation, sets aside a fixed share for a particular workload. Priority decides which work is served first when the total is short. A quota is a limit on how much a project may use; it is a ceiling, not a promise that capacity exists when you ask for it. Autoscaling adds workers when demand rises, but it takes time and has its own maximum, so it cannot be relied on for a sudden spike.

Worked example. The shared pool has 120 units. The nightly billing job needs 100 units and must finish by 06:00. Step 1: measure the critical need at its busiest, which is 100 units. Step 2: reserve 100 units for billing. Step 3: leave 20 units for everything else. Step 4: at 22:00 analysts start heavy queries; they can use only the 20 shared units and queue the rest. Step 5: billing runs at full speed and finishes at 04:30. Without the reservation, the analysts would have taken most of the pool and billing would have crawled.

Common mistake: assuming that because a platform can scale, critical work never competes with anything. Scaling takes minutes, and the maximum may already be reached when the spike arrives.

Consequence: when a critical job runs late, the systems that depend on it, such as invoices and dashboards, show stale or missing data, and the business often notices before the engineering team does. Sizing this protection requires knowing each critical job's peak need, plus headroom for growth.

questions.prompt: A freight company runs a shared pool of 48 worker nodes. Its customs manifest job must finish before a 05:30 filing window. At its busiest, the manifest job needs 36 nodes. The team's rule is to keep 25 percent headroom above peak need for growth. Step 1: the peak need is 36 nodes. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: reserve 45 nodes for the manifest job. Step 4: at 21:00 a clickstream backfill starts and can use only the unreserved nodes, so it queues the rest.
choices: Add the 25 percent headroom to the 36-node peak, giving 45 nodes
Divide the peak need by two to get the reservation, which gives 18 nodes
Skip the reservation and rely on autoscaling to add the extra nodes at run time
Reserve all 48 nodes so that no other work can start during the window
questions.why: The headroom rule says to add 25 percent to the measured peak, and 36 multiplied by 1.25 gives the 45-node reservation used in step 3.

questions.prompt: A team's project quota allows 200 vCPUs. At 02:00 the shared region has only 150 vCPUs free. Which statement about the quota is correct?
choices: The quota is a ceiling on what the team may use, so a request can still be refused or queued when the free capacity is short
The quota will automatically add the missing 50 vCPUs within seconds if autoscaling is enabled
The quota guarantees that all 200 vCPUs will be available whenever the team asks for them
The quota reserves 200 vCPUs exclusively for the team's critical jobs
questions.why: A quota is a limit on usage, not a promise that capacity exists at the moment of the request, so the 150 free vCPUs can still constrain the team.

questions.prompt: A fraud-scoring service uses autoscaling with a maximum of 30 workers. A flash sale raises demand to the equivalent of 45 workers within a few minutes. The operations team assumes autoscaling will cover the gap. What is the main failure?
choices: Priority settings will move fraud scoring ahead of every other job, so capacity is not needed
The autoscaler stops at its 30-worker maximum and takes time to add workers, so part of the spike goes unserved without a reservation sized to peak
Scoring stays on time because the spike is short enough for queued work to clear
The autoscaler will scale past its maximum once it detects the spike
questions.why: Autoscaling has its own maximum and needs time to respond, so it cannot cover a sudden spike beyond that maximum without a reserved share sized to peak need.

questions.prompt: A regulator report and a marketing export both run on one shared pool, which is short of capacity at night. Which setting decides which of the two is served first when the total is short?
choices: The quota assigned to the marketing project
The priority given to each job
The autoscaling maximum of the pool
The number of dashboards that read the export
questions.why: Priority decides which work is served first when the total capacity is short, which is what the regulator report needs when the pool is constrained.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who runs the nightly reporting pipeline how you would make sure the critical jobs get enough capacity during a busy period. Name at least one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing which jobs are business-critical and what each one needs at its peak, not on average. Then I would give those jobs guaranteed capacity, so a fixed share is held for them and cannot be taken by ad-hoc work. Lower-priority work shares whatever is left and queues when the pool is full. I would also check quotas, because a quota is a ceiling and can block a job even when the platform has spare capacity. The tradeoff is cost and waste: reserved capacity that sits idle overnight is still paid for, and an oversized reservation starves everyone else. So I would size reservations from measured peaks plus some headroom, review them monthly, and alert when a critical job's runtime creeps toward its deadline so we see trouble before it becomes a miss.
rubricPoints: Identifies which jobs are business-critical and sizes them at their peak need, not their average.
Guarantees capacity for critical work separately from shared or ad-hoc work.
Explains that a quota is a ceiling and does not guarantee that capacity is available.
Names the tradeoff: idle reserved capacity costs money, and oversizing starves other work.
Watches critical job runtime against its deadline so problems show up early.

suggested.rationale: That mission has learners work through capacity being exhausted under a surge, which is the situation this objective is about protecting against.

lessons.plain: A Dataproc cluster is a group of rented virtual machines that runs big data tools such as Apache Spark and Hadoop. You have two ways to run one. A persistent cluster is built once and left running, so many jobs can share it and it is ready the moment work arrives, but you pay for every hour it sits idle. A job-based cluster, also called an ephemeral cluster, is created for one job and deleted when that job finishes, so you pay only for the time the work actually runs. Choosing between them mostly depends on how often work arrives and how much waiting you can tolerate.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team runs one Spark job per day that takes 40 minutes, but their cluster has been running 24 hours a day for a year. What is the main reason this might be wasteful, and what is a reasonable reason someone might still keep it running? Answer in plain words.
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A cluster is a set of machines that work together on one workload. A persistent cluster keeps running between jobs. A job-based cluster, also called an ephemeral cluster, is created as part of a job and deleted when that job ends. Dataproc is Google Cloud's managed service for Apache Spark and Hadoop, so Google operates the software while you choose machine sizes, count, and how long each cluster lives.

Why it works: cloud machines are billed by the time they are running, not by the work they finish. A persistent cluster bills around the clock, so it is cost-effective only when it stays busy. A job-based cluster bills for its job plus creation time, but each run waits for a cluster to start, and it must keep its data outside the machines, for example in Cloud Storage, because local disks disappear with the cluster.

Worked example with illustrative numbers. A nightly Spark job needs 40 minutes on a 4-machine cluster. Persistent option: the cluster runs 24 hours, so 4 machines are billed for 24 hours each day. Job-based option: creation takes about 3 minutes, the job runs 40 minutes, then the cluster is deleted, so about 43 minutes are billed for those 4 machines. Step by step, the job-based choice bills for under 3 percent of the time. A persistent cluster only wins when jobs arrive so often that it is rarely idle.

Common mistake: treating a job-based cluster as storage, then deleting it and losing results that existed only on its local disks. A second mistake is creating job-based clusters but never deleting them after a failed run, which keeps billing silently.

Consequence in a running platform: an orphaned cluster is a recurring cost leak, and lost output is a data loss event. Pipelines should write results to durable storage and delete their cluster in a failure-safe final step, so a crashed job does not leave machines running.

questions.prompt: A reporting team runs a Spark job every 45 minutes, which is a data-processing program that runs on a group of machines. Each run needs 15 minutes of work on a 4-machine cluster, and creating a fresh job-based (ephemeral) cluster takes 4 minutes. Step 1, already done: runs per day = 1440 divided by 45 = 32. Step 2, already done: billed minutes per run on a job-based cluster = 4 creation + 15 job = 19. Step 3 is missing and you must supply it: multiply the billed minutes per run by the runs per day to get the total billed minutes per machine per day for the job-based option. What is that total?
choices: 480 minutes
640 minutes
1440 minutes
608 minutes
questions.why: Multiplying 19 billed minutes per run by 32 runs gives 608 minutes per machine, which is the job-based total to compare against the 1440 minutes a persistent cluster bills each day.

questions.prompt: In Dataproc, a job-based cluster is best described as which of the following?
choices: A cluster created for one job and deleted when that job ends
A cluster that keeps running between jobs so its data stays in memory
A permanent storage bucket where Spark output is kept
A cluster that Google operates without any choice of machine size or count from you
questions.why: A job-based cluster is created as part of a job and deleted when the job finishes, while the other options describe a persistent cluster, a fully unmanaged setup, or storage rather than compute.

questions.prompt: A job-based cluster wrote its only output to its local disks. The job finished, and a cleanup step then deleted the cluster. What is the consequence?
choices: The output stays because Dataproc copies local disks to a backup for every cluster
The output is kept because deleting a cluster only stops the machines and leaves their disks
The output is kept until the next job reads it, then removed
The output is lost with the machines, so results belong in durable storage such as Cloud Storage
questions.why: Local disks disappear with the cluster, so a job-based cluster must write results to storage outside the machines before it is deleted.

questions.prompt: A team runs a 3-minute job every 2 hours on a 6-machine cluster. Creating a job-based cluster takes 2 minutes. Over one day, which option bills fewer machine-minutes per machine, and why?
choices: Persistent, because 12 runs at 2 minutes each is 24 minutes, so creation dominates
Job-based, because 12 runs at 5 billed minutes each is 60 minutes against 1440 for a cluster that runs all day
Job-based, because it is free to create so only the job minutes count
Persistent, because the cluster is already warm and creation time is never billed
questions.why: Each job-based run bills 2 creation minutes plus 3 job minutes, so 12 runs total 60 minutes, far below the 1440 minutes a persistent cluster bills in a day.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks whether our Dataproc jobs should run on one always-on persistent cluster or get a fresh job-based cluster each time. Explain the difference in your own words, and name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not choose by default.
lessons.modelAnswer: A persistent cluster stays up between jobs, so jobs start immediately and can share it, but you pay for every idle hour. A job-based cluster is created for one run and deleted afterward, so cost follows actual compute time, but each run waits for the cluster to start and the data must live outside the cluster, because local disks are removed with it. I would default to job-based clusters for scheduled batch work, since idle time is the usual cost waste. The tradeoff is that a failed run can leave an orphaned cluster behind unless the pipeline deletes it reliably, and the startup delay matters if the work is interactive or needs very low latency. Persistent clusters fit frequent, interactive use where the cluster stays busy.
rubricPoints: Persistent clusters stay running between jobs and bill for idle time.
Job-based clusters are created per job and deleted after, so cost follows run time.
Job-based clusters need data stored outside the cluster and accept a startup delay.
A reliable cleanup step is required so failed runs do not leave billed clusters behind.

suggested.rationale: Comparing always-on and per-job cluster costs in fictional credits builds the cost intuition this objective needs.

lessons.plain: Imagine planning a weekend meal: you buy ingredients before you cook, chop vegetables before they go in the pan, and serve only after everything is cooked. A DAG, short for directed acyclic graph, is a diagram of that kind of plan. It has a set of steps, arrows showing which step must finish before another starts, and no loop where a step ends up waiting on itself. Cloud Composer is a managed service that runs these plans for data work. You describe the steps and their order in a Python file, and the service runs them on schedule, retries failed steps, and shows you what happened.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose task A must run before task B, B must run before task C, and C is also set to run before A. What goes wrong with this plan, and why can it never finish?
lessons.teach:
A DAG (directed acyclic graph) is a set of tasks plus dependencies. A task is one unit of work, such as copying a file or running a query. A dependency is an arrow saying one task must succeed before another starts. Directed means the arrows have a direction. Acyclic means that following the arrows never leads back to a starting point, so the plan always has a valid finish. In Cloud Composer, which is managed Apache Airflow, you write a DAG as a Python file. Each task is built from an operator, a ready-made template for a kind of work such as moving data or calling a service. The DAG also carries a schedule that says when a run starts. Each scheduled execution is called a DAG run.

Why it works: the orchestrator reads every dependency, starts each task once all its upstream tasks have succeeded, and runs independent branches in parallel. A failed task can be retried on its own without rerunning the whole plan.

Worked example: a nightly sales load has four tasks. Task A checks that the source file exists. Task B loads it into a staging table. Tasks C and D both depend on B: C rebuilds a summary table and D publishes a status file. The dependencies are A to B, B to C, and B to D. The run order is A, then B, then C and D together. If B fails, C and D never start, and the retry applies to B alone.

Common mistake: writing a dependency loop, such as C feeding back into A. The scheduler rejects it because the graph is no longer acyclic. A second frequent mistake is making tasks non-idempotent, meaning running them twice changes the result. If a retry of B appends the same rows again, the table ends up with duplicates.

Consequence: in a running system, a slow or duplicating DAG shows up as late dashboards and double-counted revenue, so task design matters as much as the arrows. A DAG's shape decides what can run in parallel and what gets blocked when something fails.

questions.prompt: A bike-share company runs one daily job. A DAG (a directed acyclic graph, a set of tasks plus arrows saying which task must finish before another starts) has four tasks: fetch_trips (P), check_schema (Q), build_weather_join (W), and load_warehouse (R). Send_alert (S) runs last. The dependencies are P to Q, P to W, and S after R. Worked trace: P runs first. Q and W are independent of each other, so the orchestrator runs them in parallel once P succeeds. R must not start until its inputs are ready. Step to fill in: R is declared as depending on ______, so it starts only after both Q and W succeed. Then S runs after R.
choices: P again, so that R restarts whenever the first task reruns
nothing, so R runs in parallel with Q and W to save time
both Q and W, so R starts only after both have succeeded
W alone, because the weather join is the slower of the two
questions.why: R needs validated trip data and the weather join, so a dependency on both Q and W makes the orchestrator hold R until both upstream tasks succeed.

questions.prompt: A university enrollment pipeline has tasks X, Y, Z, and W. Which set of dependencies describes a valid DAG, where the arrows never lead back to an earlier task?
choices: X to Y, Y to Z, and Z back to Y, so Y and Z retry each other until both are clean
X to Y and Y to X, so each waits for the other to confirm
X to Y, Y to Z, X to Z, and a Z to X arrow added for audit
X to Y, X to Z, and both Y and Z to W, with no arrow pointing back toward X
questions.why: A valid DAG has directed arrows with no path that loops back to a starting point, and only the last option meets that condition.

questions.prompt: A ride-hailing company's payments task inserts rows into a ledger table. It fails midway and is retried twice, and the ledger ends up with duplicate payment rows. Which change best prevents this?
choices: Raise the retry count to five so the load eventually succeeds in one clean pass
Disable retries on the payments task so it only ever runs once
Give each retry a new output file name so a rerun never overwrites anything
Write each row as an upsert keyed by payment ID, so a rerun updates existing rows instead of adding them
questions.why: Making the task idempotent, meaning a rerun produces the same result, is achieved by keying writes on a unique ID so repeated runs cannot add the same payment twice.

questions.prompt: In an insurance claims DAG, task A ingests claims, task B cleans them, tasks C and D both depend on B, and task E depends on both C and D. After B succeeds, C finishes successfully but D fails. What happens next?
choices: E runs anyway using C's output, because C already succeeded
C is rerun too, because the scheduler reruns every task after a failure
C's finished result stays, E stays blocked, and only D is retried
The whole DAG restarts from A, since any failure invalidates the run
questions.why: A failed task is retried on its own, completed upstream and sibling work is kept, and any task depending on the failed one waits until it succeeds.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a DAG is in Cloud Composer and how it differs from a simple list of scripts run one after another. Name one limit or tradeoff of expressing a pipeline as a DAG.
lessons.modelAnswer: A DAG is a set of tasks with dependency arrows between them, and the arrows must never form a loop, so the plan always has a finish. In Cloud Composer, which is managed Apache Airflow, we write that graph as a Python file, and the scheduler runs each task once its upstream tasks succeed. Compared with a list of scripts run in sequence, independent branches can run in parallel and a single failed task can be retried without rerunning everything. The tradeoff is that every task should be safe to run twice, because retries and reruns are normal. If a task appends rows without checking, a retry creates duplicates. We also need to keep tasks small enough that a failure is cheap to retry, and remember that the DAG file itself has to be correct and importable, or the whole schedule breaks.
rubricPoints: A DAG is tasks plus dependency arrows with no cycles.
Independent tasks can run in parallel and a failure only blocks its downstream tasks.
Tasks must be idempotent so retries do not duplicate results.
A dependency loop is rejected, so the graph shape must be checked when the DAG is written.

suggested.rationale: A planned workflow state machine engine would let the learner build ordered steps with dependencies and retries, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: Scheduling means having a job start by itself, such as at 2 a.m. every day or when a new file arrives, so nobody has to press a button. Orchestrating means coordinating several such jobs so they run in the right order, wait for each other, retry failures, and report what happened. Together they let a data pipeline run every day with the same result, without a person watching it. This matters because a pipeline that runs on time but in the wrong order, or twice, can quietly produce wrong numbers that look normal.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job copies yesterday's sales into a report table at 02:00. Sometimes the copy takes longer than usual. If a second job that builds the report is set to start at 02:30 on a plain timer, what could go wrong, and how would you prevent it without changing the clock time?
lessons.teach:
A scheduled job is a unit of data work, such as loading a day of sales files or rebuilding a summary table, that runs without a person starting it. A trigger is whatever starts it: a clock (run at 02:00 every day), an event (a new file lands in a storage bucket), or the successful finish of an upstream job. An orchestrator is the coordinator that runs several jobs in order, waits for each to finish, retries failed steps, and records status. Its plan is usually a DAG, a directed acyclic graph: each task is a node, each dependency is an arrow, and no chain of arrows can loop back to its start. Repeatable means that running the same schedule again gives the same result without damage. The main technique is idempotency, which means a step run twice for the same date overwrites that date's output rather than appending a second copy. Jobs are usually parameterized by a run date so a rerun touches exactly one slice of data.

Worked example. A nightly pipeline has three steps: extract orders for 2024-06-01, transform them, then load a summary table. The trigger fires at 02:00. Extract succeeds. Transform fails on one malformed row. The orchestrator retries transform twice, then marks it failed and never starts load, so the summary does not show half a day of data. An engineer fixes the row and reruns only transform for 2024-06-01. Because load overwrites that date's partition, the rerun yields the correct total.

Common mistake: scheduling by clock time alone, with no dependency check. The load starts while extract is still writing, reads a partial file, and publishes low revenue. If the load appends rather than overwrites, a later rerun doubles the rows.

The orchestrator's real job is therefore not only to start work on time, but to refuse to run downstream steps on incomplete input.

questions.prompt: A ride-share company runs an hourly job for run date 2024-09-14. Step 1: at 03:00 the trigger fires and the ingest task reads that day's trip files, which succeed. Step 2: the aggregate task fails because one trip file is truncated. The orchestrator retries aggregate twice, then marks it failed and does not start publish. Step 3: an engineer repairs the truncated file and reruns only aggregate for 2024-09-14. Step 4 (missing): the publish step runs for 2024-09-14 and writes its output by ____.
choices: appending the new rows under the day's label, so the table now holds two copies of that day
rebuilding every date from the start of the month, because the scheduler reruns the whole pipeline
overwriting the 2024-09-14 partition, so the day ends with one copy and the correct total
skipping the write, because the orchestrator already published the earlier partial run
questions.why: Because publish overwrites only the run date's slice, the rerun leaves exactly one correct copy of that day, which is what makes the rerun repeatable.

questions.prompt: In an orchestrator, what does a DAG (directed acyclic graph) describe?
choices: A log of every past run and its final status, kept for auditing
A list of times at which jobs should start, with no links between them
A plan where each task is a node, each dependency is an arrow, and no chain of arrows loops back to its start
A single job that retries itself on a fixed interval until it succeeds
questions.why: A DAG is the plan of tasks and their dependency arrows, with the defining rule that no chain of arrows can return to where it began.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team's nightly job adds yesterday's active-customer count to a summary table. When someone reruns the job for the same date, the count for that date doubles. Which change makes the job repeatable?
choices: Add a second trigger so the job runs twice a day for safety
Change the write so that it replaces the rows for that run date instead of appending to them
Run the job at a random minute each night to avoid collisions
Raise the retry limit from two to ten so transient failures are covered
questions.why: Replacing that date's rows means a rerun produces the same single result, which is the idempotency property; the other changes do not affect duplicate rows.

questions.prompt: An IoT platform runs an hourly job that aggregates sensor readings. The hour-14 ingest task fails and the orchestrator exhausts its retries. The downstream dashboard-refresh task depends on that aggregate. What should the orchestrator do with the dashboard-refresh task?
choices: Run it after a random delay in case the failed task recovers on its own
Run it anyway using the previous hour's aggregate, so the dashboard never goes stale
Run it with an empty input so the dashboard shows zero readings for hour 14
Never start it, and leave it marked as not run so consumers do not read incomplete data
questions.why: The orchestrator's job is to refuse to run downstream steps on incomplete input, so the dashboard task must not start; it should wait and show a clear not-run status.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between scheduling a job and orchestrating a pipeline. Then name one limit or tradeoff of running a multi-step pipeline on a simple timer.
lessons.modelAnswer: Scheduling answers when a job starts: a trigger such as a clock time or an arriving file. Orchestrating answers how several jobs work together: which step waits for which, what happens when one fails, and how often it retries. A pipeline with three steps needs orchestration because the load step must not start until the extract step has finished successfully. The limit of a plain timer is that it has no view of whether upstream work is done. If extraction runs long, the timer fires anyway and the load reads partial data. Scheduling alone also gives no safe rerun path. To fix that, I would make each step idempotent, so rerunning one date overwrites its output, and use an orchestrator that blocks downstream steps when an upstream step fails.
rubricPoints: Scheduling is a trigger that starts work at a time or on an event
Orchestration coordinates ordering, dependencies, retries and status across steps
A timer alone cannot see whether upstream work finished, so downstream steps can read incomplete data
Repeatable reruns need idempotent steps, such as overwriting a date's output

suggested.rationale: A workflow state machine engine would let the learner model steps, dependencies, retries and failure paths, which is the core of orchestration.

lessons.plain: BigQuery is Google Cloud's service for running large data queries. The processing power it uses is measured in slots, which are units of compute. Editions are different packages of BigQuery features and price levels, and you can buy slot capacity in blocks called commitments. A reservation is a named pool of slots, and you assign projects or folders to a pool so that one team's heavy workload cannot quietly starve another's. Set up well, this keeps spending predictable and makes sure critical jobs finish on time.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company runs a nightly data load and also has analysts running dashboards during the day, all on one BigQuery project with no capacity settings. At 2am the load slows the morning dashboards to a crawl. Name two changes that would stop the load and the dashboards from competing for the same processing power, and say what each one costs you.
lessons.teach:
A slot is a unit of BigQuery processing power. Queries and load jobs consume slots while they run. An edition is a tier of BigQuery that bundles a feature set with a per-slot-hour price. A commitment is a purchase of slots for a fixed term, usually one or three years, which lowers the unit price in return for paying whether or not the slots are busy. A reservation is a named pool of slots you create in a chosen location. It has a baseline, the slots always available to it, and an optional autoscale maximum, the ceiling it may grow to when demand rises. An assignment links a project, folder, or organization to a reservation and names a job type, such as query or pipeline.

Worked example. You create reservation etl with a baseline of 500 slots and an autoscale maximum of 800. You create reservation bi with a baseline of 200 slots and no autoscale. You assign the pipeline project to etl as a pipeline job type, and the dashboard project to bi as a query job type. At 2am the load needs 700 slots. It gets its 500 baseline, then autoscales 200 more, reaching 700. Dashboards draw only from bi, so they are unaffected. Idle slots from bi can also be lent to etl unless you turn idle sharing off for that reservation.

Common mistake: assigning the whole organization to one large reservation. Then a single ad hoc query can use every slot, and the nightly job waits behind it.

In a running system, if etl's autoscale maximum were left unset, the morning dashboards would share a small pool with overnight work. Commitments are billed whether used or not, so oversizing them wastes money just as undersizing causes missed deadlines.

questions.prompt: A team creates reservation marketing with a baseline of 120 slots and an autoscale maximum of 300. A reporting job in a project assigned to marketing as a query job needs 280 slots at peak. Step 1: the job first draws on the 120 baseline slots. Step 2: (missing). Step 3: the job runs with all 280 slots and does not queue.
choices: The job waits in a queue until another reservation releases 160 slots to marketing, since autoscale only works between projects
Autoscale adds 300 slots on top of the baseline, so the reservation grows to 420 slots, which is above its maximum
Autoscale adds 160 slots, bringing the reservation to 280 slots, which stays under the 300-slot ceiling
The job switches to on-demand pricing for the 160 extra slots, because a reservation cannot grow at all
questions.why: The autoscale maximum is a ceiling on the reservation's total size, so the reservation grows by the 160 slots needed to reach 280, which is within 300.

questions.prompt: A data team creates a reservation with a baseline of 400 slots and leaves the autoscale maximum unset. What does this mean for the reservation at peak demand?
choices: It can grow to any size the project quota allows, because an unset maximum removes the limit
It can never grow beyond its 400-slot baseline, so demand above that level must wait for capacity
It can grow past 400 slots only when another reservation is idle, and its size is otherwise fixed
It always runs at exactly 400 slots, and it can grow past that only after the commitment term ends
questions.why: With no autoscale maximum, the reservation has no ceiling to grow into, so it stays at its baseline and extra demand waits.

questions.prompt: An organisation assigns its whole company to one 1,000-slot reservation, so a nightly ingestion pipeline and analysts running ad hoc queries all share it. Which problem is most likely?
choices: The analysts' queries are billed twice, once for each assignment, because the organisation level adds a second charge
The pipeline is moved to on-demand pricing automatically, because a shared reservation cannot run load jobs
The 1,000 slots are reduced to the smallest project's share, so each team gets far fewer slots than the total
The nightly pipeline may wait behind a large ad hoc query, because nothing separates the two kinds of work in one shared pool
questions.why: Assigning everything to one pool lets a single large query consume many slots, leaving the scheduled job to wait, which is the failure the unit warns about.

questions.prompt: A team buys a three-year commitment of 600 slots. Their workload averages about 150 slots and rarely peaks above 200. What is the main consequence for cost?
choices: The team pays for the full 600 committed slots whether they are busy or not, so most of the spend is unused capacity
The commitment shrinks automatically to match average use after the first month, so the cost falls
The commitment is billed only for the slots actually used each hour, so the unused slots cost nothing
The extra slots are refunded at the end of each year if they went unused, so the overspend is recovered
questions.why: A commitment is billed for the purchased slots for its full term whether they are busy or not, so oversizing it wastes money.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how BigQuery slots, reservations, and assignments work together to keep one team's heavy jobs from slowing another team's work, and name one tradeoff of using commitments.
lessons.modelAnswer: Slots are the compute units BigQuery uses to run queries and loads. A reservation is a pool of slots with a guaranteed baseline and, optionally, an autoscale ceiling. An assignment points a project or folder at a reservation, so that project's jobs draw from that pool rather than from a shared free-for-all. That separation is what protects critical work: the nightly pipeline gets its own guaranteed slots, and dashboards cannot consume them. The tradeoff with commitments is that you pay a lower unit price for a fixed term whether or not the slots are busy, so sizing the baseline from real usage matters. Too large and you pay for idle capacity; too small and autoscale is doing constant work, and jobs may queue at peak times. Idle slot sharing can recover some unused capacity, but it means one reservation's jobs may run on another's spare slots, which is worth knowing before you promise a deadline.
rubricPoints: Defines slots as the compute units that BigQuery jobs consume
Explains that reservations give a pool with a baseline and optional autoscale ceiling
Explains that assignments route a project's jobs to a specific reservation to isolate workloads
Names a real tradeoff of commitments: lower price in exchange for paying whether slots are used or not
Notes that idle slot sharing can lend spare capacity between reservations

suggested.rationale: Choosing baselines, autoscale ceilings, and assignments for competing workloads is best learned by reasoning through an exam-style capacity scenario.

lessons.plain: When many people or programs ask a database a question, there are two broad ways to run it. Some questions need an answer now, like a person waiting on a dashboard chart. Others can wait a while, like a report that builds overnight before anyone arrives at work. A query job is the unit of work that runs one such question. Choosing between interactive and batch means telling the platform how long you can wait, so it can decide when your job runs and how it shares capacity with everyone else.
lessons.guessPrompt: Imagine one data warehouse shared by a live sales dashboard and a nightly report that must finish before morning. If both send queries at 9 a.m., which one would you want to get results first, and why?
lessons.teach:
A query job is one run of a SQL question against stored data. In Google BigQuery, the managed analytics warehouse, each query job gets a priority: INTERACTIVE or BATCH. INTERACTIVE is the default. An interactive job starts as soon as capacity allows and suits a person or app waiting on the answer. A batch job is queued and starts when the platform has spare capacity. It has no guaranteed start time, so it suits work whose deadline is loose. Under on-demand pricing, both kinds are billed on the bytes they scan, so the choice mainly affects timing and contention, not the bill. Check your own pricing model.

Why it works: the platform limits how many interactive queries a project can run at once. When a burst of dashboard refreshes uses those slots, extra interactive queries wait or fail. Batch jobs do not compete for those interactive slots, so they absorb load that can wait.

Worked example: a team has a nightly transformation that must finish before 07:00 and a live sales dashboard. Step 1: the transformation is submitted as BATCH at 22:00 and queues behind nothing urgent. Step 2: it starts overnight when capacity is free and finishes around 02:00. Step 3: the dashboard queries stay INTERACTIVE, so analysts see results at once during the day.

Common mistake: setting every query to BATCH to be safe. A dashboard query tagged BATCH may sit in the queue, so the chart looks frozen during the morning rush.

Consequence: if a batch job queues behind heavy load, a later pipeline step that depends on its output can miss its deadline. Use batch only where a delay is acceptable, and watch the job's end time.
