questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs a weekly reconciliation query that compares shipment records against invoices. It must finish before Monday 06:00, and it scans about 4 TB each run. Dispatchers also use a live query-backed board that shows trucks still waiting at depots. Worked steps: Step 1: the reconciliation is submitted as BATCH on Friday at 18:00, because nobody needs it before Monday. Step 2: it queues and starts over the weekend when spare capacity is free, and it finishes Sunday night. Step 3: the dispatch board queries are set to ____, because dispatchers are waiting on each result. Fill in the missing setting and the reason.
choices: INTERACTIVE, because dispatchers are waiting on the answer and need it to start as soon as capacity allows
INTERACTIVE, because the reconciliation must also be INTERACTIVE to meet its Monday deadline
BATCH, because batch queries are cheaper per scan under on-demand pricing
BATCH, because it frees interactive capacity so the reconciliation can finish sooner
questions.why: A live board that people wait on should stay INTERACTIVE so it starts as soon as capacity allows, while the loose-deadline reconciliation stays BATCH.

questions.prompt: In Google BigQuery, what does a query job with BATCH priority mean?
choices: It is queued and starts when the platform has spare capacity, with no guaranteed start time
It runs immediately and gets a larger share of the project's interactive capacity
It runs only once per day at a fixed time chosen by the platform
It scans fewer bytes, so it is billed at a lower rate than an interactive query
questions.why: A BATCH job waits in a queue and starts when spare capacity is available, and the teaching text says it has no guaranteed start time.

questions.prompt: A team runs a fraud check that must return a result within a few seconds of each card payment, and they set it to BATCH priority to keep the project tidy. What is the most likely problem?
choices: The query will scan more bytes and be billed for the extra work
The query will return results in the wrong order because batch output is unsorted
The query will be blocked from reading the stored data while batch jobs run
The query may sit in the queue with no guaranteed start, so the payment decision arrives late
questions.why: Because a BATCH job has no guaranteed start time and waits for spare capacity, a query that must answer within seconds can miss its need, which is why it should be INTERACTIVE.

questions.prompt: Under on-demand pricing, a team moves a large scheduled transformation from INTERACTIVE to BATCH expecting the monthly bill to drop. Which statement is correct?
choices: The bill rises because batch jobs are reserved in advance and billed whether they run or not
The bill drops by half because batch jobs are automatically given a discounted scan rate
The bill drops because batch jobs are priced per minute of queue time, which is always shorter
The bill is based on bytes scanned, so the same job costs about the same either way; the change mainly affects when it starts and how it contends for capacity
questions.why: The teaching text states that under on-demand pricing both priorities are billed on bytes scanned, so the priority choice affects timing and contention rather than the bill.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we should not run every BigQuery query as batch to cut costs. Explain interactive versus batch, what changes when you pick one, and one limit or tradeoff of batch.
lessons.modelAnswer: Interactive and batch are priorities that decide when a query job runs. Interactive is the default: it starts as soon as the project has capacity and is meant for people or apps waiting on the answer. Batch waits in a queue until spare capacity exists, so it has no guaranteed start time. Under on-demand pricing the bytes scanned are billed the same either way, so switching to batch rarely saves money on its own. The real effect is timing and contention. Batch keeps non-urgent work out of the interactive slots that dashboards need. The tradeoff is that a batch job may start late or finish after a downstream step expects it. So we should batch the overnight jobs that can wait and keep user-facing queries interactive.
rubricPoints: Interactive is the default and starts as soon as capacity allows, for waiting users or apps.
Batch queues and has no guaranteed start time, so it suits work with loose deadlines.
Under on-demand pricing the billed bytes are the same, so the difference is timing and contention.
Batch delay can make downstream steps miss their deadlines, so use it only where waiting is acceptable.

suggested.rationale: A planned SQL lab could let the learner submit the same query under both priorities and observe the difference in start time and queueing.

lessons.plain: Observing a data process means watching it while it runs so you notice trouble before the people relying on its output do. Cloud Monitoring collects numbers over time, such as how many rows a pipeline wrote or how long a query took, and can alert you when a number crosses a line you set. Cloud Logging keeps the detailed event records that explain what happened and when. The BigQuery admin panel shows the health of the warehouse itself: which jobs ran, how much work they did, and how much data is stored. Think of a car dashboard showing speed and fuel, paired with the mechanic's log of each trip.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly pipeline finishes without errors, but the dashboard totals are half of last week's. Would you check a number tracked over time first, or a detailed event record first, and why?
lessons.teach: A metric is a number that is measured again and again, such as rows written per hour. Its history is called a time series, and Cloud Monitoring stores these series. An alerting policy watches a series and fires when the value stays past a threshold for a set duration. A log entry is a timestamped record with a severity level, such as INFO, WARNING or ERROR, and a message or structured payload. Cloud Logging stores these and lets you filter them. The BigQuery admin panel and job history show each query or load job, with details like bytes processed and the time it ran. Metrics are cheap to scan across weeks, so they show that something changed. Logs and job records explain the cause. Worked example: on Tuesday, the rows-written metric for a load job falls from 1.2 million to 300 thousand. Step 1: an alert fires because the value stayed below its threshold for 30 minutes. Step 2: you filter Cloud Logging to that job and to WARNING and above during Tuesday's window. Step 3: you find a warning that the source file was empty. Step 4: you check the job history to confirm the load ran and wrote the rows it found. Common mistake: alerting only on job failures. A job can succeed while writing far too few rows, and then nothing errors while reports go stale. Consequence: a silent drop in data volume can corrupt decisions downstream for days before anyone notices. Monitoring the output, not only the job status, is what catches it.

questions.prompt: A clinic-scheduling company loads yesterday's appointment rows into a BigQuery table each morning. On Monday, the rows-written metric for that load drops from about 40,000 to 4,100 and stays low for over an hour, so an alerting policy (a rule that fires when a monitored value stays past a set threshold for a set duration) notifies the team. The team works through the investigation in this order. Step 1: they compare the metric over the last four weeks and see the drop only on Monday. Step 2: they open the BigQuery job history and see the Monday load marked Succeeded, with 4,100 rows written. Step 3: they filter Cloud Logging to that load job at WARNING and above and find a warning that 3 of the 12 regional export files were missing from the source folder. Step 4: [missing]. Step 5: they ask the regional export owner to re-send the three files and rerun the Monday load.
choices: Delete the Monday rows from the table and reload them with schema auto-detection turned on.
Raise the alert threshold to 4,000 rows so the alert no longer fires for this load.
Compare Monday's appointment count in the source system with the rows loaded, to confirm the missing files explain the gap.
Restart the alerting policy with a longer duration so it stops firing on short dips.
questions.why: Checking the source count confirms that the missing files account for the shortfall, which is the cause the logs pointed to, before any repair is made.

questions.prompt: In Cloud Monitoring, what is a time series?
choices: A list of log entries sorted by severity level from INFO to ERROR.
A record of the query text and bytes processed for one BigQuery job.
The stored history of a number that is measured again and again over time.
A monthly bill that shows the cost of each project in the account.
questions.why: A time series is the recorded history of a repeatedly measured value, such as rows written per hour, which Cloud Monitoring stores.

questions.prompt: An alerting policy watches rows written per hour. Its threshold is 1,000 rows and its duration is 10 minutes, so it fires only when the value stays below 1,000 for the full 10 minutes. Over one afternoon the readings are: 800 for 5 minutes, then 1,200 for 30 minutes, then 700 for 12 minutes. What happens?
choices: It fires at every single reading below 1,000, so it fires three times.
It fires once, during the final 12-minute stretch at 700, because only that stretch stays below the threshold for the full duration.
It fires during the first 5-minute stretch at 800, because that value is under the threshold.
It never fires, because the 700 reading is too brief to be a real change.
questions.why: The policy needs the value to stay past the threshold for the whole duration, so only the 12-minute stretch at 700 qualifies.

questions.prompt: A nightly load job into a BigQuery table finishes with a status of Succeeded every night, but one night it writes only 5 percent of its usual rows. Which monitoring setup would have caught this without anyone reading the logs first?
choices: A weekly review of the billing report for the project that runs the load.
Turning off Cloud Logging so that warnings do not clutter the console.
An alerting policy on the rows-written metric that fires when it falls below a set threshold for a set duration.
An alerting policy that fires only when the job status changes to Failed.
questions.why: Monitoring the output volume catches a silent drop in rows, which a job-status check cannot, since the job succeeded.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that if every pipeline job shows as succeeded, we do not need to monitor the data itself. In your own words, explain why that is wrong, and name one limit of the monitoring approach you would use instead.
lessons.modelAnswer: A job can report success while doing the wrong amount of work. A load might run, find an empty source file, and write zero rows without raising an error. So I would watch an output metric such as rows written per run, against a threshold or a comparison to the same day last week, and alert when it drops. Cloud Monitoring shows that the number changed, and Cloud Logging and the job history show why. The limit is that a threshold only catches changes we anticipated. A gradual drift or a new kind of bad data can stay inside the threshold, so I would also review the trend on a dashboard and add checks on data quality, not just volume.
rubricPoints: Job success status does not prove the data is correct or complete
Metrics over time show that something changed and can trigger alerts
Logs and job history explain the cause of the change
A named limit: thresholds only catch anticipated changes, so trends and data quality checks are needed

suggested.rationale: Setting thresholds and alerts on a metric that tracks pipeline output is what the planned metric alarm builder would practise.

lessons.plain: A budget is a spending limit you set in advance for a project or team. Planned usage is how much you expected to spend by a given point in time. Monitoring planned usage against budget means regularly comparing what you have actually spent with what you planned, and asking whether the current trend will overshoot before the period ends. Cloud bills often arrive late and in bulk, so an engineer who waits for the invoice learns about an overrun too late. The useful habit is to watch spend while it is still happening, measure the gap against the plan, and act early enough to change something.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team plans to spend 3,000 dollars on cloud data processing this month, spread evenly across 30 days. On day 10 the bill shows 1,500 dollars spent. Without doing exact arithmetic, do you expect the month to finish under or over plan, and which single number would you check first to be sure?
lessons.teach:
Budget: a spending limit for a project, team or account over a set period, such as one month. Planned usage: the spend you expected by a given day, usually the budget spread across the period. Actual spend: what has really been charged so far. Variance: actual minus planned, which tells you how far off the plan you are. Burn rate: how fast spend is accumulating per day. Projection: a simple estimate of the month-end total, made by extending the current burn rate to the end of the period. Alert threshold: a percentage of the budget, such as 80 or 100 percent, at which a notification is sent.

Why it works: a planned line gives you something to compare against every day, so a spike shows up as a gap while there is still time to respond. A projection turns a daily number into a question you can act on: will we finish over budget at this rate?

Worked example. Monthly budget is 10,000 dollars over 30 days. Planned daily spend is 333.33 dollars, so by day 10 the plan is 3,333 dollars. Actual spend on day 10 is 4,100 dollars. Variance is 4,100 minus 3,333, which is 767 dollars over plan, about 23 percent. Projection is 4,100 divided by 10, times 30, which is 12,300 dollars, or 2,300 over budget. The 80 percent threshold of 8,000 dollars was already crossed, so the owner investigates the source of the extra spend now rather than at the invoice.

Common mistake: checking only the total at month end. A budget alert also does not stop spending by default; it sends a notification, so someone must act on it.

Consequence: in a running data platform, a forgotten cluster or an unbounded query can burn through a budget within days. Pairing the alert with a named owner and a daily projection check keeps the overrun visible while it can still be corrected.

Monitoring planned usage against budget means comparing actual spend with the plan every day and projecting the period-end total, so overruns are caught while they can still be fixed.

questions.prompt: A small analytics team has a monthly budget of 6,000 dollars over 30 days. By day 12 the actual spend is 2,700 dollars. Work the monitoring steps. Step 1: planned daily spend is 6,000 divided by 30, which is 200 dollars. Step 2: planned spend by day 12 is 200 times 12, which is 2,400 dollars. Step 3: variance is actual minus planned, 2,700 minus 2,400, which is 300 dollars over plan. Step 4 is missing: the projection of the month-end total, made by extending the current burn rate to the end of the period. What is the projected month-end total, and is it over budget?
choices: Projection is 2,700 divided by 12, times 30, which is 6,750 dollars, or 750 dollars over budget
Dividing actual spend by the day count gives a burn rate of 225 dollars per day, which is the projection itself
Adding the remaining planned spend to actual, 2,700 plus 3,600, gives 6,300 dollars, which is 300 over budget
Projection equals the budget spread over 12 days, 6,000 times 12 divided by 30, which is 2,400 dollars, so the team is on track
questions.why: The projection extends the current burn rate of 2,700 divided by 12 days across all 30 days, giving 6,750 dollars, which is 750 dollars above the 6,000 dollar budget.

questions.prompt: A project has a budget of 8,000 dollars over 40 days. On day 16 its actual spend is 3,900 dollars. What is the variance, and what does its sign tell you?
choices: 700 dollars over plan, found by subtracting planned spend from actual spend
700 dollars under plan, found by subtracting actual spend from planned spend
4,600 dollars over plan, found by subtracting planned spend from the total budget
3,900 dollars over plan, because the variance is simply the actual spend figure
questions.why: Planned spend by day 16 is 3,200 dollars, so variance is actual minus planned, 3,900 minus 3,200, which is 700 dollars over plan; a positive variance means spending is ahead of the plan.

questions.prompt: A team's monthly budget has an alert threshold set at 80 percent. The spend crosses that threshold on day 20 of a 30-day month. Which statement describes what the alert does by default?
choices: It stops new charges automatically once spend reaches 80 percent of the budget
It recalculates the month-end projection and cancels any resource running above plan
It sends a notification at the threshold but does not stop spending, so someone must act on it
It fires only when spend reaches 100 percent of the budget, so 80 percent is a planning figure
questions.why: An alert threshold is a notification point: crossing 80 percent sends a message to the people set up to receive it, and spending continues unless an owner intervenes.

questions.prompt: A retail analytics team has a monthly budget of 3,000 dollars over 31 days. On day 7 its actual spend is 1,400 dollars. What is the projected month-end total, using a simple burn-rate projection?
choices: 677 dollars, found by multiplying the budget by 7 and dividing by 31
6,200 dollars, found by dividing actual spend by 7, then multiplying by 31
4,400 dollars, found by adding the budget to actual spend
316 dollars, found by dividing actual spend by 31, then multiplying by 7
questions.why: The burn rate is 1,400 divided by 7, which is 200 dollars per day, and extending that rate across 31 days gives 6,200 dollars, which is 3,200 dollars over the 3,000 dollar budget.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell, midway through the month, that a data platform is going to overshoot its budget. Name one limit of the check you describe.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would take the monthly budget, divide it evenly across the days, and compare the actual spend to date with that planned line. The gap is the variance. Then I would extend the current daily spend to the end of the month to get a projection. If the projection is over budget, or actual spend has passed an alert threshold like 80 percent early in the period, I would look at which service or job caused the rise before it continues. One limit is that an even split assumes steady usage. A batch pipeline that runs mostly at month end can look on track midway and then overshoot, so I would also check the planned schedule of heavy jobs, not only the straight-line average. Another limit is that the cost data can lag by a day or more, so the projection is an estimate, not an exact figure.
rubricPoints: Compares actual spend to date against a planned line derived from the budget.
Uses a projection of the period-end total from the current burn rate.
Explains that budget alerts notify but do not stop spending by default.
Names a limit such as uneven or scheduled workloads, or delayed cost data.

suggested.rationale: A cost model in fictional credits lets the learner build a planned-versus-actual curve and watch a projection cross a budget line, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: When a cloud data job fails, the platform usually explains why, but in terse codes and messages. Troubleshooting means reading that message and deciding which of three things happened: a bug in your job, a quota (a cap the platform sets on how much of a resource your project may use), or a billing problem (a payment or spending state that restricts your account). Each cause has a different owner and a different fix. Learning to sort a symptom into one of these buckets before changing anything saves most of the guesswork.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly load job that worked last week now fails with a message saying a limit was exceeded, and nobody changed the job's code. Before reading any documentation, what would you check first, and why?
lessons.teach:
An error message is the platform's statement of what went wrong. A good one names the resource, the project, and the rule that was broken. A quota is a limit on how much of a resource a project may use, such as the number of load jobs per day or requests per minute in one region. Quotas protect shared infrastructure. Raising one needs a request, and it does not fix a job that sends too much work. A billing account is the payment arrangement that every project's charges attach to. A budget is a spending threshold you set, and a budget alert notifies people when spend crosses it. By default it sends a message and does not stop spending.

Why this works: a rejection points to one of three causes. If the message cites the content of a request, the job is usually at fault. If it cites a quota, the job is correct but too frequent or too large. If it cites a billing state, the account itself is restricted. Sorting the symptom first tells you who should act.

Worked example. A load job that ran once a night starts failing with a message naming a daily load-job quota. Step one: read the message for the quota name, project, and region. Step two: open the quota page and compare current usage with the limit. Step three: check the schedule. A recent change now runs the same load every five minutes, which is about 288 jobs a day instead of one. Step four: fix the schedule and batch the loads, then decide whether a higher limit is still needed.

Common mistake: rerunning the failed job again and again. Each attempt is another request against the same exhausted limit, and it can add cost. Check for partial output from the rejected run before any retry, and make sure the retry is safe to repeat.

In a running system, a quota rejection during a write can leave a table half loaded, so the on-call engineer must confirm what landed before anyone reruns the job.

questions.prompt: A ride-share company's pipeline backfills two years of trip records into a table in project rideco-history, region us-east4. The backfill is rejected with a message naming a per-minute request quota for that region. Step 1: read the message and note the quota name, project rideco-history, and region us-east4. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: the backfill runs 40 workers, and each worker sends 25 requests per minute, so about 1,000 requests per minute reach the region against a limit of 600. Step 4: cut the workers to 15, which sends about 375 requests per minute, and then decide whether a higher limit is still needed. Which completion correctly fills the missing Step 2?
choices: Rerun the backfill with a longer timeout to see whether the rejection clears.
Open the quota page and compare current usage with the 600-per-minute limit.
Raise the billing budget so the backfill is not stopped by spending limits.
Ask the on-call engineer to confirm nothing landed before reading the message.
questions.why: Step 2 in this method is to open the quota page and compare observed usage with the limit, which is what confirms the job is correct but too frequent, so the schedule or worker count is the fix.

questions.prompt: A quota, in the sense used for this objective, is best described as:
choices: A cap on how much of a resource one project may use, such as requests per minute in one region.
A record of every error a pipeline has written to its log over a month.
A list of the people allowed to change the IAM roles on a shared dataset.
A fixed price per gigabyte that a billing account agrees to pay for storage.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a quota as a limit on how much of a resource a project may use, with requests per minute in one region as an example.

questions.prompt: A team sets a budget with an alert on a project that runs a streaming ingestion job. Spend crosses the threshold on Thursday afternoon. What does the default configuration do?
choices: Stops the ingestion job automatically so spending cannot grow further.
Lowers the project's quotas until the next billing cycle begins.
Sends a notification to the people configured for the alert and keeps spending.
Deletes the project's stored data to bring spend back under the threshold.
questions.why: The teaching text says a budget alert notifies people when spend crosses the threshold and that by default it sends a message and does not stop spending.

questions.prompt: A pipeline in a seed-sorting startup's project fails. The message cites row 4,112 of an inbound file and says the timestamp field is malformed. Which party should act first, and why?
choices: The quota owner, because the message names a limit that was exceeded.
The on-call engineer, who should raise the quota before any other step.
The billing administrator, because a malformed timestamp is a billing state problem.
The team that owns the pipeline's code and input, because the message cites the content of the request.
questions.why: The teaching text says that when a message cites the content of a request, the job is usually at fault, so the owner of that code and input should act first.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that whenever our pipeline hits a quota error, the right move is to request a higher quota. Explain to them when that is correct, when it is not, and what tradeoff comes with a higher limit.
lessons.modelAnswer: That is right only after we know the job is behaving correctly. First I would read the error to find which quota is hit, then compare current usage against the limit. If a schedule change or a retry loop multiplied the work, the fix is in our code or schedule, such as batching loads or spacing runs out, and a higher limit would just hide the problem. If usage is legitimately higher because the business grew, a quota increase is reasonable. The tradeoff is that a higher limit lets one runaway job consume more shared capacity and spend more money, so we should pair the increase with a budget alert and a check that retries are idempotent.
rubricPoints: Read the error to identify the specific quota or rule before acting
Compare current usage with the limit to find whether usage is legitimately high or inflated
Fix runaway retries or schedules in code rather than raising the limit
Raising a quota trades headroom for higher cost and a larger blast radius, so pair it with budget alerts

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style failing pipeline that shows a quota error and a billing symptom adds more than reading facts alone, and no listed mission covers cloud quotas directly.

lessons.plain: Think of a shared kitchen in a busy restaurant. Several cooks need the same ovens, and if one cook grabs every oven for a huge batch of bread, the lunch orders stop. Managing workloads on a data platform means deciding who gets how much of the shared compute, which jobs run when, and which ones are allowed to wait. In Google Cloud that work covers the jobs you submit, the queries analysts run, the pool of processing capacity behind them, and the reservations that set aside a share of that capacity for a particular group of work. Done well, the nightly batch finishes on time and the dashboards stay fast at the same moment.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company runs a nightly batch load and, at the same time, dashboards that managers open at 09:00. If the batch load is allowed to use all the shared processing capacity, what do you expect to happen to the dashboards, and what is one way to prevent it?
lessons.teach:
A job is one unit of work the platform runs, such as a load, an export, a pipeline run, or a query. Each job has a status and a history record. In BigQuery, the processing capacity that runs queries is measured in slots, where a slot is a unit of compute that one piece of query work can use. A reservation is a named pool of slots you set aside. An assignment links a project, folder, or organization to a reservation, so jobs from that project draw only from that pool. Unused slots can be shared with other pools by default, which is why one busy workload can look fine until another one needs its share back.

Why it works: separating work into pools means a heavy batch job can only consume the slots in its own pool. Dashboards keep their own slots and stay responsive.

Worked example. Reservation A holds 500 slots and is assigned to the analytics project that serves dashboards. Reservation B holds 300 slots and is assigned to the ETL project. At 02:00 the ETL project starts a large load that asks for 300 slots of work. Those 300 slots come from B. Dashboards queries in A still have their 500 slots, so at 09:00 they respond normally. Next, to find what was expensive, you query the job history view for the project, sort by bytes billed or slot time, and set a maximum bytes billed limit on the scheduled query so a runaway query stops instead of scanning the whole table.

Common mistake: buying more slots to fix a slow dashboard without checking which job is using them. The extra capacity is consumed by the same heavy job and the problem returns as data grows.

Consequence: when all work shares one unlabelled pool, the nightly batch can push dashboard queries past their timeouts, and users report a slow platform even though nothing is broken.

Workload management is the discipline of putting each kind of work in the pool it deserves, and checking the job history to see what really uses that capacity.

questions.prompt: A retailer has a project called storefront-reports assigned to a reservation named RPT with 150 slots, and a project called clickstream-load assigned to a reservation named LOAD with 400 slots. A backfill, which is a large one-off re-processing job, was scheduled from the storefront-reports project at 01:00 and asks for 150 slots of work. Step 1: the team opens the job history view for storefront-reports and sorts by slot time, finding the backfill at the top. Step 2: the team sees the dashboard queries in the same project queuing behind it and timing out at 08:30. Step 3 is missing from the team's notes. Which action completes the fix so the dashboards stay inside their target?
choices: Move the backfill's scheduled query into a project assigned to LOAD, and keep the dashboards' project on RPT.
Raise the maximum bytes billed limit on the dashboard queries so they finish faster.
Rename the backfill job so the job history view groups it separately.
Buy 150 more slots for RPT so the backfill and the dashboards both fit.
questions.why: Because a project draws only from the reservation it is assigned to, moving the heavy backfill into a project on LOAD keeps its slot use out of the RPT pool that the dashboards need.

questions.prompt: A health-tech company wants its nightly claims export and its clinician dashboards kept apart so neither starves the other. Using the course's terms, which setup does the teaching text describe as achieving this?
choices: Separate reservations, each assigned to the project that runs that work
A single large reservation with no assignments at all
One shared pool with a priority label on each job
A maximum bytes billed limit applied to every query
questions.why: The teaching text explains that separate reservations, each linked by an assignment to a project, mean a heavy job can only draw from its own pool.

questions.prompt: A media company has a reservation with 200 slots assigned to its ad-analytics project, and all its jobs run in that project. Dashboards become slow, and the team adds 200 more slots without checking the job history. Why might the problem come back?
choices: Unused slots stop being shared once a reservation passes 300 slots.
Slots are billed per query, so more slots always raise cost without speed.
The heavy job using the slots was never identified, so it will take the new capacity too as data grows.
Dashboards cannot draw from reservations, only from on-demand capacity.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that buying capacity without checking which job uses it means the same heavy job consumes the extra slots and the slowdown returns as data grows.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs a 04:00 nightly export in the same unlabelled pool as its customer-facing tracking queries. Users report slowness, but no component is failing. According to the teaching text, what is the most likely cause?
choices: A corrupted table in the tracking dataset
The nightly batch is pushing tracking queries past their timeouts because all work shares one pool
Users' browsers caching old results
A missing index on the export's source table
questions.why: The teaching text describes this exact consequence: when one batch job shares an unlabelled pool, it can push dashboard queries past their timeouts while nothing is actually broken.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would stop a nightly batch job from slowing down the morning dashboards on a shared BigQuery setup. Name at least one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would put the batch project and the dashboard project into separate reservations, each with its own slot count, and assign each project to its own reservation. That way the batch load can only use its own slots, and the dashboards keep theirs. Before sizing anything, I would check the job history for the project and sort by slot time and bytes billed to find which queries are actually expensive, because they are often the cause rather than the raw volume. The tradeoff is that dedicated pools can sit idle when their owner is quiet, and shared idle slots only help if sharing is allowed. Another limit is that a fixed pool caps how fast the batch can finish, so if the load grows, the schedule has to be re-checked rather than assumed to still fit.
rubricPoints: Separate workloads into reservations so one heavy job cannot take all the shared slots
Use the job history view to find expensive jobs by slot time or bytes billed before adding capacity
Name a tradeoff such as idle dedicated slots or a fixed cap on batch throughput
Mention a cost guard such as a maximum bytes billed limit on queries

suggested.rationale: Choosing which workload gets which capacity under a deadline is a situation to reason through, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it directly.

lessons.plain: Fault tolerance means a data pipeline keeps producing correct results when parts of it fail: a machine crashes, a network drops, or a service is briefly unavailable. Managing restarts means deciding what happens next, whether the work resumes from where it stopped, starts over, or is set aside for a person to look at. Think of a line of workers passing parcels. If one worker faints mid-task, the parcel must not be lost, and it must not be counted twice when someone else picks it up. The goal is that a restart repairs the damage instead of creating new damage.
lessons.guessPrompt: A pipeline reads messages from a queue, writes each one to a database, and then tells the queue it is done. If the worker crashes after writing but before telling the queue, what do you think happens to that message when the worker restarts, and what would you change so the final result is still correct?
lessons.teach:
Fault tolerance is a system's ability to keep producing correct results when a component fails. Restart management is the set of rules that decides how failed work is retried, resumed, or parked. Several terms matter here. A checkpoint is a saved record of how far processing has safely got, so a restarted job can resume rather than begin again. At-least-once delivery means a messaging service guarantees every message arrives, but may deliver the same message more than once. An idempotent write is one that produces the same final result no matter how many times it is applied, for example writing a row keyed by order ID so a repeat overwrites the row instead of adding a second one.

Why it works: at-least-once delivery protects against data loss, but it moves the duplicate problem to the consumer. Making the consumer idempotent turns 'this might run twice' into 'harmless if it does'. Checkpoints limit how much work is redone after a failure.

Worked example. A worker reads order 4471 from a queue and inserts it into a warehouse table. Step 1: the insert succeeds. Step 2: the worker crashes before acknowledging the message. Step 3: the queue, seeing no acknowledgement, redelivers order 4471 after its timeout. Step 4: a new worker inserts it again. With a plain insert, the table now holds two rows for one order. With a merge keyed on order ID, the second write updates the existing row and the totals stay correct.

Common mistake: assuming a restart is safe because the retry 'succeeded'. Retrying a non-idempotent step produces duplicates that look like valid data, so nothing fails loudly. Messages that fail every time, often called poison messages, should be routed to a dead-letter destination after a set number of attempts, so they stop blocking the rest of the stream.

Consequence: in a running system, an unbounded retry loop on one poison message can stall a whole pipeline while backlog and cost grow. Bounded retries, dead-letter handling, and idempotent writes together keep a restart from corrupting totals or halting the line.

questions.prompt: A telemetry consumer reads a batch of 500 sensor readings for van 17 and writes them into a daily-mileage table. The consumer's writes are not yet protected against repeats. Step 1: the batch is written and 500 rows are added. Step 2: the worker crashes before it confirms the batch to the broker. Step 3: the broker, seeing no confirmation, redelivers the same batch after its timeout. Step 4 is missing: the table's write rule must be changed so that a repeated batch overwrites the existing rows for the same vehicle and timestamp instead of adding new ones. Which change completes the trace?
choices: Cap the consumer at three retries and then discard the batch
Move the table to a larger storage tier so the duplicate rows fit
Keep the plain append and lower the broker's redelivery timeout so repeats arrive sooner
Switch to a merge keyed on the vehicle ID plus reading timestamp, so a second write updates the same rows
questions.why: A merge keyed on vehicle ID and timestamp is an idempotent write, so applying the same batch twice leaves the same final rows, which is the property the trace needs.

questions.prompt: In restart management, what does a checkpoint record?
choices: The list of consumers that are currently connected to a queue
The number of times a message has been redelivered
How far processing has safely got, so a restarted job can resume from there
The total cost of the last run in currency units
questions.why: A checkpoint is a saved record of safe progress, letting a restart resume rather than redo everything; the other choices describe different metrics or components.

questions.prompt: A nightly job processes 40 numbered stages and saves a checkpoint after each stage it completes. It fails while running stage 31. Roughly how many stages must be redone on restart?
choices: Only stage 31, because checkpoints are saved before a stage begins
Zero, because the failure happened after a checkpoint and the queue replays it
All 40 stages, because a checkpoint cannot be used for partial runs
About 1 stage, because checkpoints save the work in progress for stage 31
questions.why: Stages 1 to 30 are checkpointed as complete, so the restart resumes at stage 31, which is the only stage whose progress was not safely recorded; the other choices misread how checkpoints limit redone work.

questions.prompt: A stream consumer retries one malformed message every second with no attempt limit. Other messages behind it are waiting. Which rule best keeps the rest of the stream moving and bounds cost?
choices: Acknowledge every message before processing it, so no message can ever be retried
Add more consumer instances so the malformed message is spread across them
Set a maximum attempt count and route the message to a dead-letter destination after it is reached
Increase the retry interval to ten minutes so the malformed message fails less often
questions.why: A poison message that fails every time should be parked in a dead-letter destination after a bounded number of attempts, which stops it blocking the stream; the other options either keep the retry loop or skip processing guarantees.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a pipeline that guarantees no lost messages still needs its writes to be idempotent. Name one limit or tradeoff of your design, such as cost, latency, or how far back a restart can safely replay.
lessons.modelAnswer: Guaranteeing no lost messages usually means at-least-once delivery: if the consumer does not confirm a message in time, the queue sends it again. The guarantee is that the message is never dropped, but the same message can arrive twice, for instance when a worker crashes after writing and before confirming. If the write is a plain insert, the second copy creates a duplicate row and totals drift without any error. Making the write idempotent, such as a merge keyed on a unique order ID, means the second copy changes nothing. The tradeoff is cost and complexity: a merge is slower than a blind append, and the key must be truly unique and stable, so we need a decision for rows that arrive without one. Checkpoints also limit how far back a restart replays, but replaying older work still depends on the write being idempotent.
rubricPoints: Lossless delivery usually means at-least-once, which allows duplicates.
A crash between the write and the acknowledgement is the case that causes redelivery.
An idempotent write keyed on a unique identifier makes a repeat harmless.
A real tradeoff is named, such as merge cost, key design, or replay window.

suggested.rationale: That mission has you build retries with backoff and idempotency keys, which is the core reasoning this objective tests.

lessons.plain: Running a data job in more than one place means the work, and the data it touches, live in separate physical locations. A zone is one isolated data centre inside a region, and a region is a group of zones in one geographic area. If one place has an outage, another can keep going. The trade-offs are that copying data between places costs money and adds delay, and some rules require data to stay inside one country. Deciding where each piece runs affects reliability, cost and compliance all at once.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a nightly pipeline runs in one data centre and that data centre loses power in the middle of the run, what happens to the pipeline and to the data it was writing, and what would you need in place so it can finish somewhere else without someone copying files by hand?
lessons.teach:
A zone is a single isolated data centre. A region is a geographic area that contains several zones. A multi-region is a larger grouping of regions, such as a whole continent, offered for some storage services. A regional resource lives in one region, and a zonal resource lives in one zone. Cross-region transfer means moving bytes from one region to another. Cloud providers usually charge for it, and it is slower than moving data inside a region. Failover means switching work or traffic to a healthy location when the first one fails. A replica is a copy kept in another place so that failover has data to work with. Data residency is a rule that data must stay in certain places.

Worked example: a nightly job reads 500 GB from a storage bucket in europe-west1, processes it with compute in europe-west1, and writes results to a warehouse dataset in europe-west1. Step one, the job starts in the same region as its data. Step two, the reads stay inside that region. Step three, the writes stay there too. Nothing crosses a region boundary, so transfer charges stay near zero and the run is fast. Now suppose a team moves the compute to us-central1 but leaves the data in europe-west1. Every run now pulls 500 GB across the ocean. The bill rises and the job slows down.

Common mistake: assuming a multi-region storage location also makes the compute multi-region. The data can survive an outage while the job that reads it still sits in one failed place. Consequence: when a region fails, a job pinned to it stops and must be restarted in a healthy region, so it needs checkpoints or idempotent steps to resume without duplicating output. Keep compute and data in the same region unless a reliability target clearly justifies the transfer cost.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm keeps 800 GB of shipment logs in a regional storage bucket in southamerica-east1. Its nightly aggregation job runs on compute in southamerica-east1. Step 1: the job starts in the same region as its logs. Step 2: the reads stay inside that region, so nothing crosses a boundary on input. Step 3: the job writes a 2 GB summary table to a warehouse dataset in us-east1 for a reporting team. Step 4 is missing. The team asks what happens to those 2 GB on the way out. Which statement correctly completes step 4?
choices: The bucket's regional setting automatically moves the write into the same region as the reporting team.
Nothing is charged, because writes to a warehouse are free in every region.
Because only 2 GB moves, the transfer falls under a free allowance and runs at normal speed.
The 2 GB is a cross-region transfer, so it is billed and slower than an in-region write, even though the amount is small.
questions.why: Writing from a job in one region to a dataset in another region is a cross-region transfer, which providers usually charge for and which is slower, regardless of how small the amount is.

questions.prompt: A team's feature table is a zonal resource located in zone us-west1-b. Which statement about it is true?
choices: It is automatically copied to every zone in the region, so a single zone failure never affects it.
It lives across the whole multi-region that contains us-west1, so its location is wider than one region.
It can be read from any continent at no extra cost because zonal resources are global.
It lives in one zone, so if that zone fails the table is unavailable until it is recovered or restored elsewhere.
questions.why: A zonal resource lives in exactly one zone, so the failure of that zone affects it directly unless a copy exists elsewhere.

questions.prompt: A streaming job runs on compute in region A. Its input data sits in a multi-region storage location that spans region A and region B. Region A suffers an outage. Which outcome is most likely?
choices: The job keeps running in region A because the data copy in region B keeps it alive.
The job stops in region A, the data may still be readable from region B, and the job must be restarted in a healthy region.
The job moves to region B automatically with no action, since multi-region storage always fails over compute.
The data becomes unreadable everywhere, because multi-region storage depends on the compute location.
questions.why: Multi-region storage can keep the data available, but compute pinned to the failed region stops and needs to be restarted elsewhere, ideally with checkpoints to avoid duplicate output.

questions.prompt: A healthcare company must keep patient records in Germany by a data residency rule. It also wants failover protection and low transfer costs. Which design best satisfies all three?
choices: Process records in Germany but store backups in a multi-region that spans several continents.
Keep the bucket in Germany, run the job in the cheapest region available, and replicate to a US region for safety.
Keep the records bucket and the processing job in a German region, and keep any replicas in German regions.
Store records in Germany and move the processing job to the region with the lowest compute price each night.
questions.why: Keeping data, compute and replicas inside German regions meets the residency rule, avoids cross-region transfer charges, and still provides a copy for failover.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a batch pipeline should run in one region or be spread across several, and name one limit or tradeoff you would knowingly accept.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start from the targets. If the pipeline must survive a whole-region outage, I need the data replicated somewhere else and a way to restart the job in that second region. If the main constraint is cost and speed, I keep compute and data in one region, because reading data across regions adds transfer charges and latency on every run. Spreading work across regions also means I must check residency rules before moving any personal data. The tradeoff I would accept is a short recovery window: after a failover the job restarts from its last checkpoint, so some work is redone and the outputs must be safe to write twice. I would document that gap so the business can see what a regional outage actually costs them.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes zones, regions and multi-regions and what a regional resource depends on
Explains that cross-region data movement adds cost and latency
Connects reliability targets to replicas and failover
Names a concrete tradeoff such as recovery time, redone work or residency limits

suggested.rationale: The disaster-recovery planner would let the learner choose regions for compute and data and see the failover and transfer-cost tradeoffs directly.

lessons.plain: Data corruption means data is still there but wrong: a value got mangled, a file was half written, or a bad job overwrote good rows. Missing data means rows or files that should exist are simply absent, perhaps because a feed was down or a pipeline quietly dropped records. Preparing for these problems means deciding ahead of time how you will notice them, how you will get the data back, and how far back you can go. It is like keeping spare copies of a ledger and a checklist that confirms every page arrived, so a mistake is caught early and can be undone instead of discovered months later in a report.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job accidentally overwrites yesterday's sales table with an empty result. Before reading anything, what two things would you have wanted in place so that you could still produce tomorrow's report correctly?
lessons.teach:
Data corruption is data that exists but is wrong. Missing data is data that should exist but does not. Both are normal risks in a pipeline, and preparing for them means three things: detecting the problem, keeping a way to recover, and being able to rebuild from an original source. A validation check is an automated test that compares data against an expectation, such as matching row counts against the source file, or checking that no key fields are empty. A point-in-time restore brings a table back to how it looked at an earlier moment, if the storage keeps that history for a set window. Replay means reprocessing the original raw input, which only works if that input was kept. A dead-letter location holds records that failed processing so they are kept for review rather than silently dropped.

Worked example. An hourly job loads a warehouse table from raw files kept in cloud object storage for 30 days. Step 1: the job reads a file with 10,000 rows but writes only 6,000 before failing. Step 2: a validation check compares the loaded count with the file count, sees the gap, raises an alert, and blocks the table from being published. Step 3: the team restores the table to its state from 40 minutes earlier using the warehouse's time-travel window. Step 4: they reload that hour from the raw file, and the check passes.

Common mistake: treating the warehouse table as the only copy. If a transform overwrites it and the raw input was never kept, the original data is gone. Another mistake is assuming a backup exists without ever testing a restore.

Consequence: until someone notices, dashboards and models built on the bad table show wrong figures. The time between damage and detection determines how much must be rebuilt.

Preparation means guarding the raw source, checking every load, and rehearsing recovery before you need it.

questions.prompt: A nightly job loads a fare table for a ride-share company from raw JSON files that are kept in object storage for 14 days. Step 1: the job reads a file of 4,200 trip records and writes 4,200 rows, but 180 of those rows have an empty driver_id, because an upstream field was renamed and the mapping now points at nothing. Step 2: a key-field validation check finds the empty driver_id values, fails the load, and keeps the table out of reports. Step 3: the team corrects the field mapping in the job. Step 4: ? Which completes the recovery?
choices: Delete the fare table and wait for the next nightly run to recreate it from scratch
Publish the table now, since the row count of 4,200 matches the file
Replay the raw file for that night through the corrected job, then rerun the validation check until it passes before publishing
Restore the table to its state from six months ago and skip reloading the night
questions.why: Replay reprocesses the kept raw input through the fixed logic, and the validation check must pass before the table is published, so option B covers both rebuilding and verification.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a dead-letter location in a data pipeline?
choices: A log of how long each job step took, used to tune performance
A timed window in which the warehouse keeps earlier versions of a table
A place where records that failed processing are kept for review instead of being silently dropped
A backup copy of the final warehouse table, kept for disaster recovery
questions.why: A dead-letter location holds failed records so someone can examine them later rather than losing them without trace.

questions.prompt: A team keeps nightly snapshots of its reporting database and assumes they are safe. During an incident, they try to restore from a snapshot and discover it cannot be read. Which practice would have prevented being caught out?
choices: Rehearsing a restore from the snapshots on a regular schedule, before any real incident
Turning off validation checks so the snapshots are not rejected
Switching from snapshots to a second live copy of the database in the same zone
Increasing the number of snapshots kept, without ever opening one
questions.why: A backup that has never been restored in a test is unproven, so regular restore rehearsals reveal problems while there is still time to fix them.

questions.prompt: A streaming ingestion pipeline keeps its raw input for 7 days. On day 9, the team discovers that a transform corrupted a table on day 2. Which recovery option is no longer dependable, and why?
choices: A validation check on the table, because checks can run at any time against current data
A point-in-time restore of the table, because the warehouse always keeps history forever
Replaying day 2 from raw input, because that raw input was discarded before the damage was found
Publishing the table with a note, because the dashboards only show recent figures
questions.why: Replay only works while the original raw input still exists, and here the day 2 input was kept for only 7 days, so it is gone by day 9.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would protect a daily analytics table against both corrupted data and missing data. Name one limit of your approach, such as the recovery window or the cost of keeping raw copies.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would protect the table in three layers. First, I keep the raw source files in storage for longer than the warehouse's recovery window, so the data can always be reloaded. Second, each load runs validation checks: the row count must match the source, key columns must not be empty, and totals must match the source control figure. If a check fails, the table is not published and an alert fires. Third, I rely on the warehouse's point-in-time restore to roll back a bad write quickly, and I rebuild the affected period by replaying the raw files. The main limit is the window. Time-travel history only goes back a fixed number of days, and raw copies cost storage. If corruption is found after the raw files have expired, the data is lost for good, so retention periods have to be set against how long problems can take to notice.
rubricPoints: Keeps an original raw source that can be replayed to rebuild derived data.
Uses automated validation checks such as row counts and null checks, with publishing blocked on failure.
Uses point-in-time restore for fast rollback, within a limited window.
Names a real limit, such as retention windows or storage cost, and ties retention to detection time.

suggested.rationale: A disaster-recovery planner would let the learner set recovery points, retention windows, and replay steps for a data set, which is the core of this objective.

lessons.plain: Replication means keeping extra copies of a database or cache running on other machines, so that if one machine fails, another can take over. Failover is the moment the system switches traffic from the failed copy to a healthy one. Designing this means deciding how much recent data you can afford to lose if that happens, and how long the service can be down while switching. Cloud SQL is Google's managed relational database service, and Redis is an in-memory store often used as a cache. Each offers different copy and switchover options, and the right choice depends on those two limits.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose an application writes a row to a database, and the copy that takes over after a crash was updated a moment later. What might be missing after the switch, and what do you think decides how much is missing?
lessons.teach:
A primary is the copy that accepts writes. A standby or replica is a second copy that receives the primary's changes. Synchronous replication means the primary confirms a write only after the standby has recorded it too. Asynchronous replication means the primary confirms first and sends the change to the copy afterward, so the copy can trail behind. Two numbers frame every design. The recovery point objective, or RPO, is how much recent data you can afford to lose, measured as time. The recovery time objective, or RTO, is how long the service may stay down before it is usable again. Synchronous copies aim for a near-zero RPO but add write latency. Asynchronous copies are faster on writes but may lose the last moments of data.

Cloud SQL offers a high-availability configuration: a standby in a different zone of the same region, kept in synchronous step, with automatic failover that keeps the same connection address. Its read replicas are asynchronous, can sit in other regions, and are promoted only when someone decides to promote them. Memorystore for Redis, the managed in-memory store, has a Standard tier with a replica that copies asynchronously, so a fast failover can drop the newest keys. Redis Cluster splits keys into shards, each with its own replica, so one failed shard affects only its slice of keys.

Worked example: a Cloud SQL high-availability instance has its primary in zone A and its standby in zone B. Step one: the application commits an order row. Step two: the primary writes it, sends it to the standby, and waits for confirmation before reporting success. Step three: zone A fails. Step four: the standby is promoted, the connection address points to it, and the application reconnects. Because the order was confirmed only after both copies held it, no acknowledged write was lost, so the RPO is near zero. The RTO is the minutes the switch takes.

Common mistake: treating a read replica as a failover plan. It does not take over on its own, and promoting it is a deliberate step that starts from whatever lag it had. Backups are also not failover: restoring from them is far slower.

In a running system, applications holding old connections must retry after a failover, or the outage lasts longer than the switch itself. Set the RPO and RTO first, then choose the copy type that meets both.

questions.prompt: Lumen Ticketing stores seat holds in a Memorystore for Redis instance on the Standard tier, which has one replica that copies asynchronously. Here is the trace of one hold. Step 1: the app writes the key seat-hold-14C to the primary. Step 2: the primary replies OK to the app immediately. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the primary fails and the replica is promoted. Step 5: the key seat-hold-14C is absent on the new primary, so the seat looks free. Which sentence correctly fills step 3?
choices: The replica is promoted automatically with the same connection address before the primary fails.
The app retries the write against the replica because the replica rejects writes.
The primary sends the key to the replica afterward, so the replica may not hold it yet when the primary fails.
The replica must confirm the key to the primary before the primary replies OK to the app.
questions.why: Asynchronous replication means the primary confirms the write before the copy receives it, so the change can still be in transit when the primary fails.

questions.prompt: A payments team says its ledger database may lose at most 30 seconds of committed data during a failure. Which term describes that tolerance?
choices: Recovery time objective, meaning how long the service may be down
Synchronous write latency, meaning the extra delay each commit adds
Recovery point objective, meaning how much recent data may be lost, measured as time
Read replica promotion time, meaning how long a replica takes to become writable
questions.why: The recovery point objective (RPO) is defined in the teaching text as the amount of recent data you can afford to lose, measured as time.

questions.prompt: A gaming company runs Redis Cluster with six shards, each with its own replica. One shard fails. Which outcome matches how Redis Cluster is described?
choices: Every key in the cluster is lost, because keys are spread evenly across all shards.
The newest keys across the whole cluster roll back, because replicas copy asynchronously.
Every player session stops, because the cluster shares a single primary across all shards.
Only the keys in the failed shard's slice are affected, while keys on the other shards keep being served.
questions.why: Redis Cluster splits keys into shards with their own replicas, so one failed shard affects only its own slice of keys.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's Cloud SQL primary in one region fails. The team plans to point the application at a read replica in another region, which is currently about 40 seconds behind. What is the main problem with this plan?
choices: The only valid option is a backup restore, and the replica is useless for any kind of failover.
Promotion is a deliberate step that starts from the replica's existing lag, so recent writes may be missing when it takes over.
The replica takes over automatically with the same connection address, so no operator action is needed at all.
Replicas cannot be promoted, so the team has no writable copy anywhere in the second region.
questions.why: The teaching text says read replicas are asynchronous, are promoted only by a deliberate decision, and start from whatever lag they had, so recent writes can be missing.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between a synchronous standby and an asynchronous read replica for a Cloud SQL database. Name the limit or tradeoff each option carries.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from the two targets. If the business cannot accept losing any confirmed write, I need a synchronous standby, such as Cloud SQL's high-availability configuration, which gives automatic failover and a near-zero RPO. The cost is that every write waits for the standby to confirm, so write latency rises, and the standby sits in the same region, so it does not protect against losing the whole region. If some lost recent data is acceptable, an asynchronous read replica can sit in another region and be promoted for disaster recovery. Its limits are that writes are confirmed before the copy catches up, so the last moments can be lost, and promotion is a manual step that adds to the RTO. I would test both by timing a real failover and checking how much data was missing.
rubricPoints: Defines RPO and RTO and uses them to drive the choice
States that synchronous standbys trade write latency for near-zero data loss
States that asynchronous replicas can lose recent writes but may span regions
Notes that promotion of a replica or failover has a time cost that affects RTO

suggested.rationale: That mission makes the learner reason about asynchronous replica lag, which is the core tradeoff behind choosing a copy type, though it does not cover Cloud SQL or Redis specifics.

scenarios.title: Clinic data access and residency review
scenarios.scenario:
Harbor Lane Clinics is a fictional telehealth company that stores patient visit records in a cloud data warehouse. A data warehouse is a managed analytics database where tables are grouped into datasets, and datasets sit inside a project, which is the basic container that holds resources, billing, and access settings. Its patient data includes personally identifiable information (PII), meaning any detail that can identify a person, such as names, email addresses, and dates of birth. Records for European patients must stay stored and processed inside the European Union. You are the new data engineer asked to review the design before a compliance audit next month. The team wants analysts to count visits and study outcomes without seeing raw contact details. The security team wants the encryption keys for European data controlled by Harbor Lane itself, not only by the cloud provider. The company also runs a development project and a production project, and development must not be able to read live patient data. Answer the following:
1. Name the control that hides the patient_email column from analysts who can otherwise query the visits table, and explain where in the architecture it must be attached.
2. Choose the encryption option that lets Harbor Lane control and revoke the keys for European data, and state where that key must be located.
3. Describe the organization policy and project layout that keep European datasets in an EU location and stop development users from reading production patient data.
subParts: Customer-managed encryption key choice and location
modelAnswer: Use column-level security through policy tags. A policy tag is a label attached to a column, and labels are grouped into a taxonomy, which is a named set of labels. Access is granted through IAM (identity and access management, the system that decides which people and services may perform which actions on which resources). Analysts keep read access to the table so they can count visits, but they are not granted the reader role on the tag that marks patient_email, so that one column comes back as denied while the other columns stay visible. The tag must be attached to the column in the schema of the production table, because that is where the data lives. Common mistake: giving analysts owner rights at dataset level, which overrides the column restriction. Consequence: an audit finds PII visible to staff who have no need for it.

Use customer-managed encryption keys, often called CMEK. These are keys that Harbor Lane creates and manages in the cloud key management service, instead of relying only on keys the provider manages. Encryption at rest means the stored data is scrambled so it cannot be read without the key. The key should be created in the same EU location as the European datasets. A key and its data in different locations can break the residency requirement and can make the data unreadable if the key is unavailable. Revoking the key's permission cuts off access to the data, which is the control the security team wants. Common mistake: creating a multi-region or global key for EU data. Consequence: if the key is disabled during an incident, EU data cannot be decrypted until the key is restored.

Set an organization policy, which is a rule applied at the top of the cloud hierarchy and inherited by everything below it, using the resource location constraint so that new datasets can only be created in approved EU locations. Apply it at the organization or folder level so no project can override it. Split the company into separate development and production projects. Give development users access only to their own project, plus anonymised or synthetic copies of data if they need realistic test data, never direct access to production tables. Pipelines should use separate service accounts, which are non-human identities, for each environment, with IAM roles granted at project level. Common mistake: letting developers work in the production project because it is convenient. Consequence: a development query can read live patient records, which breaks the separation requirement and can create datasets in a location that violates residency rules.

scenarios.title: Cold-chain sensor data at a fictional grocery distributor
scenarios.scenario: Harbor Fresh Logistics is a made-up grocery distributor that runs about 300 refrigerated trucks. Each truck has a temperature sensor that sends a reading every 30 seconds. Dispatchers need to see a truck that is running warm within two minutes, so the readings must be processed close to real time. Separately, 40 partner depots upload one file each night containing the day's delivery records, and finance needs those records in a data warehouse by 6 a.m. Keep in mind that a streaming pipeline is one that processes each event as it arrives, while a batch pipeline processes a bounded collection of data at scheduled times. A data warehouse is a database built for large analytical queries, and BigQuery is Google Cloud's serverless warehouse, meaning you do not manage any servers for it. Pub/Sub is Google Cloud's managed messaging service: producers publish messages to a topic, and subscribers read them later, which decouples the sender from the processing. Dataflow is a managed service that runs Apache Beam pipelines, where Beam is an open programming model for describing both batch and streaming transformations. Windowing means grouping an unbounded stream into finite time slices, such as five-minute buckets, so that averages and counts can be computed. Late-arriving data is an event whose timestamp is earlier than the current window but which reaches the pipeline after that window has been considered finished. Cloud Composer is a managed version of the Apache Airflow scheduler, used to run dependent jobs in a set order. Harbor Fresh's architect asks you to design the ingestion for both sources. Answer each numbered sub-task: 1. For the truck sensor readings, name the ingestion path and the processing service you would choose, state whether the transformation is batch or streaming, and explain how you would handle readings that arrive minutes late from trucks in tunnels with poor signal. 2. For the nightly depot files, name the processing approach and the service you would choose, state whether it is batch or streaming, and explain how you would schedule the job and make sure it only starts after all 40 files have landed. 3. For both sources, define the sink (where the cleaned data ends up) and describe one cleansing step you would apply before loading, such as rejecting records with impossible temperatures or missing truck identifiers.
subParts: Sensor readings: ingestion path, processing service, batch or streaming, late-data handling
Nightly depot files: processing approach, service, batch or streaming, scheduling and dependency check
Sinks and cleansing: destination for each source and one cleansing rule before load
modelAnswer: Sensor readings are a continuous stream, so the transformation is streaming. The sensors publish each reading to a Pub/Sub topic, which holds the messages durably until a consumer reads them, so a short spike in volume does not drop data. A Dataflow job built with Apache Beam subscribes to that topic and groups readings into fixed windows, for example one-minute windows, to compute average and maximum temperature per truck. For late-arriving data, the Beam pipeline uses event time (the time the sensor recorded the reading) rather than arrival time, and it sets an allowed lateness value, such as ten minutes, so that readings from a truck that was in a tunnel are still counted into the correct window if they arrive within that allowance. Readings that arrive even later can be routed to a separate dead-letter output for review, so the dashboard result does not change unexpectedly after it was shown.

The depot files are bounded, meaning they have a clear start and end, so the transformation is batch. A Dataflow batch job, or a Dataproc Spark job if the team already has Spark code, reads all the files from a Cloud Storage bucket, applies the same parsing and validation, and writes the result. Scheduling belongs in an orchestrator. Cloud Composer can run a DAG (a directed acyclic graph, meaning a set of tasks with a fixed order and no loops) that first checks that all 40 expected files exist, then starts the batch job, and only then runs the load step. A sensor task in the DAG waits for the 40th file, and a timeout alerts the on-call engineer if one depot is missing. A common mistake is to schedule the job at a fixed clock time, which can process a partial set of files and silently undercount deliveries.

The sensor results go to a BigQuery table partitioned by reading date, so dispatchers' dashboard queries and the trend history stay fast and cheap to scan. The depot records also go to BigQuery, in a separate table with a load date column so finance can reconcile each night's batch. A useful cleansing rule for the sensor stream is to drop or quarantine readings with temperatures outside a physically possible range, or with a missing truck identifier, and count how many were rejected. For the depot records, reject rows where the delivery quantity is negative or the depot code is not in the reference list, and write them to an error table instead of discarding them, so the rejects can be explained to the depots.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Parcels: choosing where shipment data lives
scenarios.scenario: Brightwater Parcels is a fictional regional parcel delivery company. Its vans send a GPS and scan event roughly every 10 seconds, about 40 million events per day. Customer support agents need to pull the latest status for any single parcel within a second, using the parcel ID as the lookup key. Separately, the operations analytics team builds daily dashboards on delivery times by depot and by week, and the data team keeps the raw event files as a long-term archive that must be cheap to hold. Brightwater's engineering lead asks you to work through three decisions for the new platform. 1. Choose the Google Cloud storage service for the per-parcel status lookups, and explain in plain terms why a close alternative (such as Spanner or Firestore) is a weaker fit for this access pattern. 2. Decide how the analytics warehouse should be modelled, including how far to normalize the tables, and name the Google Cloud warehouse product you would use. 3. Propose a lifecycle and cost plan for the raw event archive, and say how a data lake governance tool would help the team find and control that data.
subParts: Storage choice for per-parcel lookups and why a near-miss fails
Warehouse product and data model, including normalization level
Archive lifecycle, cost control, and lake governance
modelAnswer: Choose Bigtable, Google Cloud's managed wide-column NoSQL store, which is a database that holds very large numbers of rows, each addressed by a single row key, and is built for high write throughput and fast reads by that key. Parcel status lookups are single-key reads at high volume, and the event stream is append-heavy, which matches Bigtable well if the row key is designed so that one parcel's recent events sit together (for example, a parcel ID plus a reversed timestamp so the newest event is read first). Spanner is a globally consistent relational database and is strong when you need multi-row transactions and SQL across regions; Brightwater does not need that, so paying for it would add cost without solving the stated problem. Firestore is a document database suited to app-style records with modest write volume per document; at roughly 400 events per second sustained across many parcels, its per-document and per-database limits make it a poorer fit than Bigtable for an event stream. A common mistake is choosing a row key that is the current timestamp alone, which sends all writes to one spot and creates a hotspot that slows the whole table. Consequence for the running system: a hotspotted key would make support lookups slow during peak hours, exactly when agents need them most.

Use BigQuery, Google Cloud's serverless analytical warehouse, which runs large SQL queries over columns of data without you managing servers. For this team, a star schema is the right model: one fact table of delivery events (one row per scan or GPS event, with foreign keys to parcel, depot, and date) surrounded by small dimension tables for depots, parcels, vans, and calendar dates. Normalization is the process of splitting data into many related tables to avoid repeating values; a star schema deliberately denormalizes the dimensions a little so that dashboard queries need fewer joins. Because dashboards filter by date and depot, partition the fact table by event date and cluster it by depot ID, so queries read only the blocks they need. Mistake to avoid: copying the full raw event payload into the fact table, which inflates storage and query scan costs for no dashboard benefit. Consequence: unpartitioned scans would make the daily dashboards slower and more expensive as history grows.

Keep the raw event files in Cloud Storage, Google Cloud's object store for files of any size, organized in a bucket with folders by date. Set an object lifecycle rule that moves files older than 90 days to a colder storage class (a cheaper class meant for rarely read data, with higher retrieval cost) and deletes or archives them after the agreed retention period, which the legal team must confirm. Lifecycle rules are automatic actions based on object age, so they need no manual cleanup. Mistake to avoid: applying a cold class to files the analytics team still reads weekly, because retrieval fees can exceed the storage saving. For governance, Dataplex is Google Cloud's service for organizing data across lakes and zones, and its catalog (Dataplex Catalog) records what datasets exist, who owns them, and what they contain. Use a discovery scan so that new files and tables are registered automatically, assign each zone an owner, and set access policies per zone, so the depot team sees only its own zone while the archive stays locked to the data team. Consequence without this: uncatalogued files pile up unnoticed, and storage costs grow with no owner accountable for them.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Outdoor Co. sales dashboard and partner sharing
scenarios.scenario:
Brightwater Outdoor Co. is a fictional outdoor-gear retailer. Its analytics team stores every online order in a BigQuery table named orders.
